title: [RFC]: Release all releasable GPU memory in sleep mode (tracking)
body:
> **Update (tracking).** This issue started as a report about WorkspaceManager memory (original report below, by @penguin-wwy). Investigation showed that the workspace is one of several allocations that sleep mode leaves on the GPU. This issue now tracks all of them.

### Summary

Colocated RL setups call `/sleep` to hand GPU memory back to the trainer. With only `weights` and `kv_cache` under sleep-mode management, a sleeping DeepSeek-V4 engine still holds **14–21 GiB per GPU**. We attributed that memory to its owners on 4× GB300. The PRs below make the releasable parts releasable. With all of them applied, what remains is 5.6–6.2 GiB per GPU on DeepSeek-V4 (3.9–4.7 GiB with the existing `--enable-nccl-comm-suspend` plus #59360). Most of it is driver-side state: CUDA graph executables and the CUDA context.

### Current main (2026-10-04, `bdd31c31d`, with #59156/#59158/#59160 merged)

Memory per GPU while asleep (level 1), MiB, saving vs the first column in parentheses. Every run is bit-exact against the awake run (28 greedy + 28 seeded top-k/top-p probes, 3 cycles). "Open PRs" = #59228 + #59909 + #59360 + #59939 + #59625 + #59934 applied together.

| Model / setup | Main, sleep mode | Main + `--sleep-mode-offload-cudagraph` | Open PRs + `--sleep-mode-offload-cudagraph --enable-nccl-comm-suspend` | ... + #59537 + #59540 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash, TP4 + EP4, MTP | 10869 | 8633 (−2236) | **6451 (−4418, 41%)** | **6097 (−4772, 44%)** |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DP4 + EP4, DeepGEMM MoE, fp8 KV, mbt 8192 | 9953 | 8507 (−1446) | **7355 (−2598, 26%)** | **7323 (−2630, 26%)** |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DP8 + EP8 over 2 nodes (this issue's setup) | 9941 | 8495 (−1446) | **7343 (−2598, 26%)** | **7327 (−2614, 26%)** |
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, TP8 over 2 nodes, MTP off | 13653 | 6123 (−7530) | **4481 (−9172, 67%)** | **4247 (−9406, 69%)** |
| GLM-5.2-FP8, TP8 over 2 nodes, MTP | 20945 | 11655 (−9290) | **9991 (−10954, 52%)** | **9787 (−11158, 53%)** |
| Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507-FP8, TP4 + EP4 | 7617 | 7341 (−276) | **5051 (−2566, 34%)** | **4961 (−2656, 35%)** |

- #59909 frees the same graph memory as the merged backup mode, without the CPU copy (7.4 GiB/GPU less pinned host memory on V4.1).
- #59537 moves graph-capture memory to the KV cache (+0.62 GiB/GPU on V4-Flash TP4, +4.57 GiB/GPU on GLM-5.2).
- Qwen3-235B level 2 + `reload_weights`: bit-exact, same asleep memory as level 1.
- Wake takes 0.2-1.4 s longer with `--enable-nccl-comm-suspend`.
- These numbers are higher than the 09-30 tables below. On V4-Flash TP4 the 2.3 GiB gap breaks down as: +1.3 GiB of CUDA graph executable memory from this cluster's driver (the 09-30 code measures the same on this node; the 09-30 tables are from a different GB300 cluster), +0.5 GiB of MTP runner buffers that the merged #59158 no longer tags (a follow-up puts the model runner back in the `runtime` pool), and +0.5 GiB of FlashInfer TRT-LLM allreduce workspace since #56891, which #59360 releases. Host RSS stays at the asleep level after wake because PyTorch caches the pinned backup buffers.

### What stays on the GPU, and which PR releases it

| Resident while asleep | PR | How | Contents after wake |
|---|---|---|---|
| WorkspaceManager scratch (MoE / attention workspaces, scales with DP × `max_num_batched_tokens`) | #59156 | allocated in a `workspace` cuMem pool | discarded (scratch) |
| State built with the KV cache (block tables, sparse-MLA and indexer metadata) and buffers owned by the model runner (e.g. MTP speculator hidden states) | #59158 (includes the former #59162) | runner construction and KV-init state allocated in a `runtime` cuMem pool | backed up to CPU |
| CUDA graph memory pool (Model Runner V2) | #59160 | graph pools cuMem-backed under a `cudagraph` tag, remapped at the same addresses, no recapture | backed up to CPU |
| FlashInfer MNNVL allreduce workspace | #59360 | with `--enable-nccl-comm-suspend`, detached on suspend and restored at the same address on resume | restored (Lamport flags reset) |
| Documentation of the above and of what cannot be released | #59165 | docs | — |
| Worker refactor: GPU and XPU share workspace and runner init, so the PRs above touch one place | #59200 | refactor | — |
| Freeing a cuMem allocation while asleep double-unmaps (pre-existing; more frequent once graph pools are cuMem-backed) | #59228 | skip unmap for already-released handles | — |

### Savings per PR (memory per GPU while asleep, level 1)

All runs use the same nightly image with and without the PR on 4× GB300 per node. The last two columns were measured on 09-30 at #59156 `21c7a0be4c`, #59158 `0354f3d8a9`, #59160 `57d4f411ee`, #59228 `49b5f1ae43` and #59360 `0de03c0dfc`. The per-PR columns were measured at the previous heads; the latest #59156 change frees the same memory while asleep. With all PRs, the KV cache is the same size as unpatched (e.g. 202.44 GiB on V4-Flash TP4, 192.2 GiB on V4.1). Each cell shows memory while asleep and, in parentheses, the saving against unpatched. Every column except the last runs without `--enable-nccl-comm-suspend`, like its baseline.

| Model / setup | Unpatched | #59156 workspace | #59158 runtime ¹ | #59156 + #59160 graph pool ² | All PRs | All PRs + `--enable-nccl-comm-suspend` + #59360 ³ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash, TP4 + EP4, MTP | 15178 | 13857 (−1321) | 9975 (−5203) | 11515 (−3663) | **6313 (−8865, 58%)** | **4649 (−10529, 69%)** |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DP4 + EP4, DeepGEMM MoE, fp8 KV, mbt 8192 | 14528 | 12129 (−2399) | 10227 (−4301) | 10225 (−4303) | **5925 (−8603, 59%)** | **4773 (−9755, 67%)** |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DP8 + EP8 over 2 nodes, DeepGEMM MoE, fp8 KV, mbt 8192 (this issue's setup) | 16790 | 12135 (−4655) | 12489 (−4301) | 10229 (−6561) | **5929 (−10861, 65%)** | **4777 (−12013, 72%)** |
| DeepSeek-V4.1, TP8 over 2 nodes, MTP off | 21037 | 15753 (−5284) | 18583 (−2454) | 8143 (−12894) | **5693 (−15344, 73%)** | **4029 (−17008, 81%)** |
| GLM-5.3, TP8 over 2 nodes, MTP | 9449 | 9449 (0) ⁴ | 8655 (−794) | 8199 (−1250) | **7405 (−2044, 22%)** | **5741 (−3708, 39%)** |

Values are MiB. "All PRs" is #59156 + #59158 + #59160 + #59228. One or two GPUs per run carry an extra 126–128 MiB of driver memory, awake and asleep alike; the table shows the value common to the other GPUs.

1. #59158 now includes the former #59162 (runner buffers such as the MTP speculator hidden states: 512 MiB on V4-Flash, 192 MiB on GLM-5.3, nothing with MTP off). On Model Runner V1 it also moves the block tables rebuilt after CUDA-graph profiling into the `runtime` pool (V4-Flash TP4 on V1: 9187 → 7507 MiB).
2. #59160 is stacked on #59156, so this column includes #59156. It backs the graph pool up to CPU: the `cudagraph` tag is 2.29 GiB/GPU on V4-Flash, 7.43 GiB on V4.1 and 1.22 GiB on GLM-5.3. The first level-1 sleep takes up to ~1.7 s longer; wake time is unchanged.
3. `--enable-nccl-comm-suspend` releases the NCCL buffers; #59360 also releases the FlashInfer MNNVL allreduce workspace (~510 MiB/GPU on the TP configurations; DP does not use it). Each wake takes 0.3–1.0 s longer.
4. GLM-5.3's workspace is small. #59156 still reduces its level-1 host backup by 0.38 GiB per GPU.

**Accuracy.** GSM8K (1319 questions, 5-shot, temperature 0) is unchanged by every PR across awake, level-1 full wake and level-1 selective wake on all three models:

| | V4-Flash | V4.1 | GLM-5.3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unpatched → all PRs | 0.950–0.951 → 0.947–0.949 | 0.892–0.902 → 0.898–0.906 | 0.911–0.918 → 0.911–0.916 |

Per-PR tables are in each PR. On V4-Flash TP4, outputs after wake are bit-identical to before sleep: 553/553 requests across batch sizes 1–256.

**Known upstream issue, not caused by these PRs:** `reload_weights` after a level-2 sleep produces garbage for DeepSeek-V4 models with tensor parallelism > 1 on unpatched vLLM too. `layerwise.py` fails to load the V4 attention, rotary and n-gram modules. With pure DP (DP4 / DP8, TP1 per engine) level 2 + reload works; for example, GSM8K on DP8 is 0.965.

### Validation beyond memory

All of these are on 4× GB300 per node, with the same nightly image with and without the PRs. Every issue found also occurs on unpatched vLLM.

- **Bit-exactness:**
  - DeepSeek-V4-Flash TP4: 553 deterministic requests (batch sizes 1–256) are identical to the awake run after every level-1 full wake and selective wake (weights-first and kv_cache-first).
  - Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B NVFP4, Qwen3-VL-8B (images), Kimi-Linear-48B (MLA + KDA) and Qwen3-235B-A22B FP8: also identical after level 2 + `reload_weights`.
- **Lifecycle:**
  - V4-Flash TP4, 300 consecutive cycles (alternating full and selective wake), all PRs with and without `--enable-nccl-comm-suspend` + #59360: every cycle bit-exact (34,140/34,140 requests), memory after wake equal to before sleep on every GPU (0 MiB), and a device-memory slope of 0.000 MiB/cycle.
  - Host RSS: about +5 MB/cycle of warm-up over the first ~50 cycles in every launch, patched or not. After that, slopes over 300 cycles are −1.8 to +3.6 MB/cycle patched (4 launches) and −0.5 to +0.6 unpatched (3 launches). The sign changes between launches of the same configuration, and one unpatched launch also rises steadily. All of the growth is process heap; the shared-memory backup is byte-for-byte constant.
  - Host RAM cost: the level-1 backup now also covers the `runtime`, `workspace` and `cudagraph` pools, about 8.1 GiB more host memory per GPU on V4-Flash TP4 (33 GiB per 4-GPU node). It is constant from the first sleep on, but host RAM has to be sized for it.
  - V4-Flash DP4, 100 cycles with level 2 + `reload_weights` every 10th: the first reload adds 2548 MiB/GPU outside the cuMem pools, identically on unpatched vLLM; flat afterwards.
  - Sleep before the first request.
  - Requests sent while asleep, or after a weights-only wake, are queued and complete after the full wake.
  - A double sleep or double wake is a no-op.
  - Level 1 followed by level 2 without a wake is ignored.
  - 256 concurrent requests right after wake: no errors, no NaN.
- **Configurations:**
  - Model Runner V1; `--enforce-eager`; chunked prefill; `--max-num-seqs 8`; MTP on and off.
  - PP2 × TP2, TP2 × DP2, DP4, DP8 over 2 nodes.
  - A KV connector (the `runtime` pool is skipped, as intended).
  - Custom allreduce forced (Qwen3-8B TP4) with #59160.
- **RL-style soak:** 100 iterations each on Qwen3-235B-A22B FP8 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, all PRs applied.
  - Each iteration runs a rollout of 64–256 concurrent requests, then a level-1 sleep. On about a third to a half of the iterations, another process fills ~270 GiB/GPU of the freed VRAM during the sleep.
  - Wakes alternate full and selective; every 25th iteration on Qwen3-235B is level 2 + `reload_weights`.
  - Probes stay bit-exact, with no drift in GPU memory, host RSS or latency. 16,345/16,345 requests succeeded.
- **Serving performance while awake:** unchanged (V4-Flash TP4, `vllm bench serve`, concurrency 1–256).
  - Throughput and TTFT/TPOT match unpatched within noise, on a fresh server and after sleep/wake.
  - Throughput varies by up to ~45% between launches of the same code, because the FlashInfer MoE autotuner picks different tactics on each launch. Comparisons need several launches per arm.
- **Sleep/wake latency:**
  - Wake is unchanged (V4-Flash TP4 and V4.1 ~0.95 s, GLM-5.3 ~1.45 s).
  - The first level-1 sleep can take up to ~1.7 s longer on V4.1, because #59160 backs up the 7.4 GiB/GPU graph pool; later sleeps take ~1.2–1.4 s.
  - `--enable-nccl-comm-suspend` with #59360 adds 0.3–1.0 s per wake.
- **Review:** three rounds of adversarial review (two external code-review models plus a manual pass) across all PRs. Confirmed findings were fixed: the #59156 pool-lifetime rework, the #59158 V1 block-table placement, the #59360 restore-retry flag, and the #59228 test.
- **AMD (ROCm):** see the MI355X results below.

### What remains after all PRs

Memory per GPU while asleep (level 1), attributed with a driver-API hook plus torch allocator history. The unexplained remainder is ≤ 17 MiB in every configuration. Local memory is 480 MiB everywhere: NCCL kernels raise the per-thread stack to 1616 B, × 152 SMs × 2048 threads. TP8 adds a 384 MiB NVLS buffer on its first NCCL all-reduce, which is why V4.1 and GLM show 1644 MiB of NCCL.

| Item (MiB) | V4-Flash TP4 | V4-Flash DP4 | V4-Flash DP8 (2 nodes) | V4.1 TP8 (2 nodes) | GLM-5.3 TP8 (2 nodes) | Releasable? |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| **Total asleep** | **6311** | **5923** | **5927** | **5693** | **7406** | |
| CUDA graph executables + capture-charged driver memory | 2536 | 2668 | 2668 | 1762 | 3102 | No ¹ |
| NCCL cuMem buffers | 1260 | 1260 | 1260 | 1644 | 1644 | Yes, `--enable-nccl-comm-suspend` ² |
| FlashInfer MNNVL allreduce workspace | 512 | — | — | 512 | 512 | Yes, #59360 with `--enable-nccl-comm-suspend` |
| torch SymmetricMemory | 132 | — | — | 164 | 164 | Needs suspend/resume support in torch SymmetricMemory |
| CUDA context + local memory + kernel modules | 1166 | 1162 | 1162 | 1160 | 1162 | No |
| cuBLAS, custom allreduce | ~96 | ~68 | ~68 | ~92 | ~88 | Partly, #59537 ³ |
| torch tensors outside any tag (router gate, sampler, GEMM outputs, …) | 281 | 281 | 281 | 202 | 206 | Partly, #59540 and #59537 ³ |
| FlashInfer sparse-MLA workspace (lazily allocated, untagged) | — | — | — | — | 394 | Yes, #59535 |
| Allocator fragmentation | 321 | ~480 | 483 | 151 | 122 | Mostly, once the untagged tensors above move to a tag |

1. **Graph executables:**
   - Destroying all graphs while asleep returns 0 MiB: the driver keeps graph-exec memory. Releasing it needs recapture on wake or a CUDA checkpoint (#56373).
   - The size scales with graph count. Breakable PIECEWISE capture creates about one graph per layer per batch size: GLM-5.3 (78 layers) has 6557 PIECEWISE graphs, against about 3.7–3.8k on V4 (40–43 layers).
2. **NCCL buffers:** with the existing flag plus #59360, all PRs reach:
   - **4029** MiB on V4.1 (−81% vs unpatched);
   - **4649** MiB on V4-Flash TP4 (−69%);
   - **4773** MiB on DP4 (−67%);
   - **4777** MiB on DP8 (−72%);
   - **5741** MiB on GLM-5.3 (−39%).

   Each wake takes 0.3–1.0 s longer. GSM8K was checked unchanged with the flag before #59360; with #59360, outputs after wake are bit-identical on V4-Flash TP4 (553/553).
3. **Untagged tensors:** most of them are scratch that belongs in `WorkspaceManager`, so they are released by #59156 once moved. Several "GEMM output" items are PyTorch's 32 MiB cuBLAS workspace, one per stream, kept for the process lifetime.
   - #59535 moves the FlashInfer MLA decode workspaces into `WorkspaceManager`: −394 MiB/GPU asleep on GLM-5.3, bit-exact after wake.
   - #59540 takes the top-k/top-p sampler scratch from `WorkspaceManager`: about −75 MiB/GPU on V4-Flash.
   - #59537 reuses one stream for every `graph_capture()` call instead of creating one per call: about −64 MiB/GPU on V4-Flash, bit-exact over 22 cycles.
   - Priming the remaining cuBLAS workspaces inside the `workspace` pool was prototyped. Discard and remap stay bit-exact, but destroying the profiling graphs frees the capture stream's workspace, so the real capture allocates a new untagged one. Not proposed yet.

### AMD MI355X (ROCm)

vLLM ROCm nightly image (`e975732152`, torch 2.12, RCCL 2.30.4) with each PR's diff applied, level-1 sleep. Memory per GPU while asleep, MiB (saving vs unpatched):

| Model / setup | Unpatched | #59156 | #59156 + #59158 | #59156 + #59160 (ROCm patch ¹) | All three | Graph memory ² |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| DeepSeek-V2-Lite TP1 | 5677 | −930 | −1034 | −1094 | −1198 | 948 |
| DeepSeek-V2-Lite TP2 | 7946 | −770 | −880 | −908 | −999 | 1044 |
| DeepSeek-V2-Lite DP2 | 9430 | −1536 | −1628 | −1647 | — | 1543 |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash TP4 | 12018 | −888 | −1031 | −1030 (V2 runner forced) | — | 1743 |

- **#59156 and #59158** work on ROCm unchanged. Outputs are bit-identical after full and selective wake (TP2, DP2 within its pre-sleep variation, V4-Flash). Nested pools behave as on CUDA: the innermost pool wins.
- **#59160 is CUDA-only as posted.** Enabling it on ROCm also needs a C++ change: a blocking `hipMemset` in `cumem_allocator.cpp` breaks graph capture, and making it `hipMemsetAsync` on a non-blocking stream fixes it. Custom allreduce needs the same unregistered capture path as on CUDA. With that change it stays bit-exact over 10 cycles plus a level-2 reload, but frees only 72–244 MiB, because most graph memory is held by the HIP runtime outside torch pools. Unlike CUDA, ROCm returns that memory when graphs are destroyed, so destroying graphs on sleep and recapturing on wake would recover ~1–1.5 GiB/GPU at 9–50 s per wake. Both are possible follow-ups.
- **#59360 is a no-op on ROCm** (verified): FlashInfer allreduce is unavailable, so no workspace exists. Memory, bit-exactness and wake latency match unpatched.
- **`--enable-nccl-comm-suspend` frees ~0 MiB on ROCm by default:** RCCL does not allocate its buffers with cuMem. With `NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=1`, suspend frees 505 MiB but cuMem itself adds 389 MiB, a net saving of 116 MiB.
- **Wake latency:** 0.37–0.9 s; the #59160 ROCm patch adds 0.2–0.3 s.
- **50-cycle leak test** (DeepSeek-V2-Lite TP1 / TP2 / DP2, V4-Flash TP4; unpatched, #59156, #59156 + #59158): device-memory slope 0.00 MiB/cycle and every cycle bit-exact (sequential 8-prompt check, 50/50) in every arm. Host RSS does not grow over level-1 cycles; it steps up only at level-2 `reload_weights` cycles, unpatched too. After wake, in-process memory (`hipMemGetInfo`, torch, every cuMem tag) equals the value before sleep; `rocm-smi` steps once at the first wake and then stays flat, unpatched too. #59156 + #59158 + #59523 on V4-Flash TP4 (V2 runner): 30/30 cycles bit-exact, flat at 10779 MiB.
- **GSM8K before sleep and after wake** (1319 questions, 5-shot, temperature 0): every post-wake score stays within the server's own two awake rounds, give or take one standard error.

  | V4-Flash TP4 | Awake R1 / R2 | Full wake | Selective wake | +10 cycles |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Unpatched | 0.949 / 0.945 | 0.948 | 0.944 | 0.945 |
  | #59156 + #59158 | 0.947 / 0.948 | 0.949 | 0.948 | 0.947 |
  | V2 runner, unpatched | 0.947 / 0.949 | 0.951 | 0.948 | 0.948 |
  | V2 runner, all three + #59523 | 0.943 / 0.945 | 0.948 | 0.948 | 0.945 |

  DeepSeek-V2-Lite TP2 gives the same picture at 0.34–0.36, with about 250 of 1319 answers changing between two awake rounds even without sleep.
- **Exact logprob comparison is not reproducible on this ROCm image**, even awake against awake on unpatched vLLM (about 25% of requests identical on DeepSeek-V2-Lite TP2, about 90% on V4-Flash), so bit-exactness on ROCm rests on the sequential check above.
- **Open on #59523:** one DeepSeek-V2-Lite TP2 startup with its cached-stream build hung in the kernel during KV-cache allocation (2 clean startups plus the unit test otherwise). The cause is not established; the earlier per-stream-per-call variant had no hang and is the one used for the GSM8K run.

1. #59523, stacked on #59160.
2. Asleep memory with CUDA graphs minus `--enforce-eager`, unpatched.

### Notes and related work
- **#59160 compatibility:**
  - Custom allreduce IPC-registers graph buffers, which fails on cuMem memory. #59160 makes it copy into its pre-registered buffer while capturing, which is the same approach as sgl-project/sglang#7873.
  - NCCL graph registration pins cuMem pages and goes stale after remap (see fzyzcjy/torch_memory_saver#88), so `NCCL_GRAPH_REGISTER=0` is required in this mode. Serving cost is within ±5% noise.
- **Related work:**
  - #47700 captures graphs into the `weights` pool.
  - #56373 checkpoints the whole CUDA process on one GPU, which also frees graph executables.

### Tracking

Merged: #59200, #59156, #59158, #59160. Remaining memory PRs are independent unless noted.

- [x] #59200 Share workspace and model runner init between GPU and XPU workers (merged)
- [x] #59156 Release WorkspaceManager scratch on sleep (merged)
- [x] #59158 Offload runtime state on sleep (merged)
- [x] #59160 Offload V2 CUDA graph pools in sleep mode, opt-in `sleep_mode_offload_cudagraph` (merged)
- [ ] #59228 Don't unmap cuMem allocations freed while asleep
- [ ] #59909 Release the CUDA graph pool on sleep instead of backing it up (follow-up to #59160: no CPU copy; refuses if a tensor is live in the pool)
- [ ] #59523 ROCm support for the graph pool mode (`hipMemsetAsync` in the cuMem allocator)
- [ ] #59360 Release the FlashInfer MNNVL allreduce workspace with `--enable-nccl-comm-suspend`
- [ ] #59939 Release DeepEP all2all buffers with `--enable-nccl-comm-suspend` when CUDA graphs are off (~1 GiB/GPU high-throughput, ~4.4-6 GiB/GPU low-latency on V4-Flash)
- [ ] #59535 Move FlashInfer MLA decode workspaces into `WorkspaceManager`
- [ ] #59537 Reuse one stream for every `graph_capture()` call
- [ ] #59540 Take the top-k/top-p sampler scratch from `WorkspaceManager`
- [ ] #59847 Register KV caches with the connector outside the runtime pool (fixes a #59158 regression with LMCache)
- [ ] #59165 Docs: what stays on the GPU in sleep mode

KV connectors (P/D) across sleep: sleep remaps the KV cache to new physical pages at the same addresses, so a connector that registered it with a NIC or another process keeps stale registrations.

- [ ] #59625 Connector API (`supports_sleep_mode`, `release_kv_caches`/`restore_kv_caches`), startup refusal for connectors that cannot follow the remap (NIXL, MoRIIO, non-RDMA Mooncake, MooncakeStore), and MooncakeConnector support over RDMA. Self-contained; supersedes #59624.
- [ ] #59934 MooncakeStoreConnector support (stacked on #59625)
- [ ] #59635 NIXL pull connector support (stacked on #59625; re-registers and peers re-handshake on a registration epoch, no lease)
- [ ] #59993 `pause(mode="wait")` drains requests whose async KV load is in flight (pre-existing 500 with any async-load connector)
- [ ] #59994 Offload model runner construction buffers (e.g. MTP hidden states, 512 MiB/GPU on V4-Flash); follow-up to #59158
- [x] ~~#59162~~ folded into #59158

---

<details>
<summary>Original report (by @penguin-wwy)</summary>

### Summary
In colocated RL training setups, when the training process is running, a sleep request can be used to free the GPU memory held by the vLLM process. However, I found that the memory allocated by WorkspaceManager is not covered by sleep mode.

### Root cause analysis
In `EngineCore._initialize_kv_caches`, `determine_available_memory` is called first to compute the available memory before allocating the KV cache blocks. Following the call stack, this triggers a dummy run that goes through the full inference path:

```
gpu_worker.py: determine_available_memory
                     ↓
gpu_model_runner.py: _dummy_run
                     ↓
            attention / moe
                     ↓
current_workspace_manager().get_simultaneous(...)
                     ↓
self._ensure_workspace_size(total_bytes)
                     ↓
self._current_workspaces[workspace_id] = torch.empty(
    (required_bytes,), dtype=torch.uint8, device=self._device
)
```
This path triggers the workspace manager's allocation logic, but the allocation is not covered by either `self._maybe_get_memory_pool_context(tag="weights")` or `self._maybe_get_memory_pool_context(tag="kv_cache")`. As a result, sleep mode cannot release this chunk of memory.

### Reproduction / observed impact
For example, with the following launch command:
```
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --data-parallel-size 8 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --reasoning-parser deepseek_v4
```
The leftover MoE workspace size is proportional to dp_size × max_num_batched_tokens, which amounts to roughly 6.1 GiB in this configuration.

### Question / proposal
Could this workspace memory also be brought under the management of sleep mode, so that it can be released together with weights and KV cache when the engine sleeps?

</details>

title: [Feature]: [RFC] Dynamic Latent-Trajectory Consensus Governor for Reasoning Models (DeepSeek-R1 / QwQ) to Free KV-Cache 4.5x Faster
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Research paper :
[SubNeutralize__The_Geometry_of_Reasoning_and_the_Elimination_of_the_Overthinking_Trap (4) (1).pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32702285/SubNeutralize__The_Geometry_of_Reasoning_and_the_Elimination_of_the_Overthinking_Trap.4.1.pdf)
## 1. Problem & Systems Motivation

Autoregressive reasoning models (e.g., `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B`, `QwQ-32B`) present a massive throughput bottleneck in vLLM:
* In up to 40% of coding and reasoning tasks, models derive the correct solution within early generation (80–120 tokens).
* Instead of emitting the final answer, the model enters repetitive post-deduction monologue loops ("Wait, let me double check... what if null? Actually, step 1 was right..."), consuming 1,500+ tokens.
* **The vLLM Impact:** This unnecessarily occupies PagedAttention KV-cache slots for 2+ minutes per sequence, starving the scheduler, inflating queues, and degrading global serving throughput.

---

## 2. Proposed Mechanism: Latent Trajectory Consensus

Rather than applying arbitrary token limits or heuristic string parsing, we propose an early-exit mechanism (**SubNeutralize**) computed directly from latent trajectory dynamics at the model's cognitive bottleneck layer (layer 14 on 1.5B/7B, layer 32 on 32B).

During token decoding, we track cosine velocity and momentum in Python:

```python
# 1. Directional velocity between current and previous hidden states
velocity = 1.0 - cosine_similarity(h_current, h_prev)

# 2. Update exponential moving average (alpha = 0.10)
ema_velocity = (0.10 * velocity) + (0.90 * ema_velocity_prev)

# 3. Scale-free momentum ratio
momentum_ratio = velocity / ema_velocity

# 4. Consensus check (after minimum 60 tokens, with 2-token debounce)
if token_step >= 60 and (momentum_ratio < 0.82 or velocity < 0.135):
    # Trajectory has stabilized into consensus equilibrium.
    # Transition immediately into answer/code emission.
    trigger_early_stop()
```

---

## 3. Empirical Benchmarks on NVIDIA A100-SXM4 (DeepSeek-R1-32B)

Tested under an identical **1,500-token ceiling** for both Vanilla and Governed runs on enterprise backend coding tasks (Rate limiters, SQL sanitizers, JWT claims validators, TTL LRU caches):

| Metric | Vanilla vLLM Baseline | Governed (SubNeutralize) | Improvement |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Total Tokens Consumed** | 5,698 tokens | **1,261 tokens** | **77.9% Compute Saved** |
| **Total Inference Latency** | 596.1 s | **132.3 s** | **4.51x Speedup** |
| **Average Query Latency** | 149.0 s | **33.1 s** | **-115.9 s per sequence** |
| **Verified Unit Test Pass Rate** | 4/4 (100%) | **4/4 (100%)** | **Zero Accuracy Loss** |
| **KV-Cache Eviction Speed** | ~150 s / req | **~33 s / req** | **Cache freed 4.5x faster** |

---

## 4. Kernel Overhead & Computational Budget

* The consensus check operates on a single-layer 1D hidden vector (d = 3584 or 5120).
* On an NVIDIA A100, computing cosine similarity and EMA takes **less than 15 microseconds per decode step**.
* Compared to the forward pass latency of a 32B model (~25–35 ms per token), compute overhead is **less than 0.05%** (negligible).

---

## 5. Potential vLLM Integration Points

We would love to discuss the cleanest architectural pattern for vLLM:
* **Option A (Worker forward hook):** Hook intermediate hidden states in the decoder layer prior to the lm_head logit projection.
* **Option B (Custom StoppingCriteria):** Register an opt-in reasoning governor via `SamplingParams(early_consensus_stopping=True)` or a worker plugin.

---

## 6. Resources & Reference Implementation

* **Apache-2.0 Reference Implementation:** https://github.com/Arnab758/subneutralize
* **PyPI Package:** `pip install subneutralize` (v0.1.2)
* **Research Paper (Zenodo DOI):** https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22941619

Would the maintainers be open to an RFC/PR exploring this integration for reasoning models?

title: [Feature]: [Rust Frontend][Multimodal] Add Gemma 4 image support / multimodal model spec
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Summary

Please add multimodal/image support for **Gemma 4** models to the Rust frontend's multimodal model/processor registry.

I am serving:

```text
google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it
```

with the vLLM Rust frontend enabled.

vLLM's inference engine correctly recognizes the model as multimodal and initializes the vision/encoder path, but the Rust frontend does not have a multimodal model spec registered for `model_type="gemma4"`.

As a result, the Rust frontend disables image/video support during startup and subsequently rejects otherwise valid OpenAI-compatible `image_url` content with HTTP 400.

This appears closely related to the model-family coverage item tracked in #44280.

---

## Environment

```text
vLLM version: 0.28.0
Model: google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it
Served model name: gemma-4-26b-a4b-it
Frontend: Rust frontend
Endpoint: /v1/chat/completions
```

Relevant multimodal configuration:

```text
limit_mm_per_prompt = {"image": 4, "video": 0}
```

The model is resolved by the vLLM engine as:

```text
Resolved architecture: Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration
```

---

## Relevant startup logs

The Rust frontend reports:

```text
(RustFrontend) WARNING [multimodal.rs:446]
multimodal model spec is not registered; disabling image/video support for this model
model_id="google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it" model_type="gemma4"

(RustFrontend) WARNING [multimodal.rs:413]
no multimodal modality resolved; disabling multimodal support for this model
model_id="google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it" model_type="gemma4"
```

However, the engine itself clearly initializes the multimodal portions of Gemma 4:

```text
Resolved architecture: Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration
```

and:

```text
Forcing --disable_chunked_mm_input for models with multimodal-bidirectional attention.
```

and later:

```text
Encoder cache will be initialized with a budget of 8192 tokens,
and profiled with 29 image items of the maximum feature size.
```

There is also a `SiglipImageProcessor` initialization message:

```text
[transformers] `SiglipImageProcessorFast` is deprecated.
The `Fast` suffix for image processors has been removed;
use `SiglipImageProcessor` instead.
```

This makes it appear that the inference engine supports the Gemma 4 multimodal path, while the Rust frontend independently disables multimodal request handling because `gemma4` is missing from its image model/processor registry.

---

## Reproduction

Start `google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it` with the Rust frontend enabled.

Relevant configuration:

```bash
export VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1
```

Serve the model with image inputs enabled, e.g.:

```bash
vllm serve google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it \
  --served-model-name gemma-4-26b-a4b-it \
  --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image":4,"video":0}'
```

Then send an OpenAI-compatible multimodal chat request:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "gemma-4-26b-a4b-it",
    "messages": [
      {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
          {
            "type": "text",
            "text": "What is in this image?"
          },
          {
            "type": "image_url",
            "image_url": {
              "url": "https://vllm-public-assets.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/vision_model_images/2560px-Gfp-wisconsin-madison-the-nature-boardwalk.jpg"
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }'
```

The Rust frontend returns:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "message": "unsupported multimodal content: image_url",
    "type": "invalid_request_error",
    "param": null,
    "code": "invalid_request_error"
  }
}
```

The request is rejected by the frontend rather than reaching multimodal inference.

---

## Expected behavior

Since `google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it` is a vision-capable model and vLLM's engine resolves and initializes its multimodal components, I would expect the Rust frontend to recognize `gemma4` as an image-capable model and accept standard OpenAI-compatible content such as:

```json
{
  "type": "image_url",
  "image_url": {
    "url": "https://..."
  }
}
```

Ideally, Gemma 4 would be added to the Rust frontend's registered multimodal model/processor specs.

---

## Relationship to the Rust frontend roadmap

I found #44280, **Rust Frontend Feature Parity**, which describes multimodal support as including an image path for registered image model specs and separately tracks broader model-family coverage beyond the current image processor registry.

This issue seems to be a concrete example of that remaining coverage gap:

```text
Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration
        |
        | engine recognizes multimodal model
        v
vLLM engine / vision encoder
        ✅

Rust frontend multimodal registry
        |
        | model_type="gemma4" not registered
        v
image/video support disabled
        ❌

/v1/chat/completions
        |
        v
"unsupported multimodal content: image_url"
```

I did not find a separate existing issue specifically tracking Gemma 4 multimodal support in the Rust frontend, so I am opening this separately from #44280 in case a model-specific implementation/tracking issue is useful.

---

## Alternatives

The current workaround is to use the Python frontend instead of the Rust frontend for Gemma 4 multimodal serving.

That works around the frontend registration gap, but we would prefer to use the Rust frontend in production.

---

## Additional context

I originally encountered this through LiteLLM, but reproduced the same failure by calling vLLM directly, so LiteLLM is not involved in the failure.

The full vLLM startup log also shows that the target Gemma 4 model initializes its multimodal encoder/cache successfully before the Rust frontend begins serving requests.

There is a separate warning related to the Gemma 4 MTP speculative draft model:

```text
Draft model Gemma4MTP does not support external multimodal embeddings.
Embeddings from the target model will not be passed to the drafter;
using text-only draft inputs instead.
```

I do not believe this warning is responsible for the HTTP 400, since the request is rejected by the Rust frontend due to the missing multimodal model spec before inference.

title: [Feature]: [Helm] Add configurable startupProbe for slow model initialization
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Problem

The Helm chart currently provides readiness and liveness probes against `/health`, but does not provide a startup probe.

The default liveness probe is configured as follows:

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  initialDelaySeconds: 15
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8000
```

With the current defaults, consecutive liveness probe failures can trigger a container restart as early as roughly 35 seconds after container start. The exact timing may vary slightly depending on probe scheduling and timeouts.

When starting large models, vLLM may perform several normal initialization steps, including:

- Loading model checkpoints
- Allocating the KV cache
- Kernel compilation and autotuning
- CUDA graph capture
- Model-specific warmup

These initialization steps can take substantially longer than 35 seconds.

While `/health` is still unavailable during initialization, the liveness probe cannot distinguish normal slow startup from a startup that is genuinely stuck or unhealthy.

As a result, a container that is still making normal initialization progress can be restarted repeatedly and may eventually enter `CrashLoopBackOff`.

### Proposed change

I propose adding the following startup probe as the default in `examples/deployment/chart-helm/values.yaml`:

```yaml
startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8000
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 180
```

With these proposed defaults, the startup budget would be approximately 30 minutes:

```text
10 seconds × 180 failures = 1,800 seconds = 30 minutes
```

This default is intended to accommodate cold starts for large models while remaining configurable based on model size and initialization characteristics.

A longer startup budget reduces the risk of prematurely restarting a container that is still making progress, but it also delays detection and recovery when startup is genuinely stuck.

The main goal of this proposal is therefore not simply to increase a timeout, but to separate **startup lifecycle handling from runtime liveness detection**. The exact default `failureThreshold` can be adjusted based on maintainer feedback.

Until the startup probe succeeds, Kubernetes does not execute the readiness or liveness probes. After startup succeeds, both probes run using their existing configurations.

Users who do not need a startup probe should be able to disable it completely:

```yaml
startupProbe: null
```

I propose rendering the startup probe configuration object directly, following the same pattern as the existing readiness and liveness probes.

This avoids introducing chart-specific probe fields and allows users to use standard Kubernetes probe configurations.

For example, users could replace the default HTTP probe with an exec probe:

```yaml
startupProbe:
  exec:
    command:
      - sh
      - -c
      - test -f /tmp/model-ready
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 360
```

The same approach would allow `tcpSocket` or differently configured HTTP probes.

### Deployment progress deadline

The Deployment currently hard-codes:

```yaml
progressDeadlineSeconds: 1200
```

A 20-minute progress deadline may cause the Deployment rollout to be reported as failed before the proposed startup budget is exhausted.

Kubernetes reports this using the `ProgressDeadlineExceeded` condition, but does not automatically terminate the Pods or roll back the Deployment.

I therefore propose exposing `progressDeadlineSeconds` as a Helm value, with the following default:

```yaml
progressDeadlineSeconds: 2100
```

This provides the proposed 30-minute startup budget plus a five-minute rollout margin.

Deployments that increase the startup probe's `periodSeconds` or `failureThreshold` may also need to increase `progressDeadlineSeconds` so that the rollout deadline does not expire before the expected startup window.

### Schema, documentation, and tests

I propose adding the following values schema constraints:

- `startupProbe`: object or `null`
- `progressDeadlineSeconds`: integer greater than or equal to 1

The existing readiness probe, liveness probe, and `/health` endpoint behavior would remain unchanged.

The documentation would describe the default startup budget, disabling the probe with `startupProbe: null`, custom probe configuration, and the relationship between the startup budget and `progressDeadlineSeconds`.

Helm tests would cover the default configuration, disabled and customized startup probes, and `progressDeadlineSeconds` configuration and schema validation.

### Relationship to existing issues

This proposal is related to #50282 and #6073, but addresses a different layer.

#6073 requests a separate `/ready` endpoint and a `/health` endpoint that becomes available earlier during initialization, and mentions a startup probe as a currently available workaround.

#50282 proposes a server-side management or health endpoint that would make startup state observable before the engine becomes ready.

This proposal does not introduce a new endpoint or modify the vLLM server.

Instead, it uses the existing `/health` endpoint as a Helm chart startup probe to prevent premature restarts during normal long-running initialization.

The server-side startup observability improvements and this Helm chart change are therefore complementary approaches.


### Alternatives

### Increase `livenessProbe.initialDelaySeconds`

Users can manually increase the initial delay of the liveness probe.

However, this requires each deployment to estimate its worst-case initialization time and mixes startup timing with a probe intended to detect failures during runtime.

Kubernetes provides a startup probe specifically to separate these lifecycle stages.

### Disable the liveness probe

This avoids restarts during initialization, but also removes liveness-based automatic recovery if the server becomes unhealthy after startup.

### Wait for a server endpoint that is available during initialization

The server-side changes discussed in #50282 and #6073 could improve startup observability.

However, they are broader runtime changes and do not directly address premature restarts in the current Helm chart.

A startup probe can be applied independently with the current server behavior using standard Kubernetes lifecycle semantics.

### Additional context

Relevant chart files include:

- `examples/deployment/chart-helm/values.yaml`
- `examples/deployment/chart-helm/templates/_helpers.tpl`
- `examples/deployment/chart-helm/templates/deployment.yaml`
- `examples/deployment/chart-helm/values.schema.json`
- `docs/deployment/frameworks/helm.md`

I also searched open pull requests for `startupProbe`, `startup probe`, and `helm startup probe`, and did not find an open PR implementing this change for the current Helm chart.

title: [Feature]: [ROCm][Hy4] Add calibrated FP8 KV-cache support for sparse MLA
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

While doing validation on https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58056 I noticed that `tencent/Hy4-preview-FP8` provides FP8 weights but no calibrated FP8 KV-cache scales:

```json
"kv_cache_quant_algo": null
```

When `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` is enabled, vLLM defaults the Q/K scales to `1.0`.
This causes a large accuracy regression with `ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE`.

Matched 20-example GSM8K results:

| KV-cache dtype | Accuracy | Truncated |
|---|---:|---:|
| BF16 (`auto`) | 95% | 5% |
| FP8 | 50% | 40% |

From a bit of digging, I think there are two options here:

1. **Static calibrated scales** (less work up front, but not necessary robust across workloads)
   - Calibrate and export per-layer Q and compressed-KV scales.
   - Load them following the Kimi K3 or DeepSeek V3.2 pattern.

2. **Dynamic block scales** (more impl work upfront, but scales to new workloads)
   - Add ROCm support for an embedded-scale format similar to `fp8_ds_mla`.
   - Compute per-token or per-block UE8M0 scales when writing the cache,
     following DeepSeek V4.

cc: @akii96 

### Alternatives

Use `--kv-cache-dtype auto` so Hy4 keeps a BF16 KV cache.

vLLM could also reject or require explicit opt-in for uncalibrated FP8 KV when
the checkpoint declares `kv_cache_quant_algo: null`.

### Additional context

- Hardware: 8× AMD Instinct MI350X (`gfx950`)
- Parallelism: TP8
- Backend: `ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE`
- Model revision: `4215ec29de873a998e849cee902654490c7ff4d1`
- vLLM commit: `79468c20ef23227d4e051f807e10fd54fb24e24f`
- Related: #54594, #58056

title: [Feature]: instruction-preserving truncation for `/v1/chat/completions`, and document `truncate_prompt_tokens` semantics
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

**Motivation.** We run LLM-as-judge evaluation through `/v1/chat/completions`. Each request is a system message, a grading rubric, the question, the reference answer, and the candidate model's response. Occasionally a candidate degenerates into a repetition loop; one 1,854-token response became ~16k prompt tokens after JSON escaping and overflowed a 14,336-token judge (`"This model's maximum context length is 14336 tokens. However, your request has 15995 input tokens."`).

The only server-side tool for this today is `truncate_prompt_tokens`, and for this prompt shape it is unusable:

- It keeps the **last** k tokens of the rendered prompt (`vllm/sampling_params.py`: "will use only the last k tokens from the prompt (i.e., left truncation)"). The system message, rubric and question are at the front, so they are discarded first, and the judge is left grading the tail of the garbage response with no rubric and no reference.

- For text inputs the actual side is not even guaranteed: the chat path tokenizes with `truncation=True, max_length=k`, and `vllm/inputs/preprocess.py` branches on `tokenizer.truncation_side`, so behavior depends on the model's tokenizer config.

- None of this is in the OpenAI-compatible-server docs; the semantics live only in a `SamplingParams` docstring.

Rubric-first, RAG-style and tool-instruction prompts all share this shape: the important tokens are at the start, the compressible tokens are in the middle.

**Proposal.**

1. Add an opt-in, instruction-preserving truncation mode for chat completions. Two possible surfaces:
   - a `truncation: "auto" | "disabled"` field mirroring the Responses API, implemented item-aligned (drop whole non-system messages from the front, keep the system message and the last user message, never split a message); or
   - a per-message `truncate: true` marker so the client can designate exactly which message may be shortened (from its end) to fit.
   Either is client-controlled and keeps the default strict 400.
2. Document `truncate_prompt_tokens` in `docs/serving/openai_compatible_server.md`: left truncation, `-1` = `max_model_len`, side depends on `truncation_side` for text inputs, and a note that the system message is the first thing dropped.
3. Document `/tokenize` (returns `count` and `max_model_len`, applies the chat template, skips the length check) as the intended pre-flight for clients that budget prompts themselves.


### Alternatives
- Client-side: call `/tokenize`, then shorten the designated field and retry. This is what we are doing. It works, but every client re-implements it and it costs an extra round trip per long prompt.
- `truncate_prompt_tokens` as-is: drops the wrong end (above).


### Additional context

- The Responses API already carries a `truncation: "auto"` field whose current implementation has the same left-cut problem; see https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/58421
- #37011 proposes `code: "context_length_exceeded"` so clients can detect the overflow programmatically. Together with a proper truncation mode it would give both "let the server fix it" and "let me fix it" paths.

title: [Feature]: Request observer hook for the Rust frontend
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

We run vLLM behind an API gateway and collect per-tenant usage records (prompt / cached / generated tokens) in an L7 proxy in front of it today. With the Rust frontend we would rather do this in process, as an out-of-tree module (a small crate that plugs into the frontend and writes usage records to our own store): the frontend knows the exact token counts without parsing responses, including for streams the client aborts before the final usage chunk is sent, which a proxy never sees. We don't want to patch vLLM for this, so upstream would only need a narrow, generic hook.

In the Python frontend this is possible out of tree: a stat logger plugin (`vllm.stat_logger_plugins`) receives per-request `FinishedRequestStats`, and `--middleware` can map the tenant by request id. The Rust frontend has no equivalent hook. (One gap on the Python side: requests aborted by the frontend, e.g. on client disconnect, are removed in `OutputProcessor.abort_requests` without finished stats, so they never reach stat loggers although they consumed tokens. The Rust frontend already records these aborts in Prometheus from `Drop`, so the hook below covers them.)

Today the terminal request data is computed in `RequestMetricsTracker::record_finished` and written straight to Prometheus, so nothing else can consume it. Prometheus is aggregated (no per-request or per-tenant data), and traces are sampled; the tracing plan in RFC #44757 also leaves client-initiated aborts out of the `llm_request` span, which is reasonable for tracing but means aborted streams, which still consume tokens, can't be metered from spans.

Proposal: two small, independent pieces.

**1. `vllm-llm`: a request-completion seam.** Both terminal points of `GenerateOutputStream` (`poll_next` on engine finish, `Drop` on frontend abort or stop-string match) produce one `FinishedRequest` (external / engine request id, model, LoRA, engine index, finish reason, token counts, lifecycle timestamps). The built-in Prometheus recording derives its latency breakdown from the same `FinishedRequestStats`, so metrics and other consumers cannot drift, which is the property RFC #44757 wants between metrics and the `llm_request` span. Registered observers are called synchronously, in registration order, at most once per request; panics are isolated. With no observer registered there is no extra allocation.

```rust
pub trait RequestObserver: Send + Sync + 'static {
    /// Called on the request path (possibly inside `Drop`); must not block.
    fn on_finished(&self, request: &Arc<FinishedRequest>);
    /// Called once after the engine client has shut down, e.g. to drain a queue.
    fn shutdown(&self) -> BoxFuture<'_, ()> { /* no-op */ }
}

impl Llm {
    pub fn with_request_observers(self, observers: RequestObservers) -> Self;
}
```

**2. `vllm-server`: register observers the same way as the router extension (#43774).** `ServeExtensions` (router extension + request observers) and `serve_with_extensions`; `serve` and `serve_with_router_extension` keep their behavior and delegate to it. Like
#43774, this is a composition hook for custom binaries, not a stable plugin API.

**Non-goals:** no engine protocol change, no new Prometheus metrics, no queueing or async adapter upstream (I/O-bound observers hand requests to their own task; the OTel SDK already batches spans), and no per-request attribute plumbing through the request types.

### Alternatives

- OTLP spans or logs as the metering source: spans are sampled and client aborts are left out (as planned in #44757), so they are not billing-grade. With this hook, a span emitter is just another observer.
- Scraping Prometheus: aggregated, no per-request or per-tenant data.
- Patching the frontend downstream: works, but every deployment re-patches `request_metrics.rs` / `output.rs`.

### Additional context

- Prototype: an out-of-tree crate on top of the two changes writes per-tenant usage records to a Redis Stream (the tenant is attached by a router-extension middleware keyed by request id, so no upstream change is needed for that). Verified with `vllm-mock-engine`: normal finish, client abort, Redis outage, and flush on SIGTERM.
- Both changes are small and additive: one new module plus wiring at the two terminal points in `vllm-llm`, and one new module plus entry-point wiring in `vllm-server`. Existing APIs keep their behavior; I have a working branch and would split it into two PRs.
- Related: RFC #44757 (this could serve as the base for the Phase 2 `llm_request` span; happy to coordinate with @tahsintunan), #47810, #43641 / #43774.
- #54144 and #57582 touch the same files; I would rebase onto them rather than race them.
- Disclosure: the prototype was developed with AI assistance (Claude Code). If this direction sounds reasonable, I'll open the PRs myself, having reviewed every change, and follow up on review feedback.

title: [Feature]: Improve engine RPC failure handling and shutdown
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

When one worker returns an RPC error, other workers may still have replies pending. Returning immediately can leave those replies for the next call, while waiting without a deadline can block indefinitely. If reply collection cannot finish, the executor must stop accepting work, callers must receive the failure, and workers must be cleaned up.

This proposal connects reply collection, failure propagation, and cleanup around two outcomes:

```text
worker error response
  -> collect the remaining expected replies within a shared reply collection deadline
     |-- complete: return the error; preserve reply correspondence
     |             -> caller may continue where the operation permits recovery
     +-- timeout: fail the executor and notify EngineCore
                   |-- fail pending calls and reject new RPCs
                   +-- run Core and worker cleanup
                       -> finish cleanup or let the process manager enforce its shutdown deadline
```

The timeout branch is deliberately conservative: a reply missing at the reply collection deadline makes the executor unusable, even if the worker is only delayed. This extends terminal-failure handling to RPC response timeouts, using the existing executor-failure callback and Core/process-manager shutdown path. Both outcomes depend on the following four changes.

### 1. Finish the failed call's reply collection

Worker RPC replies are matched to calls by queue order. If RPC A returns after reading one worker's error, RPC B can consume an unread reply from A:

```text
Worker 0 reply queue: [RPC B reply]
Worker 1 reply queue: [RPC A reply] [RPC B reply]
                          ^
                  incorrectly consumed by RPC B
```

Record the first error encountered in reply-queue order, then finish consuming **one reply from each worker selected for RPC A**, counting both successful and failed replies. Return the recorded error after collection completes, leaving replies for later RPCs untouched. RPC A still fails, but a subsequent operation can read its own replies.

### 2. Bound waiting for stragglers

Collecting those remaining replies requires a limit on waiting. Another worker may be a straggler, still alive but slow to reply, or may never respond.

After the first worker error, apply one reply collection deadline. Share the remaining time across all selected workers and receive stages, preserving any earlier caller deadline.

If the reply collection deadline expires, fail the executor and block both queued and new RPCs from reusing the response queues.

### 3. Propagate terminal failure to waiting callers

Blocking further RPCs does not release callers already waiting for results. Fail queued worker RPC futures when the executor becomes unusable. Client utility calls need separate handling because they wait on their own futures.

The client already detects engine death through engine-dead notifications and, for managed local processes, process monitoring. Receiver errors are forwarded to the generation output queue, which utility callers are not waiting on. Setting the engine-dead flag or stopping the receiver leaves their futures pending.

When the output receiver stops, fail all pending sync/async utility futures so those callers receive the failure too. Cover cancellation before the async receiver starts, and leave already-cancelled calls cancelled.

### 4. Let worker cleanup finish after failure is reported

Failure notification can also trigger shutdown while cleanup is still in progress. EngineCore reports fatal failure before its own teardown completes, and a client or process manager may react by sending SIGTERM. If Core has already restored the default signal handling, that signal can terminate it before worker cleanup finishes.

Ignore additional SIGTERM and SIGINT during Core cleanup. The process manager retains its existing shutdown deadline and can force termination of the process tree if cleanup does not finish in time.

These changes affect shared executor, client, and shutdown paths. Automatic retries, RPC identifiers, and new cross-node or parent-death detection protocols are outside this proposal.

### Alternatives

Treat every worker RPC error as terminal and restart the engine, without collecting the remaining replies for reuse. This simplifies reply handling but gives up recovery when all replies could be collected and a follow-up operation would be safe.

### Additional context

### Example Scenario
Consider an RL controller attempting `wake_up()` after a failed level-1 sleep in the same engine:

```text
Worker 0: releases some allocations, then returns an error
Worker 1: completes sleep
```

Inference must remain paused until the required allocations are restored and all required wake operations succeed. Otherwise, a successful-looking wake can allow the next forward pass to access released memory.

This also requires preserving `sleeping_tags` when the sleep RPC raises. Without that state, `wake_up()` can take the already-awake path and skip restoration. The shared RPC handling then ensures that the wake result comes from that wake's own replies. Together, these changes produce the following behavior:

```text
partial sleep failure; inference stays paused
  -> collect this sleep's expected replies within the reply collection deadline
     |-- complete: return the sleep error with restoration state preserved
     |             -> controller chooses wake_up()
     |             -> workers perform their required restoration
     |             -> collect this wake's own replies
     |             -> resume inference only if all required wake operations succeed
     +-- timeout: fail executor and pending calls; proceed through managed shutdown
                   -> controller receives an error and can restart or stop
                   -> no inference resumes on the failed executor
```

The controller still decides whether to request recovery. These changes do not make every allocator failure recoverable.

### Future plan

These guarantees provide a basis for automatic recovery policies. The following directions are outside this proposal:

- **Per-worker outcomes.** Report structured outcomes for each selected worker, including its rank, failure details, and whether a reply was received. This would give recovery policies more information than the first exception returned to the caller.
- **Bounded automatic recovery for partial failures.** For operations with defined retry and restoration semantics, attempt recovery on affected workers where the backend permits it. Keep inference paused until all required workers are ready and their shared state is consistent. Restart the engine if recovery is unsafe or exceeds its budget.
- **Recovery after worker loss.** Explore selective worker replacement. This requires backend support to rebuild the affected communication group and restore consistent model and cache state. An executor failed by a response timeout remains terminal; recovery must establish a fresh executor or use a separately designed channel reinitialization protocol before accepting new work.

### Roadmap alignment

This proposal contributes to the **production stability and failure ergonomics** goal under SIG Core in [#48168: vLLM Roadmap Q3 2026](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48168).

The sleep/wake scenario also supports **Section 1.2 Scheduler (Sleep/Wake/Drain)** in [#48314: 2026 Q3 vLLM and RL](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48314), tracked in [#48311: Engine Sleep/Wake/Drain Lifecycle for RL](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48311).

### Related work

| Proposal section | Existing work |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Finish reply collection** | [#49972](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/49972), [PR #49976](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49976) |
| **3. Fail waiting callers** | [PR #56416](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56416) |

title: [Feature] [KV Offload] Support sharing SimpleCPUOffload prefix caches across local DP replicas
body:
# Motivation

`SimpleCPUOffloadConnector` (#37160) keeps a private CPU prefix cache per
DP replica. Unlike the native `OffloadingConnector`, the Simple connector is
agnostic to KV organization and adapts to day-0 models without per-model
integration, which makes it a natural fit for throughput-oriented DP-heavy
deployments (e.g. 8×H100 with DP8/TP1/EP). In such deployments each
replica's CPU KV pool is small, and identical prefixes are recomputed
whenever a request is routed to a different local replica, even though a
completed CPU copy exists on the same host. Sharing the local CPU pool would
let these deployments draw on a larger combined KV pool instead of many
small private ones.

Measured on a diagnostic DP4/TP1/EP topology (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, two hosts,
two logical workers sharing each physical GB10 GPU — timings are diagnostic,
not production throughput numbers). Routing a repeated ~6K-token prefix to a
peer replica costs **14.41 s TTFT (full recompute)**; with shared offload it
costs **5.22 s (91.7% of prompt tokens restored via external KV transfer)** —
a 63.8% reduction.

# Proposed approach

Opt-in `cpu_offload_shared=true` in `kv_connector_extra_config`:
- Reuse `SharedOffloadRegion` (#50094), `BlockPool` hash/LRU, `ChunkStatus`, connector handshake; no new copy backend or allocator
- Fixed per-writer slot partitions; shared publication index + `flock` on the metadata region fd; reader references protect slots during peer DMA
- Node-local only; eager offloading; any TP×DP combination (each TP coordinate shares its own KV shard pool); startup fails closed on incompatible hash/model/layout
- PP/DCP/PCP beyond 1 is not supported yet; extending to those is desirable follow-up work, not required for the initial version

# Context

- Duplicate check against open PRs: #53474, #53073, #47324, #57418, #43483,
  #57422, #54743, #52921 — none publishes prefix hashes across DP schedulers.
- No code dependency on #53474 or #53073: peer discovery uses the existing
  `in_the_same_node_as` and region APIs. #53474 is actively reshaping the native connector's region geometry, so this feature deliberately avoids
  coupling to it; overlapping files (worker.py, docs) should need only routine rebases.

title: [Feature]:  Record model_id in bench latency/throughput --output-json
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

`vllm bench serve` records the model in its `--output-json` payload:

```python
# vllm/benchmarks/serve.py:2283
result_json["model_id"] = model_id
```

`vllm bench latency` and `vllm bench throughput` do not. Their payloads are:

```python
# vllm/benchmarks/latency.py:171
results = {
    "avg_latency": ...,
    "latencies": ...,
    "percentiles": ...,
}

# vllm/benchmarks/throughput.py:1143
results = {
    "elapsed_time": ...,
    "num_requests": ...,
    "total_num_tokens": ...,
    "requests_per_second": ...,
    "tokens_per_second": ...,
}
```

So a latency or throughput result file does not say which model produced the
numbers. Any consumer that archives, compares, or ingests these files has to
recover the model out-of-band — from the output filename, or from the shell
command that produced it. Both are lossy: filenames are chosen by the caller,
and the command is not stored next to the result.

This bites in CI/benchmark-tracking setups, where result files are collected
from many runs and loaded into a database. With no `model_id`, rows end up
attributed by filename, which silently produces wrong model labels rather than
an error.

The `.pytorch.json` sibling written under `SAVE_TO_PYTORCH_BENCHMARK_FORMAT=1`
does carry the model (inside `extra_info.args`), but that file is opt-in and
exists for the PyTorch OSS benchmark database, so relying on it is a workaround
rather than a fix for the primary `--output-json` output.

Proposal: add `model_id` to both payloads, using the same key `bench serve`
already uses.

### Alternatives

- **`--metadata KEY=VALUE`** (proposed in #41541) lets the caller pass arbitrary
  fields, including the model. That is a useful feature but a different one: it
  is opt-in and requires every caller to remember to pass the model it already
  told vLLM about on the command line. The model is not user metadata; vLLM
  knows it.
- **Parse it from the filename / invoking command** — what consumers do today,
  and the reason model names get mislabelled.
- **Depend on the `.pytorch.json` sibling** — requires setting
  `SAVE_TO_PYTORCH_BENCHMARK_FORMAT=1` and reading a file whose stated purpose
  is a different database schema.

### Additional context

The change is additive and does not alter existing fields. The in-tree consumer
of these files, `.buildkite/performance-benchmarks/scripts/convert-results-json-to-markdown.py`,
selects columns from explicit allowlists (`latency_column_mapping:19`,
`throughput_results_column_mapping:32`) and already maps `"model_id": "Model"`
for serving rows, so an added key is ignored there rather than breaking the
tables. Each file's `save_to_pytorch_benchmark_format` reads named keys only.

Happy to send the PR.

title: [Feature]: [ROCm][AITER][Hy4] Enable gfx950 MXFP8 MoE and dense linear backends
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

`tencent/Hy4-preview-FP8` runs on gfx950 through the ROCm support added in #57526, but its ModelOpt MXFP8 operations currently use Triton even when `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`:
```text
Using RocmDotScaledMxfp8LinearKernel for MXFP8 GEMM
Using 'TRITON_MXFP8' MxFp8 MoE backend.
```
This feature request tracks two independent AITER enablement categories. 

cc: @akii96 (I know you're focused on gfx942, but wanted to keep you in the loop)

### 1. MXFP8 MoE enablement
vLLM already provides `AiterMxfp8Experts`, but its compatibility check rejects Hy4.
The current AITER implementation requires:
- `SWIGLUOAI_UNINTERLEAVE`
- SwiGLU alpha `1.702`
- SwiGLU beta `1.0`
Hy4 instead uses clamped SwiGLU:
```text
gate = clamp(gate, max=limit)
up   = clamp(up, -limit, limit)
out  = silu(gate) * up
```
The published checkpoint sets `swiglu_limit=10.0`.

#### AITER work
- Support Hy4’s gate/up layout and clamped SwiGLU semantics in the gfx950 MXFP8 fused-MoE kernel.
- Preserve native 1×32 E8M0 weights/scales.
- Support Hy4 routing, expert masks and tensor-parallel execution.
- Add correctness tests against a BF16/dequantized reference.

#### vLLM work
- Represent Hy4’s activation semantics accurately in `FusedMoEConfig`.
- Update `AiterMxfp8Experts.is_supported_config`.
- Forward activation, clamp and gate-layout arguments to AITER.
- Verify automatic selection and explicit `--moe-backend aiter`.
- Preserve `TRITON_MXFP8` fallback.
- Add Hy4 MXFP8 MoE unit and end-to-end coverage.

### 2. MXFP8 dense linear/GEMM enablement
Hy4’s dense projections use ModelOpt MXFP8:
- E4M3 values
- E8M0 scales
- 1×32 scaling blocks
- BF16 output
This is not format-compatible with AITER’s conventional FP8 128×128 block-scale GEMMs. vLLM therefore selects `RocmDotScaledMxfp8LinearKernel`.

#### AITER work
- Add a gfx950 dense MXFP8 GEMM accepting the 1×32 E8M0 format.
- Support dynamic `M`, weight pre-shuffling, split-K and caller-owned output buffers.
- Add runtime configuration lookup, shape logging and a gfx950 tuner.
- Add correctness tests against dequantized BF16.

#### vLLM work
- Add an AITER-backed `Mxfp8LinearKernel`.
- Register it in `_POSSIBLE_MXFP8_KERNELS[PlatformEnum.ROCM]` ahead of Triton when supported.
- Implement gfx950, AITER and scale-layout capability checks.
- Add weight/scale preprocessing and pre-shuffling.
- Support `torch.compile` and full/piecewise cudagraph capture.
- Preserve Triton and emulation fallbacks.
- Add kernel-selection and end-to-end tests.


### Alternatives

- Continue using `RocmDotScaledMxfp8LinearKernel` and `TRITON_MXFP8`.
- Dequantize MXFP8 weights to BF16, with additional memory and performance cost.
- Generic AITER A8W8 block-scale kernels are not a valid substitute because their scale format differs from ModelOpt MXFP8.

title: [Feature]: [WideEP][CPU]: Add a CPU-only Wide Expert Parallelism well-lit path
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Add functional Expert Parallelism (EP), including DP-attention + EP-MoE deployments, to the vLLM CPU backend.

The CPU backend currently appears to partially wire up Expert Parallelism, but the default CPU all-to-all path cannot complete because the variable-size collectives required by `AgRsAll2AllManager` are not implemented by `CpuCommunicator`.

The goal is to support CPU-only MoE deployments across multiple ranks/nodes, including use cases such as llm-d Wide Expert Parallelism on x86_64 servers.

This does **not** require porting DeepEP to CPU. A functional CPU communication backend using `torch.distributed`, Gloo, oneCCL, or another appropriate CPU transport would be sufficient as an initial implementation.

### Current implementation

`CpuCommunicator` already detects EP/all-to-all usage and selects the generic `AgRsAll2AllManager`:

```python
if self.use_all2all:
    ...
    from .all2all import AgRsAll2AllManager
    self.all2all_manager = AgRsAll2AllManager(self.cpu_group)
```

GPU-specific all-to-all backends are also explicitly rejected/fallen back to `allgather_reducescatter` on CPU.

However, `AgRsAll2AllManager` requires variable-size collectives:

```python
gathered_tensors = dist_group.all_gatherv(
    tensors_to_gather,
    dim=0,
    sizes=sizes,
)
```

for dispatch, and:

```python
hidden_states = dist_group.reduce_scatterv(
    hidden_states,
    dim=0,
    sizes=sizes,
)
```

for combine.

`CpuCommunicator` currently implements regular `all_gather()`, but does not override `all_gatherv()` or `reduce_scatterv()`.

The implementations inherited from `DeviceCommunicatorBase` raise `NotImplementedError`.

As a result, the CPU backend appears to have the EP/AgRs plumbing in place, but no functional implementation of the communication primitives required for DP+EP execution.

### Desired behavior

`--enable-expert-parallel` should work with the CPU backend using the `allgather_reducescatter` backend, initially without requiring EPLB.

It would be useful to support:

* CPU implementation of `all_gatherv()` and `reduce_scatterv()`, or an alternative CPU-compatible all-to-all implementation.
* Single-node multi-rank CPU EP.
* Multi-node CPU DP+EP.
* MoE expert weights sharded across EP ranks while attention remains data parallel when TP=1.
* A CPU CI test exercising DP > 1 together with `--enable-expert-parallel`.
* Documentation identifying the supported CPU communication backend and expected network requirements.

Dynamic EPLB can remain a separate feature; currently EPLB explicitly rejects CPU platforms.

### Use case

Large MoE models can benefit substantially from expert sharding on CPU servers because the full expert weight set may otherwise exceed the memory capacity or useful memory bandwidth of a single machine.

For example, a cluster of modern x86_64 servers could use:

```text
TP = 1
DP = N
EP = N
```

with attention replicated/data-parallel across the ranks while MoE experts are distributed across the CPU nodes.

This is also the execution model required to provide a CPU variant of llm-d's Wide Expert Parallelism deployment pattern.

### Relevant code

* `vllm/distributed/device_communicators/cpu_communicator.py`

  * selects `AgRsAll2AllManager`
  * implements `all_gather()`
  * does not implement `all_gatherv()` / `reduce_scatterv()`

title: [Feature]: OutOfResources: shared memory (98304 > 65536) on Turing (SM75) — global attention layers with head_dim=512
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Title: OutOfResources: shared memory (98304 > 65536) on Turing (SM75) — global attention layers with head_dim=512

## Summary

I am unable to serve this checkpoint on NVIDIA Turing (compute capability 7.5) GPUs. vLLM fails during Triton JIT compilation of the unified attention kernel, requesting more shared memory per SM than Turing physically provides.

## Environment

- **GPUs:** 2× NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000 (Turing, SM75, 24 GB each, 64 KB shared memory per SM)
- **vLLM:** 0.26.0 (official Docker image)
- **Parallelism:** tensor-parallel-size 2, `NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1` (no NVLink, VMware passthrough)
- **Model:** `google/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-w4a16-ct`
- **Deployment:** offline / air-gapped

## Error

```
triton.runtime.errors.OutOfResources: out of resource: shared memory,
Required: 98304, Hardware limit: 65536.
Reducing block sizes or `num_stages` may help.
```

## Analysis

At startup, vLLM logs the Gemma 4 attention configuration:

```
head_dim=256, global_head_dim=512
```

Gemma 4 interleaves local sliding-window attention layers (`head_dim=256`) with full **global** attention layers (`global_head_dim=512`).

In `vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_unified_attention.py`, the kernel launch parameters are computed as:

```python
head_size = q.shape[2]

BLOCK_M = (
    16 if num_queries_per_kv <= 16 else triton.next_power_of_2(num_queries_per_kv)
)
BLOCK_Q = BLOCK_M // num_queries_per_kv

launch_num_warps: int | None = None
launch_num_stages: int | None = None

tuned_large_head = (
    head_size == 256
    and max_seqlen_q > 1
    and num_queries_per_kv <= 16
    and current_platform.is_device_capability_family(100)
)
if tuned_large_head:
    BLOCK_M = 32
    BLOCK_Q = BLOCK_M // num_queries_per_kv
    launch_num_warps = 8
    launch_num_stages = 2
```

The reported shared-memory requirement matches the default path exactly:

```
BLOCK_M × head_size × 2 bytes (fp16) × 3 (Q/K/V) × num_stages
= 16 × 512 × 2 × 3 × 2
= 98304 bytes
```

This is precisely the number in the error message, and 1.5× Turing's 65536-byte limit.

Two observations:

1. The `tuned_large_head` branch matches only `head_size == 256`, and is additionally gated on `current_platform.is_device_capability_family(100)` (Blackwell). The `head_size == 512` global attention layers therefore receive no special handling on **any** platform, and on Turing this branch is dead code regardless.
2. I diffed the file between vLLM 0.26.0 and 0.30.0rc1 — this logic is byte-for-byte identical in both, so upgrading vLLM does not change this code path.

This is consistent with an earlier experiment: I manually changed `launch_num_stages = 2` → `1` *inside* the `if tuned_large_head:` block and it had **zero** effect on the error — expected, since that block never executes on SM75.

## Already attempted

- Alternative attention backends: `FLASHINFER`, `XFORMERS`
- Various `--block-size` values
- Lowering `--max-num-batched-tokens`
- `--limit-mm-per-prompt` (to disable image input)
- Both `--tensor-parallel-size 1` and `2`

None of these changed the outcome.

## Proposed workaround

Forcing a single pipeline stage when the head size exceeds 256 brings the allocation to `16 × 512 × 2 × 3 × 1 = 49152` bytes, which fits within the Turing limit:

```python
if launch_num_stages is None and head_size > 256:
    launch_num_stages = 1
```

Placed immediately **after** the `if tuned_large_head:` block, this leaves all existing tuned paths untouched and only affects head sizes that currently have no handling at all.

## Questions

1. Are Turing (SM75) GPUs considered supported for this checkpoint, or for Gemma 4 on vLLM in general?
2. Is there a supported configuration flag that avoids this, rather than patching the kernel source?
3. If a kernel-level fix for `head_size > 256` on pre-Ampere hardware would be welcome upstream, I'm happy to open a vLLM issue or PR with the above analysis.

Thanks in advance for any pointers.

_No response_

_No response_

title: [Feature]: Share non-streaming chat message assembly between `OpenAIServingChat` and batch derender
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Tracking issue for the "Unify (not mirror) the assembly path" item in #42729, raised by @sagearc in the #48617 review (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48617#pullrequestreview-4695988048).

#### Why

Batch chat derender (`OnlineDerenderer._derender_chat`) builds the assistant message itself instead of  sharing the code in `OpenAIServingChat.chat_completion_full_generator`. Both run the same `Parser.parse()` over the same tokens. They differ in what happens after:

- which `tool_choice` branch applies
- `content or ""` for named / required tool choice
- tool call IDs
- the `finish_reason` rewrite to `tool_calls`

The two have already drifted three times:

- `null` vs `""` content, fixed in #48617
- `finish_reason`: batch derender passes through the generate side's `stop` for tool calls (fix in open PR #47931)
- tool call IDs: batch derender builds `ToolCall(id=random_uuid())` and drops the parser's ID, while coupled chat uses `tc.id or make_tool_call_id()`. Batch IDs lose the `chatcmpl-tool-` prefix, and Kimi K2 `functions.<name>:<idx>` IDs are lost. A fix will follow once #47931 merges, since both change the same block of `_derender_chat`.

The round trip parity test (`test_derender_parity.py`) missed the last two. It compares only tool names and arguments, and it feeds the coupled response's `finish_reason` into derender instead of the engine's.

#### Proposal

Pull the post parse message assembly out of `chat_completion_full_generator` into a helper that both paths call. It takes the parser output (`reasoning`, `content`, `tool_calls`), the request and the tool config and returns the `ChatMessage` fields and the final `finish_reason`. It owns:

- the `tool_choice` branches (none / named / required / auto)
- tool call IDs (`tc.id or make_tool_call_id()`)
- `content or ""` for named / required
- `auto_tools_called` and the `finish_reason` rewrite

Constraints:

- **Subclass hooks stay.** `_create_chat_message` and `_finalize_response_message` are overridden by the Cohere v2 handler (`cohere/serving.py`). The helper returns fields and serving still builds the message through the hooks. Derender doesn't subclass `OpenAIServingChat`.
- **No behavior change for `/v1/chat/completions`.** This is the hot non-streaming path.
- **Batch only.** Streaming is #57572.

#56851 `derender` level reuses `OnlineDerenderer.derender_chat`, so it picks this up without adding a third copy.

#### Done when

- [ ] Helper extracted from `chat_completion_full_generator`. Existing chat completion and tool / reasoning parser tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] `_derender_chat` uses it.
- [ ] #47931 and the tool call ID fix have landed first, so the refactor changes no behavior on either path. The tool call ID fix also makes `test_derender_parity.py` feed the engine's `finish_reason` and check tool call ID format.

### Alternatives

- **Rely on the parity test.** Cheaper  and it should be tightened anyway. But it runs one model with one parser configuration and it has already missed two of three drifts.
- **Fold this into #57572.** Both touch `OpenAIServingChat` but the streaming step works on deltas and this one builds a whole message. Keeping them apart keeps each serving change reviewable on its own. If the helpers end up sharing code (the `finish_reason` rewrite, tool call IDs), that can happen in whichever lands second.

### Additional context

- RFC #42729, "Unify (not mirror) the parse/assembly path"
- #48617 (parity test), #47931 (`finish_reason` fix, open). The tool call ID fix follows after #47931.
- #57572: streaming counterpart
- #56851: reuses `derender_chat` for its `derender` level
