title: [Feature] Support KV-cache events & KV-transfer for hybrid-attention models
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

The KV-transfer connector (`--kv-transfer-config`, e.g. mooncake) currently does **not** work for **hybrid-attention** models — models whose `layer_types` mix `full_attention` with `linear_attention` / state-space layers and are flagged `IsHybrid` (e.g. Qwen3.5, which alternates `linear_attention` (GatedDeltaNet) with `full_attention` every 4 layers). It hard-crashes at startup. KV-cache events (`--kv-events-config`), by contrast, **work** for hybrid models on v0.21 (one gotcha around the inflated hybrid `block_size`, noted below).

I'm building cache-aware request routing and want to use a KV-transfer connector for KV migration across hybrid-model replicas; the crash blocks that. Matrix (reproduced end-to-end, logs available on request):

| vLLM | `--kv-transfer-config` only | `--kv-events-config` only | both | neither (control) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0.18.0** | 💥 hard crash | 💥 hard crash | 💥 hard crash | ✅ serves |
| **0.21.0** | 💥 hard crash | ✅ works (see note below) | 💥 hard crash | ✅ serves |

#### Note on `--kv-events-config` — works for hybrid (one gotcha: large `block_size`)

KV-cache events work correctly for hybrid models on v0.21. There is no bug here; this note records one non-obvious behavior so anyone validating hybrid kv-events isn't misled.

For an `IsHybrid` model, vLLM aligns the attention page size to be `>=` the mamba page size, which inflates the attention `block_size`. For Qwen3.5-9B this lands at **528 tokens** (log: `Setting attention block size to 528 tokens to ensure that attention page size is >= mamba page size`), vs the standard **16** for a full-attention model. `BlockStored` is emitted only once a full `block_size` worth of tokens is filled (`block_pool.py`, `cache_blocks` path), so:

```bash
python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
  --model <MODEL> --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --enable-prefix-caching --enforce-eager \
  --kv-events-config '{"enable_kv_cache_events": true, "publisher": "zmq",
                       "topic": "kv-events",
                       "endpoint": "tcp://*:5557", "replay_endpoint": "tcp://*:5558"}'
```

| Model | `layer_types` | attention `block_size` | prompt tokens sent | KV-cache events emitted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507` (standard) | all `full_attention` | 16 | ~48 | **3 × BlockStored** (`group_idx=0`, `block_size=16`) ✅ |
| `Qwen3.5-9B` (`IsHybrid`) | `linear_attention` + `full_attention` (interval 4) | **528** | 1202 (≥ 528) | **4 × BlockStored** (`block_size=528`, `n_tokens=1056`, `medium=GPU`, `group_idx` ∈ {0,1,2,3}) ✅ |

The hybrid model publishes KV-cache events normally once a request fills at least one 528-token block (`Prefix cache hit rate` 70.3% confirms prefix caching engaged). In mamba `'align'` mode the linear-attention layers produce null blocks that `block_pool` intentionally skips (`if blk.is_null: continue` — those layers have no paged KV to hash); this does not affect the full-attention group, and `BlockStored.group_idx` is emitted as designed.

#### Symptom B — hard crash (v0.18.0 any flag; v0.21.0 + `--kv-transfer-config`)

Setting `--kv-transfer-config` (mooncake) on a hybrid model crashes the engine at startup. v0.18.0 crashes with `--kv-events-config` too. The model weights load, then worker KV-cache-group construction raises:

```
ValueError: Hybrid KV cache manager is disabled but failed to convert the KV cache specs to one unified type.
  File ".../vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py", line 1213 (v0.18) / 1409 (v0.21), in unify_hybrid_kv_cache_specs
```

#### Symptom B — hard crash (v0.18.0 any flag; v0.21.0 + `--kv-transfer-config`)

Setting `--kv-transfer-config` (mooncake) on a hybrid model crashes the engine at startup. v0.18.0 crashes with `--kv-events-config` too. The model weights load, then worker KV-cache-group construction raises:

```
ValueError: Hybrid KV cache manager is disabled but failed to convert the KV cache specs to one unified type.
  File ".../vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py", line 1213 (v0.18) / 1409 (v0.21), in unify_hybrid_kv_cache_specs
```

followed by `RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed` / `SERVER_EXIT=1`. vLLM also logs the cause explicitly:

```
WARNING [vllm.py] Turning off hybrid kv cache manager because `--kv-transfer-config` is set. ...
If you are a developer of kv connector, please consider supporting hybrid kv cache manager for your connector
by making sure your connector is a subclass of `SupportsHMA` defined in kv_connector/v1/base.py and use
--no-disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager to start vLLM.
```

### Alternatives

**Root-cause analysis** (what I verified while reproducing; not a fix proposal):

The "hybrid KV cache manager" the warnings refer to is the **Hybrid Memory Allocator (HMA)** — the mechanism that lets a model's multiple KV-cache groups (e.g. mamba SSM/conv-state layers + full-attention paged-KV layers) coexist with different block sizes instead of being collapsed into one unified type (`vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/base.py:84`, `SupportsHMA`). Hybrid models require HMA; disabling it forces all groups into one type, which is where the failure comes from.

- `--kv-transfer-config`: in `VllmConfig.resolve()` an unconditional `kv_transfer_config is not None → need_disable_hybrid_kv_cache_manager = True` fires, regardless of whether the connector declares `SupportsHMA`. With HMA off, `unify_hybrid_kv_cache_specs` tries to collapse `MambaSpec` + `FullAttentionSpec` into one type, but it only has conversion paths for `SlidingWindow` / `ChunkedLocal` / `SlidingWindowMLA` — not `MambaSpec` → `ValueError` (Symptom B).
- `--kv-events-config` on v0.18: the same unconditional disable (`vllm/config/vllm.py:1138-1140`, comment "Hybrid KV cache manager is not compatible with KV events"). On v0.21.0 (the build I tested, `ad7125a`) that branch is gone, so the engine no longer crashes and **KV-cache events work correctly for hybrid models** — the full-attention group emits `BlockStored` (with the multi-group `group_idx` field) once a request fills a block. The only nuance is that the hybrid `block_size` is inflated (528 for Qwen3.5-9B), so prompts shorter than that naturally emit nothing (see note above).

One nuance worth noting: `MooncakeConnector` does declare `SupportsHMA` (the marker was added by #42584), but its store worker/scheduler still carry `TODO: support HMA` / `TODO(yifan): we haven't supported HMA yet` and assume a single group (`block_ids[0]`). So the `SupportsHMA` marker alone is necessary-but-not-sufficient — the per-group store/load implementation also has to land.

**Related work (upstream):**

- #42584 (merged) — adds `SupportsHMA` + per-group `block_ids` (`tuple[list[int], ...]`) to `MooncakeStoreConnector`. This is why the marker exists on `MooncakeConnector` in v0.21.
- #39269 (open) — "allow HMA with KV events when explicitly enabled". Directly addresses the unconditional `kv_events_config → disable-HMA` logic; points out `NixlConnector` already implements full Mamba support (`_has_mamba` detection + `MAMBA2_ATTN` backend), so a working reference implementation exists.
- #38261 (open) — "Hybrid KV offload: planner, MultiConnector, and mamba alignment for hybrid models". Targets Qwen3.5-class models; the core difficulty it calls out matches the root cause here — the stock offload path needs the LCM of all group block sizes, which is impractical when mamba groups have very different sizes from attention groups. Adds a `HybridOffloadPlanner` with per-group coverage tracking.

**Tentative directions for consideration** (not validated; mostly mapping onto the above):

- Respect `--no-disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager` / check `SupportsHMA` instead of unconditionally disabling when `kv_events_config` / `kv_transfer_config` is set (≈ #39269).
- Give `unify_hybrid_kv_cache_specs` a path for `MambaSpec`, or allow Mamba+Full groups to coexist without forcing a single unified type (≈ the planner direction in #38261).
- In mamba `'align'` mode, the linear-attention layers' null blocks are intentionally not emitted as `BlockStored` (no paged KV to hash). If a consumer wants to track mamba-layer occupancy it should read `kv_cache_usage_perc` from `/metrics` rather than `BlockStored`; this is a documentation/expectation note, not a defect.
- Complete the mooncake store-layer HMA implementation (per-group buffer registration / `block_ids` dispatch), using `NixlConnector` as the reference.

### Additional context

- Reproduced standalone with vLLM only (no router or RL framework). 6 experiments (0.18/0.21 × kv-transfer/kv-events/both) + 2 controls (neither flag → both versions serve normally) all run end-to-end; logs available on request. The v0.21 + kv-events-only case was additionally re-tested with long prompts (≥ block_size) to confirm events emit normally — see Symptom A.
- vLLM versions: `0.18.0` and `0.21.0` (commit `ad7125a`).
- Hybrid model: `Qwen3.5-9B`, `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration` (`IsHybrid`). `config.json` `layer_types` = `[linear_attention, linear_attention, linear_attention, full_attention]` × 8 (`full_attention_interval=4`), 32 layers; linear layers use GatedDeltaNet with SSM/conv state.
- Crash function: `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py::unify_hybrid_kv_cache_specs` (line 1213 on v0.18, 1409 on v0.21 — same function, body grew across versions).
- Platform-independent: both GPU (`vllm/platforms/cuda.py`) and Ascend (`vllm_ascend/platform.py`) return `support_hybrid_kv_cache() = True`; the failure is purely a version × flag config-layer issue, not hardware.
- Inspection trick: live ZMQ SUB drops the first event (PUB/SUB slow-joiner); use the replay ROUTER socket (`tcp://*:5558`, DEALER → `send_multipart((b"", (0).to_bytes(8,"big")))`, decode with `msgspec` `KVEventBatch`) to read all buffered events.

title: [Feature]: Support for Responses API `/v1/responses/input_tokens`
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

The Open AI Responses API exposes `/v1/responses/input_tokens` operation is very useful for a preflight requests. You can use it to find out how many input tokens the request contains, through the Open AI compatible API.

We send it the same request as to a `/v1/responses` operation but it just returns a count of input tokens in a request. Similar to already supported Anthropic `/v1/messages/count_tokens` operation.

### Alternatives

Using the Anthropic API `/v1/messages/count_tokens` operation.

### Additional context

We have a Gen AI Gateway in front of multiple vLLM servers with a different models.
On a gateway, we expose both, Anthropic and OpenAI compatible APIs. Unfortunately, when we try to count tokens using the OpenAI compatible API, the call fails with 405 on vLLM server.

title: [Feature]: Support for GLM-5.2 NVFP4 on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (SM120 Architecture)
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Request Description

Hi vLLM team,

I am planning to deploy the **GLM-5.2** model using **NVFP4 (4-bit floating point)** quantization on a setup powered by **NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (SM120 / Blackwell architecture)** GPUs.

Since the RTX PRO 6000 (96GB VRAM, SM120) takes full advantage of Blackwell's native FP4 Tensor Cores, NVFP4 is critical for us to serve large models like GLM-5.2 efficiently within available VRAM constraints.

I would like to inquire about the current roadmap and official support for this specific combination:
1. **SM120 NVFP4 Kernel Support:** Is official support for NVFP4 MoE / attention kernels (e.g., via FlashInfer `b12x` or CUTLASS / ModelOpt) planned or currently being actively integrated for SM120 in upstream vLLM?
2. **GLM-5.2 Integration:** Are there any known blockers (such as sparse attention patterns, MTP speculative decoding, or specialized GEMM layouts) when running GLM-5.2 NVFP4 checkpoints on SM120 in standard vLLM builds?
3. **Recommended Workarounds / Nightly Images:** Is there an experimental branch, nightly Docker image, or recommended build configuration (e.g., specific FlashInfer / CUDA 12.8+ flags) that we should test in the interim?

---

### Environment Details

- **GPU:** NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell, SM120, 96GB VRAM)
- **Model:** `zai-org/GLM-5.2` (or NVFP4 quantized variants, e.g., via ModelOpt)
- **Quantization:** NVFP4
- **Framework / Runtime:** vLLM

title: [Feature]: Recency-based progressive mixed-precision KV cache
body:
## The feature, motivation and pitch

## Summary

I would like to propose a generic recency-based progressive mixed-precision KV cache.

Instead of storing the entire KV cache using one uniform format, vLLM would keep recently created KV blocks in a user-selected higher-precision tier and progressively quantize older completed blocks into lower-precision tiers.

The feature should **not be hardcoded to BF16 as the highest tier**. The ordered precision policy should be configurable. Examples include:

```text
BF16 -> FP8
BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4
BF16 -> NVFP4
FP8 -> NVFP4
NVFP4 -> a future lower-precision format
```

Example percentage-based policies:

```text
newest 20%: BF16
next 20%: FP8 E4M3
oldest 60%: NVFP4
```

or, for a cache whose highest selected precision is FP8:

```text
newest 20%: FP8 E4M3
oldest 80%: NVFP4
```

New KV entries and the active partially filled tail block would be written into the **first/highest tier selected by the policy**, which may be BF16, FP8, NVFP4, or another supported format. Once a block is complete and crosses a configured age boundary, it could be asynchronously quantized and moved to the next lower-precision pool.

This proposal is specifically about using different KV-cache formats **within the same attention layer based on block age**. It is different from layer-wise mixed precision, where different transformer layers use different formats.

## Motivation

Long-context KV caches consume a substantial amount of GPU memory. A uniform low-precision KV cache reduces memory usage, but it applies the same precision to recent and old entries.

For long-context and agentic workloads, it may be useful to preserve a recent window in the policy's selected highest precision while compressing older context more aggressively.

The intended abstraction is not a single special-case mode such as BF16 + FP8 + NVFP4. It is a generic ordered list of storage tiers. For example:

- a BF16-based policy can progressively demote blocks into FP8 and NVFP4;
- an FP8-based policy can progressively demote blocks into NVFP4;
- an NVFP4-based policy could use a future lower-precision storage format when one is supported;
- different hardware backends may expose different valid tier combinations.

This should be treated as a hypothesis that needs quality and performance benchmarking rather than an assumption that recent tokens are always more important.

## Example memory calculation

The following example uses a Llama-3.1-70B-style GQA configuration:

- context length: 64,000 tokens
- number of layers: 80
- KV heads: 8
- head dimension: 128
- both K and V are stored
- one fully populated sequence
- values are aggregated across all tensor-parallel ranks

The number of stored scalar values is:

```text
64,000 tokens × 80 layers × 2 (K and V) × 8 KV heads × 128 dimensions
= 10,485,760,000 values
```

The generic calculation for a progressive policy is:

```text
effective bits/value = sum(tier_fraction × tier_effective_bits)

KV-cache size =
    number_of_values × effective_bits_per_value / 8
```

For NVFP4, the estimates below assume packed 4-bit data and one FP8 block scale per 16 values, or approximately 4.5 effective bits per value. FP8 is approximated as 8 bits per value. Small allocator, alignment, block-table, tensor-scale, and kernel-workspace overheads are not included.

### Absolute VRAM comparison

| KV-cache policy | Effective bits/value | Total KV cache | Per GPU with TP=8 | Saving vs uniform BF16 | Capacity vs uniform BF16 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Uniform BF16 | 16.0 | 19.53 GiB | 2.44 GiB | 0.00% | 1.00x |
| Progressive: 20% BF16 + 80% FP8 | 9.6 | 11.72 GiB | 1.46 GiB | 40.00% | 1.67x |
| Uniform FP8 | 8.0 | 9.77 GiB | 1.22 GiB | 50.00% | 2.00x |
| Progressive: 20% BF16 + 20% FP8 + 60% NVFP4 | 7.5 | 9.16 GiB | 1.14 GiB | 53.13% | 2.13x |
| Progressive: 20% BF16 + 80% NVFP4 | 6.8 | 8.30 GiB | 1.04 GiB | 57.50% | 2.35x |
| Progressive: 20% FP8 + 80% NVFP4 | 5.2 | 6.35 GiB | 0.79 GiB | 67.50% | 3.08x |
| Uniform NVFP4 | ~4.5 | 5.49 GiB | 0.69 GiB | 71.88% | 3.56x |

### Correct baseline for each progressive policy

A progressive policy should be compared with a uniform cache using the policy's own highest selected precision.

| Progressive policy | Uniform reference | Progressive KV size | Uniform reference size | Saving vs its own reference | Capacity vs its own reference |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 20% BF16 + 80% FP8 | Uniform BF16 | 11.72 GiB | 19.53 GiB | 40.00% | 1.67x |
| 20% BF16 + 20% FP8 + 60% NVFP4 | Uniform BF16 | 9.16 GiB | 19.53 GiB | 53.13% | 2.13x |
| 20% BF16 + 80% NVFP4 | Uniform BF16 | 8.30 GiB | 19.53 GiB | 57.50% | 2.35x |
| 20% FP8 + 80% NVFP4 | Uniform FP8 | 6.35 GiB | 9.77 GiB | 35.00% | 1.54x |

This distinction is important:

- `BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4` is a BF16-based progressive policy and should primarily be compared with uniform BF16.
- `FP8 -> NVFP4` is an FP8-based progressive policy and should primarily be compared with uniform FP8.
- Uniform FP8 is therefore not merely a competing alternative to one BF16-based progressive mode; it can itself be the highest tier of another progressive policy.
- Uniform NVFP4 is the lowest uniform format in this example. The same abstraction should extend below NVFP4 when a supported lower-precision format becomes available.

### Breakdown: BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4

Policy:

```text
newest 20%: BF16
next 20%: FP8
oldest 60%: NVFP4
```

| Tier | Tokens | Format | Estimated memory |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Recent/hot | 12,800 | BF16 | 3.91 GiB |
| Intermediate/warm | 12,800 | FP8 | 1.95 GiB |
| Old/cold | 38,400 | NVFP4 | 3.30 GiB |
| **Total** | **64,000** | Mixed | **9.16 GiB** |

Compared with uniform BF16, this policy saves approximately **10.38 GiB**, or **53.13%**, per 64K sequence.

### Breakdown: FP8 -> NVFP4

Policy:

```text
newest 20%: FP8
oldest 80%: NVFP4
```

| Tier | Tokens | Format | Estimated memory |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Recent/hot | 12,800 | FP8 | 1.95 GiB |
| Old/cold | 51,200 | NVFP4 | 4.39 GiB |
| **Total** | **64,000** | Mixed | **6.35 GiB** |

Compared with uniform FP8, this policy saves approximately **3.42 GiB**, or **35.00%**, per 64K sequence.

This is the appropriate FP8-level comparison. It demonstrates that recency-based progression can be applied even when the selected hot tier is already quantized.

## Possible user-facing configuration

The configuration should accept an arbitrary ordered list of supported tiers rather than enabling one hardcoded BF16-based layout.

Percentage-based policies:

```bash
--kv-cache-dtype-policy "bf16:20%,fp8_e4m3:20%,nvfp4:60%"
```

```bash
--kv-cache-dtype-policy "fp8_e4m3:20%,nvfp4:80%"
```

```bash
--kv-cache-dtype-policy "bf16:20%,nvfp4:80%"
```

An absolute-window policy may be easier to provision in production:

```bash
--kv-cache-dtype-policy \
  "bf16:last=4096,fp8_e4m3:last=12288,nvfp4:rest"
```

or:

```bash
--kv-cache-dtype-policy \
  "fp8_e4m3:last=4096,nvfp4:rest"
```

The exact CLI and configuration format are open for discussion. The key requirement is that the first tier must not be implicitly fixed to BF16.

## Possible implementation direction

PagedAttention already manages KV data in blocks, so the feature could be implemented using multiple physical page pools selected by the configured policy.

For example:

```text
Policy A:
BF16 hot pool
FP8 warm pool
NVFP4 cold pool

Policy B:
FP8 hot pool
NVFP4 cold pool
```

A logical KV block ID could map to a physical location:

```text
logical_block_id -> (tier_id, physical_page_id)
```

The lifecycle would be:

1. Allocate and write new KV blocks in the policy's first/highest tier.
2. Keep partially filled blocks in that tier.
3. When a completed block becomes old enough, allocate a page in the next configured tier.
4. Quantize/copy the block asynchronously.
5. Atomically update its logical-to-physical mapping.
6. Release the source page after the migration completes.
7. Never promote a quantized block to a higher precision unless an original higher-precision copy is still available.

Each block would normally move only in one direction through the configured tier list:

```text
tier[0] -> tier[1] -> ... -> tier[n - 1]
```

Concrete examples:

```text
BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4
FP8 -> NVFP4
BF16 -> NVFP4
```

Attention could initially be implemented as one attention operation per non-empty tier, followed by an LSE-aware merge of the partial attention states. A later optimized implementation could process all contiguous age segments in one mixed-tier online-softmax kernel.

## Suggested MVP

A smaller first implementation could support:

- a generic two-tier policy;
- an absolute recent window;
- completed-block demotion only;
- Triton attention backend only;
- decode workloads;
- no prefix caching;
- no speculative decoding.

The first validated pair could be:

```text
newest 4,096 tokens: BF16
all older tokens: FP8 E4M3
```

The abstraction should not assume that this is the only valid pair. A subsequent backend-supported policy could be:

```text
newest 4,096 tokens: FP8 E4M3
all older tokens: NVFP4
```

This would allow the project to measure:

1. quality relative to the corresponding uniform highest-tier format;
2. quantization and migration overhead;
3. decode latency and memory-bandwidth changes;
4. scheduler and allocator complexity;
5. whether multi-pass attention is fast enough before implementing a fused kernel;
6. whether the same abstraction works correctly for both BF16-based and FP8-based policies.

## Important design questions

### Supported precision graph

The cache policy should be validated against backend-supported conversions.

Examples may include:

```text
BF16 -> FP8
BF16 -> NVFP4
FP8 -> NVFP4
BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4
```

The core interface should remain generic enough for future lower-precision formats, while each attention backend advertises the tier combinations and conversion paths it actually supports.

### Prefix caching

A shared prefix block can have different logical ages for different requests. For an MVP, progressive quantization could be declared incompatible with prefix caching.

Possible later policies include:

- shared prefix blocks are always stored in the lowest configured tier;
- copy-on-write when a request requires a different precision;
- store precision as a property of the physical shared block rather than each request.

### Pool sizing and scheduling

The scheduler would need to account for capacity separately for each configured tier.

When a higher-precision pool is full, it could first demote eligible blocks into the next configured tier. If that tier is full, the scheduler could continue cascading demotions through the policy before preempting a request.

This logic should operate over a generic ordered tier list rather than hardcoded BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 pool names.

### Block boundaries

Precision transitions should happen only at KV block boundaries. Requested percentages or token windows therefore need to be rounded according to the configured block size.

### Backend support

The supported tier combinations would depend on attention backend and hardware capabilities. A backend may initially expose only BF16 + FP8, while another may also support FP8 + NVFP4 or BF16 + FP8 + NVFP4.

### Accuracy evaluation

Each progressive policy should be benchmarked against its corresponding uniform highest-tier cache.

Useful comparisons include:

- uniform BF16 vs BF16 -> FP8;
- uniform BF16 vs BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4;
- uniform BF16 vs BF16 -> NVFP4;
- uniform FP8 vs FP8 -> NVFP4;
- uniform NVFP4 vs future NVFP4-based lower-precision policies;
- multiple recent-window sizes;
- percentage-based versus fixed-size windows.

Possible metrics include perplexity, long-context retrieval accuracy, task accuracy, TTFT, ITL, throughput, migration bandwidth, and peak KV-cache memory.

## Expected behavior when disabled

The feature should be opt-in. Existing uniform KV-cache configurations and their allocation, scheduling, and kernel paths should remain unchanged when no progressive policy is configured.

---

## Alternatives

### Uniform single-format KV cache

Uniform BF16, FP8, or NVFP4 cache is simpler to allocate and execute, but it uses the same format for every token regardless of age.

Each of these formats should also be considered a possible highest or lowest tier in a progressive policy rather than only as an alternative to the feature.

For example:

```text
uniform BF16 reference -> progressive BF16 + FP8 or BF16 + FP8 + NVFP4
uniform FP8 reference  -> progressive FP8 + NVFP4
uniform NVFP4 reference -> future progressive NVFP4 + lower format
```

### Layer-wise mixed precision

Related to #22195.

Layer-wise mixed precision assigns formats based on transformer layer sensitivity. This is complementary to the proposed feature: recency-based quantization assigns formats based on the age of blocks within each layer.

Both approaches could eventually be combined, but supporting both dimensions in an initial implementation would substantially increase allocator and kernel complexity.

### Sparse KV-cache eviction

Related to #5751.

Sparse eviction reduces memory by removing selected KV entries. Progressive quantization retains all tokens and instead changes their storage precision.

The approaches are complementary but have different correctness and kernel requirements.

### CPU or remote KV-cache offloading

Related to #33526.

Offloading moves older blocks out of GPU memory. It can save more HBM, but retrieving an offloaded block adds data-transfer latency. Progressive quantization keeps all configured precision tiers in GPU memory and targets reduced storage and attention bandwidth.

Offloading could eventually be represented as an additional terminal tier, but it is not required for the initial precision-tier abstraction.

### Application-level context truncation or retrieval

Applications can truncate old messages, summarize conversation history, or use retrieval to reconstruct relevant context. These techniques change the model input and are not a transparent replacement for retaining the full KV cache.

---

## Additional context

Related issues and roadmap items:

- #22195 — layer-wise mixed-precision KV-cache configuration
- #32220 — NVFP4 KV-cache support
- #5751 — sparse KV-cache framework
- #33526 — progressive KV-cache CPU onloading
- #48168 — Q3 2026 roadmap, including production KV-cache compression

This proposal is intentionally narrower than a general sparse-cache or tiered-offloading framework. The key requested abstraction is the ability for blocks belonging to the same attention layer to use different storage formats based on block age.

The proposed `20% BF16 / 20% FP8 / 60% NVFP4` policy is only one illustrative configuration. The implementation should also support policies whose highest tier is already quantized, such as `20% FP8 / 80% NVFP4`.

The policy should therefore be modeled as an ordered list:

```text
[(format, age range), ...]
```

rather than as a special BF16 cache with optional quantized older blocks.

Feedback would be especially useful on whether this should be implemented as:

1. an extension of the existing KV-cache specification and allocator;
2. a specialized cache manager;
3. an attention-backend capability;
4. or part of a more general KV-cache compression policy interface.

title: [Feature]: Support fast weight updates from disk
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

vLLM currently uses layerwise reloading while updating weights during RL training without recompilation:  
https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/training/layerwise/#what-is-layerwise-reloading

This currently assumes that weights for a given layer are loaded in order because the layerwise reloading logic allocates buffers per layer:

https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/training/layerwise/#troubleshooting-excessive-memory-usage

There can be excessive memory usage when weights are received out of order. 

In some use-cases like disaggregated RL, it is desirable to update weights from disk. In this case, it would be good to leverage GPU Direct Storage to directly load weights into GPU memory. 

Users would like to do something like:

```
# in gpu_worker.py
from vllm.model_executor.model_loader.weight_utils import fastsafetensors_weights_iterator

self.model.load_weights(fastsafetensors_weights_iterator(files, use_tqdm_on_load=False))
```

However, the current `fastsafetensors` iterator will lead to large temporary memory allocation due to out of order loading. 

For Qwen 3.5 35B, I saw temporary memory grow to > 40 GB due to the out of order loading issue, with warnings like:

title: [Feature][KV-offloading]: Relax Offloading Block Size asserts
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Setting offloading block size for some models like, 
- deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and
- google/gemma-4-31B-it

trips the assert https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/1ff9429655f01c804a7b17412144323e804f1324/vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py#L547 
This is the "all kv groups must have the same block size" assert.

How to run, 

### Deepseek V4 
```
MODEL="deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash"
DSV4_EXTRA="--kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 256 --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v4 --tool-call-parser deepseek_v4 --enable-auto-tool-choice --reasoning-parser deepseek_v4"
TP_SIZE=4
CPU_BYTES=26843545600

KV_TRANSFER_CONFIG=$(cat <<EOF
{
  "kv_connector": "OffloadingConnector",
  "kv_role": "kv_both",
  "kv_connector_extra_config": {
    "block_size": 512,
    "spec_name": "CPUOffloadingSpec",
    "cpu_bytes_to_use": ${CPU_BYTES},
    "eviction_policy": "lru"
  }
}
EOF
)

vllm serve "${MODEL}" \
      --tensor-parallel-size="${TP_SIZE}" \
      --kv-transfer-config "${KV_TRANSFER_CONFIG}" \
      --enable-prefix-caching \
      --no-disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager \
      ${DSV4_EXTRA} \
      --port 8000
```

### Gemma4
```
MODEL="google/gemma-4-31B-it"
TP_SIZE=2
CPU_BYTES=26843545600

KV_TRANSFER_CONFIG=$(cat <<EOF
{
  "kv_connector": "OffloadingConnector",
  "kv_role": "kv_both",
  "kv_connector_extra_config": {
    "block_size": 512,
    "spec_name": "CPUOffloadingSpec",
    "cpu_bytes_to_use": ${CPU_BYTES},
    "eviction_policy": "lru"
  }
}
EOF
)

vllm serve "${MODEL}" \
      --tensor-parallel-size="${TP_SIZE}" \
      --kv-transfer-config "${KV_TRANSFER_CONFIG}" \
      --enable-prefix-caching \
      --no-disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager \
      --port 8000
```

Request: 
This feature request is to relax the assertion allowing models with disparate KV group block sizes to still accommodate/align on a common offloading block size. 

Motivation: 
This is important for disk offloading as we very quickly hit the IOPs bottleneck with large quantities of small file read/writes. Relaxing the assert lets the user tune the offloading block size per their disk capacity. 


### Alternatives

The users can still set the top-level GPU block size and benefit that way. But this is not ideal and is not supported by all models. For example, setting the gpu block size to anything other than 256 for deepseek-v4-flash hits the assert, https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/1ff9429655f01c804a7b17412144323e804f1324/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/attn_utils.py#L221 . No issues with gemma4 when setting this.

title: [Feature]: [Batch-Invariant-Kernels] GDN_ATTN does not support batch-invariant mode for Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6 GDN models
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Summary

I would like to request (and offer to implement) batch-invariant compute support for the `GDN_ATTN` backend used by public Qwen GDN architectures.

Today, `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` is unsupported for these models. The `GDN_ATTN` backend inherits the default `supports_batch_invariance() = False`, so vLLM correctly rejects these models during engine initialization rather than running them under an unsupported BIC path.

I validated the current support boundary with:

- `Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B`
- `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`
- vLLM `0.25.1`

As a control, `Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct` works for a small image-request BIC smoke test with `tp=1` and `tp=2`. The unsupported path appears when moving to Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6 architectures that include GDN layers.

## Motivation

My motivation is to help extend BIC coverage to newer hybrid/GDN architectures used in VLA-style models. We do large scale post-training of models in this family and would like to contribute upstream support for bitwise-deterministic serving paths where possible, starting from public Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6 validation cases rather than any private model-specific setup.

## Public validation cases

### Small public repro

```bash
VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 \
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len 4096 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.80 \
  --trust-remote-code
```

Current behavior:

```text
Resolved architecture: Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration
Using backend AttentionBackendEnum.FLASH_ATTN for vit attention
Using FlashInfer GDN prefill kernel (requested=auto, head_k_dim=128).
Using FLASH_ATTN attention backend out of potential backends: ['FLASH_ATTN', 'TRITON_ATTN', 'FLEX_ATTENTION'].
Loading weights took 0.37 seconds
Model loading took 1.72 GiB memory and 7.535573 seconds
RuntimeError: VLLM batch_invariant mode is not supported for GDN_ATTN.
```

### Larger public repro

```bash
VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 \
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 \
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --max-model-len 4096 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --max-num-seqs 32 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --mm-encoder-tp-mode data \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --safetensors-load-strategy prefetch
```

Current behavior:

```text
Resolved architecture: Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration
Using backend AttentionBackendEnum.FLASH_ATTN for vit attention
Using FlashInfer GDN prefill kernel (requested=auto, head_k_dim=128).
Using FLASH_ATTN attention backend out of potential backends: ['FLASH_ATTN', 'TRITON_ATTN', 'FLEX_ATTENTION'].
Loading weights took 11.58 seconds
Model loading took 33.27 GiB memory and 42.684858 seconds
RuntimeError: VLLM batch_invariant mode is not supported for GDN_ATTN.
```

## Implementation starting points

Potential places to start:

- [`vllm/v1/attention/selector.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/attention/selector.py): contains the BIC support check for Mamba/GDN-style attention backends.
- [`vllm/v1/attention/backends/gdn_attn.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/attention/backends/gdn_attn.py): defines `GDNAttentionBackend`, which reports `GDN_ATTN`.
- [`vllm/v1/attention/backend.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/attention/backend.py): defines the default `supports_batch_invariance() = False` behavior inherited by unsupported backends.
- [`vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/gdn/qwen_gdn_linear_attn.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/gdn/qwen_gdn_linear_attn.py): Qwen GDN implementation path selected during the validation runs.

The validation logs show this path selecting the GDN prefill backend:

```text
Using FlashInfer GDN prefill kernel (requested=auto, head_k_dim=128).
```

## Requested support

Add BIC support for `GDN_ATTN` so Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6 GDN models can run under `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`.

A conservative implementation path could be:

1. Add a public validation harness using `Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B`.
2. Validate deterministic solo-vs-batched behavior for the supported GDN backend/backend combination.
3. Enable `supports_batch_invariance()` only for the GDN path that passes those invariance checks.
4. Document any remaining unsupported GDN backend combinations explicitly.

## Environment

- vLLM: `0.25.1`
- GPU: NVIDIA H100 80GB
- CUDA runtime as packaged in the vLLM environment
- Models:
  - `Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B`
  - `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`

## Question

Would a contribution adding `GDN_ATTN` batch-invariance support be welcome?

I am happy to start with a small public validation harness using `Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B`, then narrow the implementation to the supported GDN backend path. A first pass could be conservative, for example enabling BIC only for the GDN backend/backend combination that passes invariance checks, rather than broadly marking all GDN paths as supported.

title: [Feature]: Support response_format=diarized_json for OpenMOSS Transcribe-Diarize
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

OpenMOSS Transcribe-Diarize already exposes speaker diarization through the OpenAI-compatible "/v1/audio/transcriptions" endpoint. However, diarization is currently returned using the Whisper-style "verbose_json" response format.

It would be useful for vLLM to also support OpenAI's dedicated "response_format=diarized_json", used by "gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize", while keeping "verbose_json" for backward compatibility.

Motivation

Supporting "diarized_json" would:

- improve compatibility with the official OpenAI API;
- allow applications to switch between OpenAI and vLLM without custom response conversion;
- allow OpenAI SDK users to receive the existing "TranscriptionDiarized" type directly;
- make libraries built around the OpenAI diarization contract work with vLLM out of the box.

Example request:

```python
transcription = client.audio.transcriptions.create(
    model="OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize",
    file=audio_file,
    response_format="diarized_json",
)
```

The OpenAI Python SDK represents this response using "TranscriptionDiarized", with the transcription text, duration, and diarized segments:

```json
{
  "text": "Hello. Hi, how are you?",
  "duration": 6.1,
  "segments": [
    {
      "type": "transcript.text.segment",
      "id": "segment_0",
      "start": 0.0,
      "end": 2.8,
      "text": "Hello.",
      "speaker": "A"
    },
    {
      "type": "transcript.text.segment",
      "id": "segment_1",
      "start": 2.8,
      "end": 6.1,
      "text": "Hi, how are you?",
      "speaker": "B"
    }
  ]
}
```

Since OpenMOSS Transcribe-Diarize already produces speaker and timestamp information, this could be implemented as an additional response serializer without changing the existing transcription pipeline.

"verbose_json" should remain supported for existing users, with "diarized_json" added as an OpenAI-compatible alternative.

title: [Feature]:  Proposal for an Automated Request Validation and Normalization Module at the Upstream of vLLM (Hard Interception) to Fundamentally Solve DSML Leakage, Garbled Output, and Empty Responses
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Your current environment

Inference Framework: vllm-ascend 0.24.0
LLM: DeepSeek-V4 (Flash & Pro)

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Overview

This issue proposes a systematic improvement: add an **automated request body validation and normalization module** at the very upstream of vLLM's request processing pipeline (e.g., API gateway or `/v1/chat/completions` entry point). This module upgrades the current "soft interception" (relying on system prompts) to a **hard interception** based on Python hard-coded logic, fundamentally eliminating DSML leakage, tag corruption, empty outputs, and other issues caused by illegal request bodies.

---

## Background and Problem Statement

### Case 1: Non‑standard Request Body Format Leading to DSML Leakage

**Case Link**: [Detailed analysis of Case 1](https://3ms.huawei.com/km/groups/3959141/blogs/details/22374443?l=zh-cn&moduleId=1047283487341719552) *(internal link)*

**Root Cause**: The request body does not follow the vLLM official Tool Calling standard format – the functions to be called are not registered in the `tools` dictionary.  
- The model cannot recognize the tool call format and fails to generate structured outputs via constrained decoding.  
- DSML tags (e.g., `<| DSML |>`) leak into the `content` field.  
- Function calls are missed, causing the expected tool invocation functionality to fail.

**Solution**: Manually normalize the request body according to the official standard, i.e., correctly place function definitions into the `tools` array.

### Case 2: Fundamental Defects of the System Prompt “Soft Interception”

**Case Link**: [Detailed analysis of Case 2](https://3ms.huawei.com/km/groups/3959141/blogs/details/22379454?l=zh-cn&moduleId=1047283487341719552) *(internal link)*

**Root Cause**: Currently, the industry (including DS official APIs) commonly uses system prompts as a “soft interception” for illegal requests. However, this approach has fatal flaws:  
1. **Instruction Priority Conflict**: When the request body contains `response_format={"type": "json_object"}` or `tool_choice: "auto"`   with thinking mode or other unknown illegal requests, the structured decoding constraint or tool invocation directive takes higher priority than the system prompt, causing the validation logic in the system prompt to be overridden or “swallowed”.  
2. **Inability to Cover All Bad Cases**: For some extreme illegal request bodies (e.g., combinations of multiple high‑priority parameters), the system prompt fails to intercept, and the illegal request reaches the core inference engine, leading to tag leakage, empty outputs, etc.  
3. **Extra Token Overhead**: The system prompt occupies context length and computational resources as part of the input.

**Experimental Verification**: Local reproduction using a system prompt successfully intercepted most illegal request bodies, but failed on a few extreme cases – exactly matching the behavior of the DS official API. This confirms that the DS official API uses a similar system prompt mechanism and also exposes its fundamental limitation.

---

## Proposed Improvement: From “Soft Interception” to “Hard Interception”

### Core Idea

Add a **Python‑hardcoded request body validation and normalization module** at the very upstream of vLLM’s request processing pipeline (e.g., API gateway or `/v1/chat/completions` entry). Before the request enters the inference chain, the module performs the following:

1. **Legality Validation**: Detect whether the request body conforms to the OpenAI‑compatible `/v1/chat/completions` interface standard.  
2. **Automatic Normalization**: Automatically fix non‑standard request bodies, including but not limited to:  
   - Check whether the `tools` field exists and is correctly formatted; if missing, attempt to extract function call information from `messages` and auto‑populate.  
   - Check the combination of `response_format` and `tool_choice`; if conflicting, adjust according to priority rules.  
   - Filter or escape illegal characters, empty characters, or unregistered DSML tags.  
   - Check each `content` field in `messages` for emptiness, garbled text, or excessive length.  
3. **Reject Irreparable Requests**: For extreme illegal requests that cannot be automatically fixed, directly return `400 Bad Request` to prevent them from entering the inference pipeline (exactly what  the DS offical API does).

### Three Core Advantages

#### 1. Cost Reduction (Reduce Token Overhead)
- **Current Solution**: The system prompt occupies extra context as a pre‑processing instruction, consuming tokens for every request.  
- **Improved Solution**: Request body validation and normalization are performed by Python code outside the inference pipeline, **zero token overhead**.

#### 2. Efficiency Increase (Improve Inference Throughput)
- **Current Solution**: The system prompt forces the model to process additional validation logic, consuming model computational resources; the KV cache generated by the system prompt also occupies GPU memory.  
- **Improved Solution**: Validation logic is executed efficiently on CPU, **consuming no manual efforts or GPU compute resources or memory**, thus improving overall hardware utilization. Moreover, normalized request bodies are more uniform, leading to higher inference efficiency.

#### 3. Quality Assurance (Fundamental Solution)
- **Current Solution**: The system prompt risks being overridden or “swallowed” by illegal requests (e.g., `response_format` or `tool_choice` high‑priority parameters), causing validation failure.  
- **Improved Solution**: Validation occurs **outside the inference pipeline**; every input is processed **before** entering the formal inference chain. This fundamentally prevents the validation logic from being overridden or skipped. All illegal requests are intercepted or fixed before reaching the model, **completely eliminating DSML leakage, garbled output, empty responses, etc.**

---

### Alternatives

## Technical Implementation Suggestions

### Module Location

Add a pre‑processing hook in the request handler of vLLM’s `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint. For example:

```python
# vllm/entrypoints/openai/api_server.py or similar
# Insert pre‑processing before the request enters LLMEngine
```

### Validation and Normalization Rules (Based on Bad Cases from Case 2)

1. **Check `tools` field**  
   - If `tool_choice` is `auto` or `required` but `tools` is missing or empty, return `400` or attempt to extract from `messages`.  
   - If function definitions in `tools` do not conform to JSON Schema, auto‑fix or reject.

2. **Check combination of `response_format` and `tool_choice`**  
   - If both `response_format: {"type": "json_object"}` and `tool_choice: "auto"` are set, adjust according to priority rules (e.g., prioritize `response_format`, or return an error asking the user to choose one).

3. **Check illegal content in `messages`**  
   - Detect and filter DSML tags like `<tool_call>`, `<function_call>` (unless properly registered in `tools`).  
   - Detect and filter empty characters, garbled text, or overly long content.  
   - Check if `system` role messages have been overridden or tampered with by user messages.

4. **Check combination of `tool_choice` and thinking mode**  
   - If both thinking mode (e.g., `thinking: true`) and `tool_choice: "auto"` are enabled, return an error instructing the user to select only one mode.

### Return Values

- **Valid request**: Pass through to the inference pipeline.  
- **Fixable invalid request**: Automatically normalize and pass through, logging the repair operation.  
- **Unfixable invalid request**: Return `400 Bad Request` with a detailed error message guiding the user on how to correct the request body.

---

## Summary

This issue proposes a **hard interception** solution that fundamentally improves upon the current **soft interception** (system prompt). By decoupling request body validation and normalization from the model inference pipeline, we achieve:  
- **Zero token overhead** – no context length consumed.  
- ** Zero manual efforts** – no manually requests normalization.
- **Zero GPU compute consumption** – no model compute resources or memory wasted.  
- **100% coverage of all bad cases** – fundamentally preventing the system prompt from being overridden or skipped.

This solution not only completely resolves the DSML leakage problem in vLLM’s Tool Calling scenarios but also provides a more robust request protection mechanism for the entire inference system, improving system stability and reliability for the long-lasting future ecosystem.

**It is recommended to add this feature as an optional configuration item (e.g., `--enable-request-validation`) in a future vLLM release, allowing users to enable it on demand.**

---


### Additional context

## References

- [Case 1: DSML Leakage Due to Non‑standard Request Body and Its Root Solution](https://3ms.huawei.com/km/groups/3959141/blogs/details/22374443?l=zh-cn&moduleId=1047283487341719552) *(internal link)*  
- [Case 2: Analysis of Fundamental Defects of System Prompt “Soft Interception”](https://3ms.huawei.com/km/groups/3959141/blogs/details/22379454?l=zh-cn&moduleId=1047283487341719552) *(internal link)*  
- [vLLM Tool Calling Official Documentation](https://docs.vllm.com.cn/en/latest/features/tool_calling/)

body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

In reference to PR [https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46754](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46754) ROCM_ATTN in vLLM currently does not support PrefixLM attention paths that consume mm_range_tensors. This support exists in other attention paths such as NVIDIA FA4 on sm100 and Triton Unified Attention, and is required for correctness in multimodal models that rely on `mm_range_tensors`

Right now these cases need to defer to Triton for correctness, but the requested feature is to add native support on the vLLM ROCM_ATTN side so AMD ROCm users can run these PrefixLM multimodal workloads correctly while still using optimized ROCm attention kernels.

This request is specifically for the vLLM ROCM_ATTN backend. ROCM_UNIFIED_AITER_ATTN / AITER support is tracked separately in `ROCm/aiter#4168` and should not block native ROCM_ATTN support in vLLM. [ https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/issues/4168](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/issues/4168)

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

**Enable support for jina-embeddings-v2-small-en  https://huggingface.co/jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-small-en**

Hugging Face Link: https://huggingface.co/jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-small-en

Model Architecture: JinaBertForMaskedLM / JinaBertModel

The model architecture JinaBertForMaskedLM is not currently supported. I manually verified this in the source code (model_executor/models/registry.py) and confirmed that this architecture is not listed among the supported models.

The server fails during the model loading phase and terminates with the following error:

`ValueError: Model architectures ['JinaBertForMaskedLM'] are not supported for now.
`
old ticket: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/38633

To support this model family, vLLM needs to handle two non-standard features in the JinaBert architecture:

- ALiBi positional embeddings instead of BERT's standard absolute position embeddings. vLLM already supports ALiBi in several models 

```
"position_embedding_type": "alibi",
"max_position_embeddings": 8192
```

- GeGLU feed-forward layers instead of standard BERT FFN. vLLM already has GeluAndMul in activation.py and bert_with_rope.py handles geglu for BERT variants 
```
"feed_forward_type": "geglu",
"hidden_act": "gelu",
"intermediate_size": 2048
```

title: [RFC][Feature]: First-class session id for conversation aware routing
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

# vLLM Session Identity Roadmap

This plan is for plumbing session-aware identity into vLLM such that it is available for:
(1) consumption by external routing / serving frameworks. **This proposal is specifically for Dynamo integration**.
(2) vLLM-internal scheduling optimizations for agentic workflows

## Goal

Dynamo already extracts session identity from headers into `PreprocessedRequest.agent_context.session_id` and can use it in the Dynamo router. The missing piece is that vLLM needs a typed request-level session identity that engine internals, KV connectors, cache policy, or schedulers can consume without overloading `request_id` or hiding identity in `SamplingParams.extra_args`.

The target flow is:

```text
X-Dynamo-Session-ID / normalized agent session header
  -> Dynamo AgentContext.session_id
  -> Dynamo router session-aware behavior
  -> vLLM typed request-level session identity
  -> vLLM KV/cache/scheduler/connectors can optionally consume it
```

This is deliberately not:

```text
Dynamo session routing
  -> vLLM router feature
```

vLLM should receive stable request metadata. Dynamo should continue to own cluster-level routing.

## Current Context

- vLLM PR `vllm-project/vllm#46547` and commit [aac37e94](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/aac37e94ccae81382423f0449c5ed52f27f24fab#diff-60dbf8f976bb75c15f59e23e8c760dff094523375c9ef90cf78e1264c7f101a9) is the current vLLM-side workaround. They plumb `session_id` from HTTP headers `X-Session-ID` or `X-Correlation-ID` as `SamplingParams.extra_args["session_id"]` and forward that into Mooncake metadata.
- SGLang PR `sgl-project/sglang#29436` is useful reference for making `session_id` request-level engine state.
- `request_id` remains per-request and should keep its existing lifecycle semantics for aborts, output routing, scheduler maps, and request-local bookkeeping.
- `session_id` is stable across related requests in one conversation, agent run, or session.

## Proposal

Add a first-class scalar `session_id: str | None` to vLLM's request path.

The key design rule is:

```python
request.session_id
```

not:

```python
request.sampling_params.extra_args["session_id"]
```

`SamplingParams.extra_args["session_id"]` can remain a temporary compatibility input for existing experimental users, but it should not be the stable engine contract.

## Ingress Paths

There are two distinct ways session identity can reach vLLM.

When a client calls vLLM directly:

```text
OpenAI body session_id or HTTP X-Session-ID
  -> vLLM OpenAI serving layer
  -> vLLM EngineCoreRequest.session_id
  -> vLLM Request.session_id
```

When a client calls Dynamo first:

```text
HTTP X-Dynamo-Session-ID / normalized agent session header
  -> Dynamo AgentContext.session_id
  -> Dynamo router
  -> Dynamo vLLM backend calls vLLM with session_id=<AgentContext.session_id>
  -> vLLM EngineCoreRequest.session_id
  -> vLLM Request.session_id
```

The Dynamo bridge carries Dynamo's already-normalized session identity into vLLM. vLLM does not read the original client HTTP header in that path because it is behind Dynamo and receives an internal backend call.

## vLLM Public Ingress

Add optional `session_id` to the OpenAI-compatible request models:

```text
vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/protocol.py
vllm/entrypoints/openai/completion/protocol.py
vllm/entrypoints/openai/responses/protocol.py
```

Suggested field:

```python
session_id: str | None = Field(
    default=None,
    description=(
        "Stable session identity shared by related requests. Unlike request_id, "
        "this value is expected to remain stable across multiple requests in "
        "the same conversation or agent session."
    ),
)
```

Resolve the effective session id in the serving layer, not inside `SamplingParams`:

```text
vllm/entrypoints/generate/base/serving.py
vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/serving.py
vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/batch_serving.py
vllm/entrypoints/openai/completion/serving.py
vllm/entrypoints/openai/responses/serving.py
```

Suggested precedence:

```text
request.session_id
  > X-Session-ID
  > X-Correlation-ID, if maintainers want to preserve compatibility with PR #46547
  > request.vllm_xargs["session_id"], as temporary compatibility only
```

Maintainer sanity checks:

- Should `X-Correlation-ID` be accepted at all, or should vLLM use only `X-Session-ID`?
- Should body `session_id` always win over headers?
- Should conflicting body/header/xargs values be ignored by precedence or rejected?

## vLLM Engine API

Add `session_id` beside existing non-sampling request controls like `priority`, `trace_headers`, and `data_parallel_rank`:

```text
vllm/engine/protocol.py
vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py
vllm/v1/engine/llm_engine.py
vllm/v1/engine/input_processor.py
vllm/v1/engine/__init__.py
vllm/v1/request.py
```

Expected shape:

```python
AsyncLLM.generate(..., session_id: str | None = None)
AsyncLLM.add_request(..., session_id: str | None = None)
LLMEngine.add_request(..., session_id: str | None = None)
InputProcessor.process_inputs(..., session_id: str | None = None)
EngineCoreRequest.session_id: str | None
Request.session_id: str | None
```

Where `EngineCoreRequest` is converted into internal `Request`, copy the field:

```text
EngineCoreRequest.session_id -> Request.session_id
```

The current vLLM path includes:

```text
vllm/v1/engine/core.py
vllm/v1/request.py
```

For parallel sampling / child requests, preserve the parent request's `session_id` on every child request. `request_id` should still remain unique per child request.

For beam search, preserve the same `session_id` across the generated one-token subrequests:

```text
vllm/entrypoints/generate/beam_search/online.py
```

## vLLM Native / Offline API

The first PR can expose `session_id` through engine APIs and OpenAI serving first. Ask maintainers whether native/offline callers should also get parity immediately.

Possible follow-up surfaces:

```text
vllm/entrypoints/llm.py
vllm/inputs/engine.py
vllm/inputs/llm.py
vllm/inputs/preprocess.py
```

Two plausible native/offline designs:

- Add a `session_id: list[str | None] | None` argument to `LLM.generate`, analogous to per-prompt `priority`.
- Allow `session_id` in `EngineInput`, analogous to `cache_salt`.

Do not include this in the first patch unless maintainers ask for direct/offline parity.

## vLLM Rust Server / Engine-Core Client

Mirror the field in the Rust request path if the Rust server/client path is in scope:

```text
rust/src/server/src/utils.rs
rust/src/server/src/routes/openai/chat_completions/types.rs
rust/src/server/src/routes/openai/chat_completions/convert.rs
rust/src/server/src/routes/openai/completions/types.rs
rust/src/server/src/routes/openai/completions/convert.rs
rust/src/server/src/routes/inference/generate/convert.rs
rust/src/server/src/routes/tokenize/types.rs
rust/src/server/src/grpc/convert.rs
rust/src/text/src/request.rs
rust/src/text/src/lower.rs
rust/src/chat/src/request.rs
rust/src/chat/src/lib.rs
rust/src/llm/src/request.rs
rust/src/engine-core-client/src/protocol/request.rs
```

`rust/src/engine-core-client/src/protocol/request.rs` is especially important because it defines the Rust-side `EngineCoreRequest` that serializes compatibly with Python's `EngineCoreRequest`.

Add the new field with a default so older callers that omit it keep working:

```rust
#[serde(default)]
pub session_id: Option<String>,
```

In Rust HTTP/OpenAI lowering, use the same effective precedence as Python:

```text
request.session_id
  > X-Session-ID
  > X-Correlation-ID
  > request.vllm_xargs["session_id"]
```

The gRPC proto can be handled as a follow-up if maintainers want body-level gRPC parity. In the first patch, the Rust gRPC path can leave `session_id` unset unless the proto is already being changed for adjacent work.

## vLLM Consumers

Move consumers toward:

```python
request.session_id
```

and away from:

```python
request.sampling_params.extra_args["session_id"]
```

For the Mooncake work from PR `#46547`, the relevant files are:

```text
vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/store/scheduler.py
vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/store/data.py
```

The first consumer update can use:

```python
session_id = request.session_id
if session_id is None:
    session_id = request.sampling_params.extra_args.get("session_id")
```

The fallback should be treated as temporary compatibility for older `vllm_xargs` callers.

## vLLM Tests

Add focused tests for:

- OpenAI body `session_id` is accepted for chat, completions, and responses.
- `X-Session-ID` is accepted by the OpenAI serving path.
- Header/body/xargs precedence is deterministic.
- `EngineCoreRequest.session_id` survives serialization and reaches `Request.session_id`.
- Parallel sampling children preserve `session_id` while retaining distinct request ids.
- Beam search subrequests preserve `session_id`.
- Mooncake metadata receives the typed `request.session_id` once consumers are updated.
- Existing `extra_args` / `vllm_xargs` behavior is not broken.

Likely test areas:

```text
tests/entrypoints/openai/
tests/v1/engine/
tests/v1/worker/
rust/src/engine-core-client/src/tests/
rust/src/server/src/routes/tests.rs
rust/src/server/src/grpc/tests.rs, if gRPC body-level parity is included
```

## vLLM Maintainer Questions

- Should vLLM accept `X-Correlation-ID` as a session identity input at all, or should this PR use only `X-Session-ID`?
- Is the desired precedence `request.session_id > X-Session-ID > X-Correlation-ID > request.vllm_xargs["session_id"]`? (see `serving.py` `_get_session_id()`)
- Should conflicting body/header/xargs values be ignored by precedence or rejected with a clear error?
- Should native/offline `LLM.generate` expose `session_id` in this PR, or should direct/offline API parity be a follow-up?
- Should PR 1 include the Rust frontend HTTP/OpenAI surface, or should it only add Python ingress plus the shared typed engine/protocol plumbing and leave Rust frontend parity to a separate Rust frontend PR?
- If Rust frontend HTTP/OpenAI parity is included, should it mirror the Python body/header/xargs precedence exactly?
- Should gRPC body-level `session_id` be added now, or should the Rust gRPC converter leave `session_id` unset until a proto follow-up?

## Dynamo Follow-Up

Current Dynamo behavior:

Relevant PRs:

- [ai-dynamo/dynamo#10875](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/10875) is the merged implementation for header-based session affinity and the `X-Dynamo-Session-ID` behavior below.

```text
X-Dynamo-Session-ID
  -> AgentContext.session_id
  -> SessionAffinityId
```

These two Dynamo objects have different lifecycles and consumers:

```text
AgentContext.session_id
  -> stored in request Context under AGENT_CONTEXT_CONTEXT_KEY
  -> copied by preprocessor into PreprocessedRequest.agent_context
  -> visible to router/backend request logic

SessionAffinityId
  -> stored in request Context under SESSION_AFFINITY_CONTEXT_KEY
  -> consumed directly by session-affinity router/coordinator
  -> not copied into PreprocessedRequest.agent_context
```

Native agent headers, such as Codex `session-id`, Claude Code `x-claude-code-session-id`, and OpenCode `x-session-id`, currently populate `AgentContext.session_id`. They do not populate `SessionAffinityId`; hard session affinity is tied to the canonical `X-Dynamo-Session-ID` header.

The missing bridge is from Dynamo's backend-visible request identity into vLLM. Once vLLM has a typed field, Dynamo should pass `agent_context.session_id` into vLLM's typed `session_id` field instead of using `SamplingParams.extra_args["session_id"]` as the primary path.

Python vLLM backend:

```text
components/src/dynamo/vllm/handlers.py
components/src/dynamo/vllm/llm_engine.py
```

Add a small helper:

```python
def _session_id_for_vllm(request: Mapping[str, Any]) -> str | None:
    agent_context = request.get("agent_context")
    if isinstance(agent_context, Mapping):
        value = agent_context.get("session_id")
        if isinstance(value, str) and value:
            return value
    return None
```

Then pass it on every vLLM `generate` call:

```python
self.engine_client.generate(
    ...,
    session_id=_session_id_for_vllm(request),
)
```

Important call sites:

```text
components/src/dynamo/vllm/handlers.py
components/src/dynamo/vllm/llm_engine.py
```

Cover the normal generation path, decode worker path, prefill worker path, and local engine path.

Rust vLLM backend:

```text
lib/vllm-rs-backend/src/convert.rs
```

Map:

```rust
request.agent_context.as_ref().map(|ctx| ctx.session_id.clone())
```

into the vLLM `GenerateRequest` / `EngineCoreRequest` typed `session_id` field.

Add tests in:

```text
components/src/dynamo/vllm/tests/test_vllm_worker_handler.py
components/src/dynamo/vllm/tests/test_vllm_engine.py
lib/vllm-rs-backend/src/convert.rs
```

Test that `agent_context.session_id` reaches the engine call and that unrelated `extra_args` are preserved.

## Dynamo Compatibility Choice

During migration, Dynamo can optionally also populate `sampling_params.extra_args["session_id"]` for older vLLM versions. Avoid making that the long-term behavior.

If both a caller-provided vLLM `session_id` and Dynamo `agent_context.session_id` exist and disagree, prefer one explicit policy:

- strict policy: reject with a clear error
- permissive policy: Dynamo `agent_context.session_id` wins because the router already used it

For consistency between router and backend, the strict policy is easier to reason about.

## Future Extension

If vLLM maintainers want a broader home for non-sampling request metadata, this scalar field can later grow into a typed object, for example:

```python
class RequestMetadata(msgspec.Struct, omit_defaults=True):
    session_id: str | None = None
```

In that design, public request bodies can still expose top-level `session_id`, while the serving layer lowers it into `RequestMetadata(session_id=...)`. Avoid naming the public OpenAI field `metadata`; OpenAI-compatible APIs already use `metadata` for user/application metadata, especially Responses.

Potential future metadata fields could include tenant, cache namespace, parent session, session finality, or cache lineage. Do not include those in the first session-id PR unless maintainers explicitly ask for a broader metadata object.

## Suggested PR Split

### vLLM PR 1: Typed Session Identity Plumbing https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48048

- Add `session_id` as typed request-level state.
- Include OpenAI ingress, Python engine path, Rust server/client path, and tests.
- Keep legacy `vllm_xargs["session_id"]` only as compatibility input.
- Do not introduce new scheduling/cache policy.

### vLLM PR 2: Consumers Use Typed Session Identity

- Update Mooncake / KV connector consumers to read `request.session_id`.
- Preserve temporary fallback to `extra_args["session_id"]` if maintainers want migration compatibility.
- Add focused connector tests.

### Dynamo PR: Bridge AgentContext To vLLM

- Python backend: pass `agent_context.session_id` into vLLM generate calls.
- Rust backend: lower `PreprocessedRequest.agent_context.session_id` into vLLM `GenerateRequest`.
- Add tests proving Dynamo does not need to smuggle session identity through `SamplingParams.extra_args`.

## Non-Goals

- Do not add conversation-aware routing to vLLM's router.
- Do not overload `request_id`.
- Do not require SGLang-style `/open_session` lifecycle semantics.
- Do not make `SamplingParams.extra_args["session_id"]` the stable contract.
- Do not plumb Dynamo-only agent hints directly into vLLM unless there is a separate vLLM design discussion for them.

_No response_

title: [Feature]: Add Prometheus metrics for the multimodal preprocessing pipeline
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Motivation

When serving multimodal models, a non-trivial portion of Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) is spent in the APIServer process *before* the request reaches the engine: downloading media over HTTP/object storage, decoding images/video, resolving multi-modal items, and rendering + tokenizing the prompt.

Today this time is invisible. Per the [metrics docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/design/metrics/), `arrival_time` starts when tokenization begins, so all of the above is absorbed into TTFT. Operators serving vision/audio/video models cannot answer basic questions:

- Is high TTFT caused by slow media downloads, slow CPU decode, or the engine?
- Which media type (image/video/audio) dominates preprocessing cost?
- How does preprocessing latency scale with the number of media items per request?

### Current state

vLLM exposes rich engine-side metrics (TTFT, queue time, prefill/decode, KV cache, prefix cache, LoRA). However, there is **no metric** for:

- media download latency
- media decode (`load_bytes`) latency
- total `resolve_items` time per request
- total preprocessing (render + tokenize) time

The broader observability RFC #39979 (OpenTelemetry tracing) mentions "maybe add download for multimodal models" in passing but does not cover the preprocessing pipeline. This is a lighter, Prometheus-first addition that complements that RFC.

### Proposal

Add Histogram metrics in the APIServer (P0) process, independent of EngineCore (P1+) metrics:

| Metric | Scope | Labels |
|---|---|---|
| `vllm:mm_media_download_latency_seconds` | per media item | `media_type` |
| `vllm:mm_media_decode_latency_seconds` | per media item | `media_type` |
| `vllm:mm_download_bytes` | per media item | `media_type` |
| `vllm:mm_resolve_items_latency_seconds` | per request | — |
| `vllm:mm_preprocessing_total_latency_seconds` | per request batch (render+tokenize) | — |

**Why Histogram (not Gauge):** every observation is accumulated losslessly. A Gauge's `.set()` overwrites prior values between Prometheus scrapes, losing data under high QPS. Histogram supports `histogram_quantile(sum by (le)(...))` for cross-instance percentile aggregation; a recording rule can precompute the quantile for cheap dashboard queries.

**Instrumentation points:**

- `vllm/multimodal/media/connector.py` — `load_from_url` / `load_from_url_async` (HTTP/OSS/etc.), plus `_load_data_url` / `_load_file_url` decode timing
- `vllm/entrypoints/chat_utils.py` — `AsyncMultiModalItemTracker.resolve_items`
- `vllm/renderers/base.py` — `render_chat_async`

All metrics use lazy init and gracefully degrade if `prometheus_client` is unavailable. `time.monotonic()` overhead is ~50ns/call, off the GPU path.

### Ask

Would maintainers be open to this in core? Looking for feedback on:

- metric naming / label design (is `media_type` = `ImageMediaIO`/`VideoMediaIO` the right cardinality?)
- bucket choices
- namespace (`vllm:mm_*` vs something else)

Happy to open a PR if there's interest.

### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

title: [Feature]: Priority scheduling is not reflected in KV/prefix cache retention under cache pressure
body: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch I ran a minimal experiment to check whether the `priority` field in vLLM affects only request scheduling, or whether it is also considered by KV/prefix cache management. The result suggests that `priority` works for request scheduling, but does not appear to affect KV/prefix cache retention. Under KV cache pressure, high-priority requests are not protected from losing cached prompt tokens compared with low-priority requests. This may be expected behavior today, but it creates a gap for priority-based serving: high-priority requests can be scheduled earlier while still losing their KV cache benefit under memory pressure. ## Environment - vLLM version: `0.19.0` - Model: `Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` - GPU: NVIDIA A800 80GB - Dataset: MMLU validation split - Prefix caching enabled The KV cache was intentionally limited to create cache pressure: GPU KV cache size: 8,192 tokens ## Experiment Design The experiment has two parts. 1. Scheduling probe I first verified that `priority` affects request scheduling. Setup: - Submit 32 low-priority requests first. - Wait 0.5 seconds. - Submit 8 high-priority requests. - Use streaming completions and record first-token time. - `priority=0` is treated as high priority. - `priority=10` is treated as low priority. Result: high priority first-token range: 1.448s - 1.483s queued low-priority tail first-token range: 2.697s - 2.723s The high-priority requests, despite being submitted later, were scheduled before the tail of the low-priority queue. This confirms that priority scheduling is active. 2. KV/prefix cache retention probe Then I tested whether priority affects cache retention. Each trial has three phases: warm -> pressure -> probe - `warm`: send sentinel prompts A and B to populate prefix/KV cache. - `pressure`: send MMLU filler prompts to create KV cache pressure. - `probe`: send the same sentinel prompts again and inspect `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`. Two sentinel groups are used: - Group A - Group B For each pressure setting, I run two priority assignments: swap_priorities = false: A: high priority B: low priority swap_priorities = true: A: low priority B: high priority If KV cache retention uses request priority, then the group assigned high priority should retain more cached tokens after pressure. ## Observed Results No pressure control:pressure_count = 0 A:high cached_tokens = 1808 B:low cached_tokens = 1828 A:low cached_tokens = 1808 B:high cached_tokens = 1828 With cache pressure:pressure_count = 64 A:high cached_tokens = 1324 A:low cached_tokens = 1324 B:low cached_tokens = 1320 B:high cached_tokens = 1320 The cached token count follows the prompt group, not the assigned priority. Swapping priority between A and B does not change the number of retained cached tokens. ### Alternatives For priority-based serving, it would be useful if request priority could also influence KV/prefix cache retention or eviction. For example, under KV cache pressure, vLLM could optionally prefer retaining KV blocks associated with higher-priority requests, or expose a policy hook such as: --kv-cache-eviction-policy priority-aware or integrate request priority into the existing eviction score. ### Additional context ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Feature]: Support llmcompressor W8A8-FP8-Dynamic quantization for ModernBERT
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Summary

`vllm/model_executor/models/modernbert.py` currently does not thread
`quant_config` through its Linear layers. Loading a ModernBERT checkpoint
produced by `llmcompressor` with the `FP8_DYNAMIC` recipe fails with:

```
File ".../vllm/model_executor/models/modernbert.py", line 269, in load_weights
    param = params_dict[name]
KeyError: 'encoder_layer.layers.0.attn.Wo.weight_scale'
```

This issue proposes adding **W8A8-FP8-Dynamic** (per-channel weight, per-token
dynamic activation) support for ModernBERT by threading `quant_config` through
the encoder stack, mirroring the pattern already used in
`vllm/model_executor/models/bert.py`.

## Motivation

- ModernBERT is a widely used encoder-only backbone (classification /
  cross-encoder / embedding). FP8 gives measurable throughput gains on Ada
  (SM89, e.g. L20) and Hopper (SM90+) hardware without requiring to
  drop to smaller models.
- The compressed-tensors format produced by `llmcompressor` is the standard
  quantization path already supported by vLLM for many decoder models. Making
  it work for ModernBERT is a natural fit.

## Current failure point

`modernbert.py` has four Linear layers per encoder layer, none of which
receive `quant_config`:

| Layer | Current | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| `ModernBertAttention.Wqkv` | `QKVParallelLinear`, no `quant_config` | `weight_scale` not registered |
| `ModernBertAttention.Wo` | `RowParallelLinear`, no `quant_config` | same |
| `ModernBertMLP.Wi` | plain `nn.Linear` | does not go through vLLM linear at all |
| `ModernBertMLP.Wo` | `RowParallelLinear`, no `quant_config` | same |

`vllm_config.quant_config` is never accessed inside this file.

## Proposed scope (single PR)

- **In scope**:
  - TP=1 only
  - Scheme: `CompressedTensorsW8A8Fp8`
  - Thread `quant_config` through
    `ModernBertEncoderLayer → ModernBertLayer → {ModernBertAttention, ModernBertMLP}` and pass to all Linear
    constructors.
  - Replace `ModernBertMLP.Wi` (currently `nn.Linear`) with
    `ColumnParallelLinear` so it participates in the quantization pipeline.

- **Explicitly out of scope** (deferred to separate PRs):
  - TP > 1 (per-channel `weight_scale` sharding + fused-QKV/Wi shard
    semantics)
  - AWQ / GPTQ / INT8
  - Static-activation FP8 (checkpoint contains `input_scale`)
  - Group-wise / block-wise weight quantization

## Related work

- #43896 (open, needs rebase) — corrects `hf_to_vllm_mapper` and adds a
  `params_dict` skip safeguard in `load_weights`. Complementary to this
  proposal, not overlapping: #43896 does not thread `quant_config` or change
  any Linear type. Whichever merges first, the other rebases.

## Validation plan for the PR

1. Load a compressed-tensors ModernBERT checkpoint (llmcompressor
   `FP8_DYNAMIC`) and confirm `named_parameters()` exposes `.weight`,
   `.weight_scale` for all linears and no `.input_scale`.
2. Accuracy delta vs BF16 baseline on a held-out set.
3. Throughput delta vs BF16 baseline on identical workload.
4. Nsight kernel-name check to confirm FP8 CUTLASS kernels
   (`scaled_mm_c3x` / `sm89_fp8_*`) are actually dispatched.
5. BF16 loading path unchanged (regression check).

## Would love feedback on

1. Is TP=1-only an acceptable first PR, with TP>1 as follow-up? (I want to
   avoid ballooning the initial PR.)
2. Should `Wi` use `ColumnParallelLinear` or `MergedColumnParallelLinear`?
