title: [Performance]: Resize video frames while decoding to skip full-resolution copies
body:
### Proposal to improve performance **TL;DR:** Resize video frames right after decoding instead of in the HF processor. For Qwen3-VL on 1080p video: 10–60× smaller frame arrays, 35–46% less decode + processor time, 1.8–2.5× throughput when preprocessing-bound, and `pixel_values_videos` stays bit-identical. **Problem.** vLLM's video loaders keep every sampled frame at full resolution; the HF processor then copies and resizes them. Most video processors downscale (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, GLM-4.xV, LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL, ...). For Qwen3-VL, a 5-min 1080p video at 2 fps is 600 frames ≈ 3.5 GiB per request, resized down to 256×128 (W×H). **Proposal.** Resize each frame right after decoding, using the same op and target size as the HF processor (Qwen3-VL: torchvision bicubic + antialias on uint8, size from `smart_resize`). The processor then computes the same target size from the already-resized frames, so its resize changes nothing and `pixel_values_videos` is bit-identical. That holds for common aspect ratios but not always (e.g. 480×1920 with ≥258 frames shrinks one more step), so the loader checks it and otherwise keeps the current path. The resize is generic; each model only supplies its target size. Starting with Qwen3-VL, the only one measured so far. **Results** (Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, Big Buck Bunny 1080p h264, RTX 4090 + 16 vCPU EPYC 7542; OpenCV decode backend, fps=2; bit-identical on both clips): | Video | Frame array (MiB) | Decode + processor (s) | req/s, c=4 | req/s, c=8 | |---|---|---|---|---| | 60 s (120 frames) | 712 → 67 | 3.84 → 2.51 | 0.37 → 0.68 | 0.33 → 0.65 | | 300 s (600 frames) | 3560 → 56 | 15.5 → 8.31 | 0.10 → 0.23 | 0.11 → 0.27 | - The 300 s clip ends up smaller because Qwen3-VL caps total pixels across all frames, so frames shrink as the frame count grows (120 frames → 608×320, 600 frames → 256×128). - Memory and time columns: one process, no engine, 1 torch thread, median of 3 (the repro script below). - Throughput columns: `vllm serve` with the change applied as a runtime patch, `max_tokens=1` (so this is preprocessing + prefill bound; the gain shrinks with long outputs), processor cache and prefix caching off, 16 requests per level for 60 s and 8 for 300 s, simple async client. - The resize moves work into the decode stage: with 1 torch thread it adds ~0.6 s (60 s) / ~1.9 s (300 s) there, included in the totals above. Decode threads then touch torch, so if #60612 moves OpenCV decode into a child process, the resize should move with it (1 torch thread in that thread was enough; more was slower in our runs). - Per-request `mm_processor_kwargs` (e.g. a custom `max_pixels`) are not handled yet: such requests must keep the current path, otherwise frames are resampled twice. The chat parser sees those kwargs, so the fallback can be decided there. **Question.** The loader needs the processor's size config, which it doesn't have currently. Three options: 1. An off-by-default `--media-io-kwargs` option, usable now. Users copy the budget from the model's `preprocessor_config.json` (`size.shortest_edge`, `size.longest_edge`, `patch_size × merge_size`, `temporal_patch_size`). If it doesn't match the processor's config, the processor resizes again: the output is still valid but no longer bit-identical, and nothing reports it. 2. Override `get_media_io()` (added in #57752) in Qwen3-VL, so it's on by default with the right config. Depends on #57752 landing. 3. Extend the hook `main` already has: the chat parser passes the HF video processor class name to `MediaConnector.fetch_video(video_processor=...)` to pick the backend. Passing the processor's size budget the same way lets `Qwen3VLVideoBackend` compute the target itself, on by default, without waiting on #57752. Option 1 is usable now but easy to misconfigure; 3 is small and self-contained; 2 is the cleanest if #57752 lands. This should be complementary to #57752 either way: its benchmark showed no gain on video cache misses (−4%), which is the path this speeds up. @Isotr0py which would you prefer? Related: #57752, #60612 (same file), #58266.
Repro script: memory/time columns and bit-identity (CPU only, no model weights; throughput needs vllm serve) ```python # SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 """Resize video frames while decoding: bit-identity and timing check. Compares, for one video: baseline: vLLM's OpenCV loader (full-resolution frames) -> HF video processor proposed: same frames, each resized right after decoding with the op the HF processor uses (torchvision bicubic, antialias) -> HF video processor and reports whether `pixel_values_videos` is bit-identical, plus decode / processor time and the size of the frame array each path holds. Usage: python repro_decode_resize.py video.mp4 [video2.mp4 ...] Public test video used in the issue: Big Buck Bunny 1080p (CC-BY, Blender Foundation), big_buck_bunny_1080p_h264.mov.zip from https://download.blender.org/peach/bigbuckbunny_movies/, cut losslessly with ffmpeg -ss 60 -i big_buck_bunny_1080p_h264.mov -t 60 -map 0:v:0 -c copy \ -an -write_tmcd 0 bbb_1080p_60s.mp4 ffmpeg -ss 30 -i big_buck_bunny_1080p_h264.mov -t 300 -map 0:v:0 -c copy \ -an -write_tmcd 0 bbb_1080p_300s.mp4 """ import argparse import statistics import time import cv2 import numpy as np import torch from torchvision.transforms.v2 import functional as tvF from transformers import AutoProcessor from transformers.models.qwen3_vl.video_processing_qwen3_vl import smart_resize from transformers.video_utils import VideoMetadata from vllm.multimodal.media import ImageMediaIO, VideoMediaIO from vllm.multimodal.video_decoders.opencv import OpenCVVideoBackendMixin def target_size(vp, num_frames: int, height: int, width: int) -> tuple[int, int] | None: """The size the HF processor will pick, or None if resizing early is unsafe.""" kwargs = dict( temporal_factor=vp.temporal_patch_size, factor=vp.patch_size * vp.merge_size, min_pixels=vp.size["shortest_edge"], max_pixels=vp.size["longest_edge"], ) try: h, w = smart_resize(num_frames=num_frames, height=height, width=width, **kwargs) except ValueError: return None # The processor recomputes the size from the already-resized frames. Only # resize early if that recomputation is a no-op (it isn't for a few # odd frame counts with very large or very wide frames). if smart_resize(num_frames=num_frames, height=h, width=w, **kwargs) != (h, w): return None return h, w def decode_resized(data: bytes, indices: list[int], size: tuple[int, int]) -> np.ndarray: """vLLM's no-recovery OpenCV loop, resizing each kept frame immediately.""" cap = OpenCVVideoBackendMixin.open_video_capture(data) OpenCVVideoBackendMixin.get_video_metadata(cap) # same seeks as vLLM frames = np.empty((len(indices), *size, 3), dtype=np.uint8) wanted, i = set(indices), 0 for idx in range(max(indices) + 1): if not cap.grab(): continue if idx in wanted: ok, bgr = cap.retrieve() if ok: chw = torch.from_numpy(bgr).permute(2, 0, 1) small = tvF.resize( chw, list(size), interpolation=tvF.InterpolationMode.BICUBIC, antialias=True, ) frames[i] = small.permute(1, 2, 0).flip(-1).numpy() # BGR -> RGB i += 1 return frames[:i] def main() -> None: parser = argparse.ArgumentParser() parser.add_argument("videos", nargs="+") parser.add_argument("--model", default="Qwen/Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct") parser.add_argument("--repeats", type=int, default=3) args = parser.parse_args() # vLLM runs the multimodal processor with 1 torch thread. torch.set_num_threads(1) vp = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(args.model).video_processor io = VideoMediaIO(ImageMediaIO(), num_frames=-1, video_backend="qwen3_vl") for path in args.videos: data = open(path, "rb").read() frames, meta = io.load_bytes(data).media indices = list(meta["frames_indices"]) md = VideoMetadata(**{k: v for k, v in meta.items() if k != "do_sample_frames"}) size = target_size(vp, *frames.shape[:3]) if size is None: print(f"{path}: resizing early is unsafe for this video, skipped") continue del frames def process(frames): return vp( videos=[frames], video_metadata=[md], do_sample_frames=False, return_tensors="pt", ) paths = { "baseline": lambda: io.load_bytes(data).media[0], "proposed": lambda: decode_resized(data, indices, size), } outputs = {} for name, decode in paths.items(): dec_t, proc_t = [], [] for _ in range(args.repeats): t0 = time.perf_counter() frames = decode() t1 = time.perf_counter() outputs[name] = process(frames) t2 = time.perf_counter() dec_t.append(t1 - t0) proc_t.append(t2 - t1) dec, proc = statistics.median(dec_t), statistics.median(proc_t) print( f"{path} {name:8s} frames {tuple(frames.shape)} " f"({frames.nbytes / 2**20:.0f} MiB) decode {dec:.2f} s " f"processor {proc:.2f} s total {dec + proc:.2f} s" ) base, new = outputs["baseline"], outputs["proposed"] same = torch.equal( base["video_grid_thw"], new["video_grid_thw"] ) and torch.equal(base["pixel_values_videos"], new["pixel_values_videos"]) print(f"{path} target {size} bit_identical={same}") if __name__ == "__main__": main() ```
*Written with AI assistance (Claude Code); I reviewed the code and results.* ### Report of performance regression _No response_ ### Misc discussion on performance _No response_ ### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary) Measured on 1× RTX 4090 24 GB, 16 vCPU AMD EPYC 7542, Ubuntu VM. vLLM `0.1.dev20475+g32ad1400d` (editable install from `main`), torch 2.13.0+cu129, transformers 5.16.1, opencv-python 5.0.0, torchcodec 0.16.0. Model `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct`, served with `--max-model-len 32768 --mm-processor-cache-gb 0 --no-enable-prefix-caching`. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [ ] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Performance]: Reduce load_weights synchronization overhead for DeepSeek V4 Flash weight updates on H200
body:
### Proposal to improve performance

Profiling repeated weight updates for **DeepSeek V4 Flash on NVIDIA H200** revealed substantial CPU waiting and accounting overhead inside `load_weights`.

The transfer method involves sorting all weights by layer into buckets of ≤8 GB, with each bucket triggering a `load_weights` operation.

For the second `load_weights` invocation in each trace, the combined experimental optimizations reduced profiled CPU duration from **1,923.691 ms to 276.823 ms**, an **85.61% reduction / 6.95× speedup**.

**Original loading flow**

The baseline follows the existing layerwise reload path:

1. `load_weights` routes incoming weight names to parameters, shards, and experts.
2. `online_process_loader` buffers weights and calls `get_numel_loaded` to track layer completion. Accounting executes the original loader against meta parameters under `CopyCounter`.
3. Once a layer is ready, `_layerwise_process` materializes its parameters and replays the buffered loaders for actual loading.
4. Quantization post-processing prepares MXFP4 MoE weights for Marlin: repack `w13` and `w2`, then permute and encode their scales per expert.
5. Processed values are copied into the existing kernel tensor storage.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller as Caller
    participant Model as DeepSeek V4 load_weights
    participant Loader as Reload / weight_loader
    participant Map as Expert ID map
    participant Marlin as Marlin preparation
    participant GPU as CUDA runtime / GPU
    rect rgb(255, 242, 238)
    Note over Caller,GPU: main - second call - relative offsets in ms
    Caller->>Model: load_weights() [t=0.000 ms]
    activate Model
    Note over Model,Loader: Loading / dispatch before Marlin: t=0.000 to 1297.992 ms
    loop Interleaved accounting and actual loading (aggregated, not expanded)
        Model->>Loader: get_numel_loaded x1552
        Note over Model,Loader: Exclusive totals: accounting 94.848 ms
        Loader->>Map: map_global_to_local x3048
        Note over Loader,Map: Mapping cumulative CPU duration: 959.661 ms
        Map->>GPU: GPU expert_map scalar read / item() x3048
        Note over Map,GPU: D2H x3048
        GPU-->>Map: Scalar result after synchronization
        Map-->>Loader: Local expert ID
    end
    Model->>Marlin: prepare_moe_mxfp4_layer_for_marlin [t=1297.992 ms]
    activate Marlin
    Marlin->>GPU: repack_weight #1 [t=1298.015 to 1301.462 ms]
    Note over Marlin,GPU: CPU invocation duration 3.447 ms
    Marlin->>GPU: repack_weight #2 [t=1301.492 to 1304.639 ms]
    Note over Marlin,GPU: CPU invocation duration 3.146 ms
    Marlin->>Marlin: scales preparation #1 [t=1304.668 to 1612.284 ms]
    Note over Marlin,GPU: CPU duration 307.616 ms
    Marlin->>Marlin: scales preparation #2 [t=1612.320 to 1919.894 ms]
    Note over Marlin,GPU: CPU duration 307.574 ms
    Note over Marlin,GPU: Across both scales entries: permutation x128 / 304.153 ms
    Note over Marlin,GPU: H2D x256
    Marlin-->>Model: Preparation returns [t=1919.963 ms]
    deactivate Marlin
    Model-->>Caller: load_weights returns [t=1923.691 ms]
    deactivate Model
    end
```

Accounting and actual loading are interleaved as layers become ready. Expert ID mapping occurs in both paths.

**Bottlenecks and implemented optimizations**

1. **GPU scalar reads during expert ID mapping**

   The baseline reads `expert_map[global_id].item()` from a GPU tensor for host-side decisions. Across **3,048 lookups**, the trace records **3,048 D2H transfers and 3,048 stream synchronizations**.

   Mapping consumes **959.661 ms**, including **870.633 ms** in CPU stream synchronization, while the corresponding D2H transfers total only **7.177 ms** of GPU time. This identifies frequent host waiting as the main cost.

   **Optimization:** cache a Python list whenever the expert map is created or recalculated, and use it for host-side ID and locality queries. #60779 

   **Observed result:** mapping duration falls to **0.287 ms**. Lookup count remains **3,048**, while D2H transfers and stream synchronizations inside these lookups fall to **zero**.

2. **Replaying expert loaders for loaded-element accounting**

   The baseline invokes `RoutedExperts.weight_loader` both for accounting and for actual loading: **3,048 calls**, including **1,524 accounting calls**.

   **Optimization:** use a counting fast path that determines the loaded-element count without re-entering the expert loader.

   **Observed result:** total expert-loader calls fall to **1,524**, all on the actual loading path. `CopyCounter.__torch_dispatch__` invocations fall from **4,936 to 96**.

   The fast path still checks expert placement, so expert-map lookup count remains unchanged.

3. **Synchronization in Marlin scales preparation**

   The baseline PyTorch scales path performs permutation and MXFP4 encoding per expert. These operations account for **256 H2D transfers and 256 stream synchronizations**, with **594.433 ms** spent in CPU stream synchronization.

   **Optimization:** implement scale permutation and encoding with CUDA operators. #60780

   **Observed result:** the two scales-preparation entries fall from **615.190 ms to 7.704 ms**, and their H2D transfers and stream synchronizations fall to **zero**.

   Permutation and encoding still each execute **128 times** in this experiment. Scales-related GPU kernel time improves from **1.983 ms to 1.230 ms (1.61×)**; the much larger CPU-duration improvement reflects reduced host waiting and dispatch overhead.

### Report of performance regression

_No response_

### Misc discussion on performance

**Performance comparison**

The following breakdown assigns non-overlapping intervals within the selected `load_weights` invocation. Nested mapping time is removed from accounting and loader rows, and scale substeps are separated from their parent entries.

| Step | Baseline CPU duration (ms) | Optimized CPU duration (ms) | Baseline share | Optimized share |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Expert ID mapping | 959.661 | 0.287 | 49.89% | 0.10% |
| Loaded-element accounting, excluding mapping | 94.848 | 24.382 | 4.93% | 8.81% |
| Actual loader work, excluding mapping/accounting | 18.955 | 17.966 | 0.99% | 6.49% |
| Scales permutation | 304.153 | 2.591 | 15.81% | 0.94% |
| MXFP4 scales encoding | 308.717 | 3.183 | 16.05% | 1.15% |
| Other scales-entry work | 2.320 | 1.931 | 0.12% | 0.70% |
| Weight repack | 6.593 | 6.613 | 0.34% | 2.39% |
| Other work / gaps | 228.444 | 219.871 | 11.88% | 79.43% |
| **Total** | **1,923.691** | **276.823** | **100%** | **100%** |

Rounded rows may differ slightly from the total.

Expert mapping and scales preparation account for approximately **81.87%** of the baseline window. Actual loader work excluding mapping and accounting changes only modestly, from **18.955 ms to 17.966 ms**.

**Measurement scope**

- The window includes accounting, actual loaders, Marlin preparation, and CPU waiting. It excludes outer broadcast, bucket reconstruction, final synchronization/finalization, GC, and `empty_cache`.
- These are **profiled inclusive CPU durations**. GPU work can remain outstanding when the function returns.
- Matching operation counts do not establish identical tensor inputs or numerical correctness. The optimized full-update trace broadcasts approximately **0.0400% more bytes**.
- Repeated measurements with identical inputs and profiling disabled, plus CUDA numerical parity and model-output validation, are needed to establish the end-to-end benefit.

Related discussion: [#54477 — Direct Weight Reload for RL Training](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54477). This report contributes measurements and targeted optimizations within the existing layerwise reload path.

AI assistance was used to review the code and draft this issue.

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

```text
Model: DeepSeek V4 Flash
GPU: NVIDIA H200
Profiled rank: 0
World size: 4
Profiled MoE preparation: MXFP4 → Marlin
CUDA runtime: 13.0
NCCL: 2.28.9
Profiler setting: with_stack=True
TP / EP configuration: 4 / 4
```

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Performance]: Hybrid Mamba prefix caching (`mamba_cache_mode="align"`) costs 11-16% throughput on Nemotron-3.5-Lightning with no cache hits: per-group eager block-table ops, per-step align kernels outside CUDA graphs, and block-boundary prefill splits
body:
## Summary

Turning on prefix caching for a hybrid Mamba2 model forces `mamba_cache_mode="align"`
(`vllm/model_executor/models/config.py:640-656`; since
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58997 the only modes are `none` and `align`).
On NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 (4x GB200, DP4/EP4, Model Runner V2),
with a random 8K-in / 1K-out workload where nothing ever hits the cache, align mode
costs:

- **Output throughput: -13.4% to -16.2%** (median of 6 paired rounds, c=1/8/32/64).
- **TPOT: +14% to +20%** from align mode itself, independent of block size and of
  prefill splitting. The decode step has **28 extra eager launches**: 4 Mamba
  KV-cache groups x 7 torch ops in `mamba_get_block_table_tensor`. The V2 align
  pre-process / pre-copy / post-process kernels also run every step outside the
  CUDA graph. GPU compute per step is unchanged; **GPU idle time per step grows by
  0.55-0.75 ms**.
- **TTFT at c=1: x1.8** (125 -> 229 ms). The scheduler splits an 8192-token prompt at
  the block boundary (4176 + 4016), and each prefill step carries 70-90 ms of fixed
  non-GPU cost, which is now paid twice.
- Block size and KV capacity are **not** the cause. With prefix caching off, changing
  the block size to 6768 or 8192 stays within run-to-run noise. All configurations
  have >= 576x max concurrency and zero preemptions.

With `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, prefix caching for Mamba2 is currently rejected at
startup. A two-line fix (copy all 5 exact-replay states in align mode) makes hits and
misses bitwise equal to prefix caching off. The extra copy costs about 9.4 us per step.
That fix is not a PR yet; see the batch-invariance section below.

This issue collects the measurements, the root cause and what the open PRs cover, so
that someone can pick up the remaining work.

## Environment

- Hardware: 1 node, 4x NVIDIA GB200 (NVLink).
- Model: `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4` (ModelOpt mixed
  precision: W4A16 NVFP4 routed and shared experts and lm_head, FP8 Mamba
  in_proj/out_proj). 23 Mamba2 layers, `chunk_size=128`.
- vLLM: upstream `main` at `6e517b15c1` (2026-10-02, already contains #58997) plus
  12 out-of-tree commits (build `a92e2ac3c4`). The out-of-tree commits add a
  FlashInfer CuTe-DSL W4A16 MoE expert backend (selected by
  `--moe-backend flashinfer_cutedsl`), the batch-invariant Mamba2 exact-replay stack
  from https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55905, and two DP sampler-seed
  fixes. None of them touches the align-mode path: `vllm/v1/core/`,
  `vllm/v1/attention/backends/utils.py` and
  `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/mamba_hybrid.py` are identical to `6e517b15c1`,
  and the `mamba_utils.py` changes only take effect under `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`.
  All file:line references below are against `6e517b15c1`.
- Runtime: Model Runner V2 (`VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1`), `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=0`
  unless stated, async scheduling default, CUDA graph mode `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`
  (default for this model).
- Parallelism: TP1, DP4, expert parallel (EP4), all2all
  `flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided`.
- MoE: `flashinfer_cutedsl` (CuTe-DSL W4A16 experts). Attention: FlashInfer, FP8 KV
  cache (`fp8_e4m3`).
- Client: `vllm-rs bench serve` (in-tree Rust benchmark, `rust/src/bench`), random
  dataset with token-id prompts, 8192 in / 1024 out, `--ignore-eos`, temperature 0,
  `--request-rate inf`, `--max-concurrency` 1/8/32/64,
  `--num-prompts max(4c, 8)` after a warmup point of `max(c, 4)` requests.

## Measurements (`VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=0`)

Five server configurations. All share the serve arguments in Reproduction and differ
only as listed. The effective block size is what vLLM auto-derived or was given.

| Arm | Config | Attention block / Mamba mode | KV tokens (max concurrency at 9216) |
|---|---|---|---|
| a1 | PC off | 4176 (auto) / none | 14.88M (1615x) |
| a2 | PC off, `--block-size 6768` | 6768 / none | 10.71M (1162x) |
| a3 | **PC on** (default) | 4176 (auto) / align, mamba block 4176 | 9.47M (1027x) |
| a4 | PC on, `--block-size 8192` | 8192 / align | 5.31M (576x) |
| a5 | PC off, `--block-size 8192` | 8192 / none | 8.85M (960x) |

In align mode, `--mamba-block-size` is overwritten with the attention block size
(`vllm/platforms/interface.py:977`), so 4176 is also the smallest valid Mamba block
here. a4 exists to separate the two effects: with block 8192, an 8192-token prompt fits
in one block and is never split.

Protocol: 6 rounds on 2 nodes (3 per node, arm order forward / reverse / forward), a
fresh server per arm, and the same client seed for every arm within a round. 119 of
120 points are valid; one a3 c=32 point had an accidental 4176-token hit and does not
change any conclusion. Zero preemptions, all servers exited cleanly.

**Output throughput (tok/s), median of 6 rounds [min..max]; delta = median of paired
per-round deltas vs a1**

| c | a1 PC off | a2 bs6768 | a5 bs8192 | **a3 PC on** | a4 PC on + bs8192 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 317 [305..354] | 339 (+4.7%) | 334 (+1.5%) | **277 [246..298] (-14.9%)** | 297 (-8.9%) |
| 8 | 2178 [2076..2420] | 2072 (-4.9%) | 2168 (-1.0%) | **1879 [1718..2181] (-13.5%)** | 1808 (-15.7%) |
| 32 | 7174 [6302..7422] | 6691 (-4.8%) | 6277 (-8.7%) | **5476 [4432..6316] (-16.2%)** | 5725 (-15.5%) |
| 64 | 10371 [9055..11340] | 9781 (-3.6%) | 10387 (-0.6%) | **9109 [8173..9532] (-13.4%)** | 9303 (-12.4%) |

Per-round a3 deltas range from -30% to -3% at c=1 and from -38% to -13% at c=32. The
BI=0 baseline is bimodal (a1 at c=64 ranges 9055-11340), which is why the deltas are
paired per round.

**TTFT / TPOT medians (ms)**

| c | a1 | a3 PC on | a4 PC on + bs8192 | a5 bs8192 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 125 / 3.07 | 229 / 3.30 | 126 / 3.16 | 125 / 2.79 |
| 8 | 257 / 3.42 | 338 / 3.91 | 250 / 4.11 | 236 / 3.52 |
| 32 | 413 / 3.79 | 549 / 4.46 | 467 / 4.71 | 438 / 4.02 |
| 64 | 506 / 4.80 | 589 / 5.56 | 543 / 5.73 | 560 / 4.97 |

**Paired deltas (median of per-round ratios)**

| Comparison | c=1 TTFT / TPOT | c=8 | c=32 | c=64 TPOT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a3 vs a1 (PC on vs off) | +80% / +9% | +39% / +13% | +26% / +18% | +17% |
| **a4 vs a5** (both block 8192, only PC differs) | **+1% / +14%** | +3% / +16% | +8% / +20% | +14% |
| a3 vs a4 (only the prefill split differs) | **+85%** / +4% | +41% / -4% | +17% / -6% | -2% |

How to read this:

- a2 and a5 vs a1 are within noise, so block size is not the cause.
- a4 vs a5: the TPOT cost (+14-20%) comes from align mode itself, even with no
  prefill split.
- a3 vs a4: the TTFT doubling comes from the prefill split. a4 and a5 have the same
  TTFT.

## Profiling breakdown

Torch profiler (`--profiler-config '{"profiler":"torch",...,"torch_profiler_with_stack":false}'`,
`/start_profile` and `/stop_profile`), CUDA activity only.

### Decode (c=64 steady state, ~1 s window, ~180 steps per rank, 4 ranks)

| | Step time | GPU idle / step | Eager launches outside graphs / step | GPU compute (excl. a2a wait) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a1 PC off | 5318 us | 913 us | 10 | ~3.8 ms |
| a3 PC on | 5750 us | 1468 us | 38 | ~3.7 ms |
| a4 PC on + bs8192 | 6591 us | 1676 us | 38 | n/a |

The extra kernels are all small, about 80 us of GPU time per step in total:

- `mamba_get_block_table_tensor` (`vllm/v1/attention/backends/utils.py:1159-1190`),
  called once per Mamba KV-cache group from the Mamba metadata builder
  (`vllm/v1/attention/backends/mamba_attn.py:440`, and `:700` in
  `update_block_table`). In align mode it runs as 7 torch ops (floordiv, clamp_,
  arange, add, `.to(int64)`, gather, copy). This model has 4 Mamba KV-cache groups,
  so that is **28 launches per step** on the host critical path.
- The V2 align hooks in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/mamba_hybrid.py`, which run
  every step: `preprocess_mamba_align_fused_kernel` and `run_fused_precopy` ->
  `precopy_mamba_align_fused_kernel` (`preprocess_state`, lines 179-226), and
  `postprocess_mamba_fused_kernel` via `run_fused_postprocess_align`
  (`postprocess_state`, lines 342-394). Kernels are in
  `vllm/v1/worker/mamba_utils.py:369/504/550`. There is also one DtoD snapshot.

GPU compute does not change. GPU idle time grows by 0.55-0.75 ms per step, so the
decode loop was already partly host-bound with PC off (0.9 ms idle), and each added
eager op and piece of Python metadata work lengthens the step almost one for one. With
DP+EP the all2all synchronizes the 4 ranks every step, so the slowest rank's host
overhead sets the step time for all of them.

The comment at `mamba_hybrid.py:200-205` says the launch cost is "~0.3% of TPOT".
That estimate counts the one Triton launch, not the 28 torch ops across 4 groups or
the per-step pre/post kernels.

### Prefill (c=1, one 8192-token request)

- PC off: one step `execute_context_1(8192)`, 121 ms wall, 50 ms of GPU kernels.
- PC on: two steps, `(4176)` then `(4016)`, about 118 ms wall each, about 27 ms of
  GPU kernels each.
- The split comes from `Scheduler._mamba_block_aligned_split`
  (`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:426`, enabled at `:359-361` whenever the model
  has Mamba layers and the mode is `align`):
  `last_cache_position = num_tokens - num_tokens % block_size = 8192 - 8192 % 4176 = 4176`.
  The chunk must stop there so that the Mamba state at 4176 is materialized.
- Each prefill step has about 70-90 ms of non-GPU fixed cost here: the step is far
  above the CUDA graph capture range, plus the per-step DP synchronization. Splitting
  pays it twice.

Not measured: per-op CPU time of the eager ops (stacks were off), and the cause of
the BI=0 bimodality, which is unrelated to prefix caching.

## Root cause

### Decode: per-step align overhead on the host critical path

1. **Per-group duplication.** Each of the 4 Mamba KV-cache groups rebuilds the same
   batch-level state indices with its own `mamba_get_block_table_tensor` call. The
   groups differ only in their block tables, so the arithmetic (`(seq_lens - 1) //
   block_size`, clamp, arange, add, cast) is repeated 4 times. Only the final gather
   is group-specific.
2. **7 launches per call.** The align branch is written as eager torch ops on a
   `(num_reqs,)` tensor, so its cost is launch overhead, flat in batch size.
3. **Align pre/post kernels run every step, outside the CUDA graph.**
   `preprocess_state` launches the state-advance kernel and the fused pre-copy kernel
   on every real batch. The pre-copy kernel fast-exits per request when no block
   boundary is crossed, but its grid is `(num_reqs, num_states, 16)`, so all the
   programs are still launched. Skipping the launch on the host would need the true
   `num_computed_tokens` on the host, which async scheduling only has as an
   optimistic mirror (comment at `mamba_hybrid.py:200-205`).

Because the decode loop is host-bound in this configuration (DP4/EP4 with an a2a
barrier, 3.7-3.8 ms of GPU work per 5.3 ms step), these launches turn directly into
TPOT.

### Prefill: block-boundary split

In align mode the reusable Mamba state exists only at block boundaries, so the
scheduler ends a prefill chunk at the last block boundary below `num_tokens`. For an
8192-token prompt and block 4176 that is one extra prefill step, even when no cache
hit is possible. Its cost is the per-step fixed overhead (70-90 ms here), not GPU
work: the two halves take 27 + 27 ms of GPU time vs 50 ms unsplit. The effect is
largest at c=1 (TTFT x1.8, about 5 points of the throughput loss) and is amortized at
higher concurrency.

Mamba2 does not use the in-prefill checkpoint path:
`num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks > 0` (and `MambaPrefillCheckpointBuilder`) exists only
for GDN/KDA, so Mamba2 always pays the split.

## Related open PRs and their measured effect

- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58737: fuses the align branch of
  `mamba_get_block_table_tensor` into one Triton kernel (7 launches -> 1 per call).
  Kernel-level microbenchmark only in the PR (10.8 -> 1.8 us on MI355X); no
  end-to-end claim.
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59726: the same fusion behind an opt-in
  flag `VLLM_MAMBA_FUSED_STATE_INDEX=1` (overlaps with #58737). The PR reports
  -1.9% time per verify iteration at BS1 on a Nemotron-H MTP setup on B200.
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58851: shares GDN / Mamba / KDA batch
  metadata across KV-cache groups in MRV2 and uses the multi-group aligned-index
  precompute for Mamba1/2. The PR reports Mamba2 x 9 groups, align decode c=1: 637 ->
  258 us and 73 -> 10 CUDA API calls per `build_attn_metadata`. Serving step time on
  Granite-4.0-H-micro is -0.7%.

**Measured on this setup: in progress.** We are applying #58737, #59726, #58851 and
combinations on top of the build above and rerunning the a1 vs a3 protocol (throughput,
TPOT, launches and GPU idle per step). Results will be posted as a follow-up comment.

Other related work, not overlapping with the per-step overhead:

- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/26201: tracking issue for prefix
  caching on hybrid models.
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52959: RFC, internal state checkpoints
  for Mamba align mode (relevant to the prefill split).
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/55697: RFC, application-directed prefix
  checkpoints for hybrid prefix caching.
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50551: retain finalized Mamba decode
  checkpoints for prefix caching (hit retention policy, not overhead).
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59826: fix inconsistent hybrid Mamba
  prefix-cache boundaries and tail saves (correctness).

## What remains uncovered, with concrete ideas

Even with #58737 / #59726 / #58851, these remain:

1. **Per-step align pre/post kernels outside the CUDA graph.**
   - Capture `preprocess_mamba_align_fused_kernel` and the pre-copy inside the decode
     CUDA graph. Both read only device tensors (`idx_mapping`, `num_computed_tokens`,
     `query_start_loc`, the state-index buffers), so they could run as graph nodes
     against persistent buffers.
   - Or fuse state-advance + pre-copy (+ the block-table gather) into one launch per
     step.
   - Change the pre-copy grid so each request checks `src_col` first, and only
     requests that cross a block expand to `(num_states, 16)` programs. This also
     removes the batch-invariance overhead below (~9.4 us per step).
   - Skip the post-process launch when spec decode is off (it only matters when
     acceptance leaves the sequence unaligned).
2. **Per-group duplication.** #58851 shares metadata across groups under MRV2. Check
   that it covers the 4-group Nemotron-H layout with FULL_AND_PIECEWISE graphs, and
   that the remaining per-group work is only the gather.
3. **Prefill split at the block boundary.**
   - Extend the in-prefill checkpoint mechanism (`num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks`,
     `MambaPrefillCheckpointBuilder`) to Mamba2. The SSD kernels already compute
     chunk-boundary states, so the state at a block boundary can be written from
     inside a single prefill step when the boundary is a multiple of `chunk_size`.
     Otherwise, the partial chunk can be written separately. This would remove the
     extra step entirely.
   - Cheaper interim option: only split when the boundary state can actually be
     reused (for example skip splits for requests with no prefix hash match in the
     pool and no `cache_salt`/sharing hint). This trades away future hits on the
     first occurrence of a prefix, so it needs a policy knob.
   - Reduce the fixed per-prefill-step host cost, which would shrink the penalty for
     every split.
4. **Documentation.** Update the "~0.3% of TPOT" comment at `mamba_hybrid.py:200-205`
   and document that `--enable-prefix-caching` on hybrids costs TPOT even at a 0% hit
   rate.

## `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`: prefix caching is rejected; minimal fix (not yet a PR)

### Why it is rejected

With https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55905 (RFC
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/55524), batch-invariant Mamba2 uses exact
replay. The Mamba2 slot holds 5 states: conv, the fp32 SSM state at the last chunk
boundary, and the `x` / raw `dt` / `B` inputs buffered since that boundary (shape
`(chunk_size, ...)` each, from `mamba2_state_shape`).
`Mamba2AttentionBackend.check_batch_invariant_config` rejects prefix caching at
startup (#55627 / #55905 / #56244 all keep the `mamba_cache_mode != "none"`
rejection).

The rejection is necessary as written. Align mode copies state across block
boundaries with the model's state copy functions, and
`MambaStateCopyFuncCalculator.mamba2_state_copy_func` returns only `(conv, temporal)`.
`validate_mamba_state_copy_funcs` deliberately accepts a copyable prefix (ReplaySSM
rings must not be copied), so the three buffers would be silently left behind.
Lifting only the check (a negative control) breaks every prompt longer than one block,
**including cold requests with zero hits**, because the prefill split itself crosses a
boundary.

### Minimal fix

- `mamba2_state_copy_func` returns a whole-slot copy for each of the 3 buffers under
  `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT`, the same condition under which `mamba2_state_shape` and
  `mamba2_state_dtype` add them. BI=0 is unchanged. All align paths (V2 fused
  pre-copy, V1 `MambaCopyBuffers`, `--prefix-match-unit` tail hits) take the copy
  functions per layer, so nothing else changes. This covers every `MambaMixer2` model
  (nemotron_h, mamba2, zamba2, falcon_h1, granitemoehybrid).
- Remove the prefix-caching rejection in `check_batch_invariant_config`. Since
  #58997 the only non-`none` mode is `align`, which is the tested one.
- Rejected alternative: require `block_size % chunk_size == 0`. It does not remove
  the copy (`--prefix-match-unit` tail hits and decode positions land mid-chunk), it
  needs new block-size derivation (6768 -> 6784 here), and it does not shrink the
  per-step pre-copy grid.

### Validation (on GB200, same model, BI=1, DP4/EP, V2 runner, attention block 6768)

- Unit and e2e tests (`mamba2-130m`, block 400, chunk 256, V1 and V2 runners): hits
  and misses are bitwise equal to PC off. The negative control (two-state copy) fails
  as expected.
- Real model: 11 scenarios x 3 runs x DP ranks 0-3, 684 requests (456 with PC on).
  All are bitwise equal to PC off (token ids and logprob bit patterns), including
  hits at 13536 / 6768 / 1488 / 6688 tokens, all mid-chunk (mod 128 = 96 / 112 / 80 /
  32).
- Forced preemption (`--num-gpu-blocks-override 32 --max-num-seqs 16`): 174
  preemptions with PC on, all 360 outputs bitwise equal. 49 recomputations hit 6768
  cached tokens.

### Measured cost of the extra copy (torch profiler, c=64 shared-prefix load, 400 steps x 4 ranks, 3 runs per arm)

| | 5-state copy (fix) | 2-state copy (control) | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-copy fast-exit launch | 17.1 us | 7.8 us | **+9.3 us / step** |
| Pre-copy launch that copies (2-4 per rank per 400 steps) | ~105 us | ~58 us | +47 us |
| Share of GPU kernel time | 0.20% | 0.10% | +0.1 pt |

The cost is dominated by the per-step grid (`(num_reqs, num_states, 16)`, with
`num_states` 46 -> 115), not by the actual copies. That is about 0.2% of a 5.3 ms
TPOT. Item 1 above would remove it.

### Throughput with the fix, BI=1, PC on vs off (3 pairs, 8K/1K)

| c | Random prompts (0 hits) | Shared prefix (90% share 7168 tokens, hit rate 21-77%) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 283 -> 256 (-9.2%) | 279 -> 253 (-9.7%) |
| 8 | 1981 -> 1697 (-17.6%) | 1984 -> 1859 (-5.5%) |
| 32 | 6190 -> 5439 (-10.9%) | 6203 -> 6560 (**+7.8%**), TTFT -30 to -50% |
| 64 | 9048 -> 8218 (-9.7%) | 10029 -> 10746 (**+9.8%**), TTFT -30 to -40% |

On random prompts the loss is align mode's own overhead (TTFT about x2 at c=1, TPOT
+2-20%), the same mechanism as BI=0. Prefix caching only pays off under batch
invariance when long prefixes (at least one 6768-token block) are reused at high
concurrency. The decode-side fixes in this issue would move that break-even point.

Status: the change is a local branch stacked on #55905, with tests. It has not been
opened as a PR.

## Reproduction

The model is copied to local disk and served from there. Every arm uses a fresh
server.

```bash
export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1
export VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=0          # 1 for the batch-invariance arms
MODEL=nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4   # or a local copy

COMMON="--served-model-name nemotron-nvfp4 --dtype bfloat16 --seed 42 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel \
  --moe-backend flashinfer_cutedsl --all2all-backend flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --max-model-len 9216 --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 \
  --max-num-seqs 64 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.8 --logprobs-mode raw_logprobs \
  --shutdown-timeout 30"

# a1: PC off
vllm serve $MODEL --port 8000 $COMMON --no-enable-prefix-caching
# a2: PC off, block 6768
vllm serve $MODEL --port 8000 $COMMON --no-enable-prefix-caching --block-size 6768
# a3: PC on (align mode is selected automatically)
vllm serve $MODEL --port 8000 $COMMON --enable-prefix-caching
# a4: PC on, block 8192 (no prefill split for 8192-token prompts)
vllm serve $MODEL --port 8000 $COMMON --enable-prefix-caching --block-size 8192
# a5: PC off, block 8192
vllm serve $MODEL --port 8000 $COMMON --no-enable-prefix-caching --block-size 8192
```

`--moe-backend flashinfer_cutedsl` with this W4A16 checkpoint needs the CuTe-DSL
W4A16 expert backend, which is not on `main`. To reproduce on `main`, use another
supported NVFP4 W4A16 MoE backend for both arms. The align-mode path is independent
of the MoE backend.

Benchmark (per concurrency `c` in 1 8 32 64; one warmup point with `max(c, 4)`
prompts, then `max(4c, 8)` prompts; use the same `--seed` for every arm in a round):

```bash
vllm-rs bench serve --backend openai \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 --model $MODEL \
  --served-model-name nemotron-nvfp4 --tokenizer $MODEL \
  --dataset-name random --prompt-token-ids --random-input-len 8192 \
  --random-output-len 1024 --random-range-ratio 0 --ignore-eos \
  --temperature 0 --request-rate inf --max-concurrency $c \
  --num-prompts $n --seed $seed --save-result --save-detailed \
  --result-dir out/c$c --result-filename result.json
```

For the shared-prefix variant (BI=1 table), add
`--random-cache-hit-fraction 0.9 --random-cache-ratio 0.875`.

Validity check per point: compare `vllm:prefix_cache_hits` in `/metrics` before and
after the point. Any hit on the random workload invalidates the pair. Also check that
preemptions are 0 and that request and token counts match.

Profiling: add
`--profiler-config '{"profiler":"torch","torch_profiler_dir":"<dir>","ignore_frontend":true,"torch_profiler_with_stack":false}'`.
Then:

- Prefill: `POST /start_profile`, one 8192/64 request at c=1, `POST /stop_profile`.
- Decode: start a c=64 8192/1024 run, wait about 4 s, then `/start_profile`, sleep
  1 s, `/stop_profile`.

Count launches outside CUDA graphs per step, and GPU idle per step, from the trace.

## Owner / next steps

- [ ] Rerun a1 vs a3 with #58737, #59726, #58851 and their combinations. Report
      TPOT, the launch count and GPU idle per step (in progress, see above).
- [ ] Decide between #58737 and #59726 (same fusion; default-on vs opt-in), and
      confirm that #58851 composes with it for the 4-group Nemotron-H layout.
- [ ] Move the V2 align pre-process / pre-copy into the decode CUDA graph, or fuse
      them into one launch. Change the pre-copy grid to expand to the state
      dimension only for requests that cross a block.
- [ ] Prototype in-prefill block-boundary checkpoints for Mamba2 (extend
      `num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks` / `MambaPrefillCheckpointBuilder`) to remove
      the block-aligned prefill split. Coordinate with
      https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52959.
- [ ] Update the "~0.3% of TPOT" comment and the prefix-caching docs for hybrid
      models.
- [ ] Batch invariance: open the 5-state copy + rejection removal as a PR stacked on
      https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55905, after a human review of every
      line and a rerun of the tests.
- [ ] Re-measure BI=0 and BI=1 PC on vs off after the decode fixes, on random and
      shared-prefix workloads.

---

Duplicate search done before filing (open issues): "mamba align prefix caching",
"hybrid prefix caching overhead", "mamba_get_block_table_tensor", "Nemotron-H prefix
caching", "mamba prefix caching slow", "mamba_cache_mode align performance". No open
issue covers the align-mode per-step overhead or the prefill split cost. Related
issues and PRs are linked above. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59770 (Nemotron-3.5-Lightning decode regression on GB10 since v0.29) is a different problem.

This issue was drafted with AI assistance (Claude Code). The measurements come from our
own benchmark and profiler runs on the setup above.

title: [RFC]: Octave KV, a native 3-bit KV cache for AMD GPUs
body:
PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59774

### Proposal to improve performance

## Where this comes from

We serve Qwen3.8-27B (GPTQ W4A16) on boxes with four RX 7900 XTX, 96 GB in
total, with tensor parallel 4 and MTP. Our users send long prompts: whole
repositories, long documents, agent sessions that run for hours. With an fp16
KV cache and 8 GB per GPU for it, a box holds about 446k tokens, so one long
request fills it.

On ROCm today the options below 8 bits are TurboQuant, UltraQuant (#57057,
gfx950 only) and KVarN (#46613, CUDA-first). We tried TurboQuant first, since
it is merged and its idea (random rotation plus a Lloyd-Max codebook) is the
right one. On our hardware three things got in the way:

- With MTP on (`qwen3_next_mtp`, k=3) every preset produced garbage, and
  GSM8K fell to around 1%. Without MTP it was correct.
- Its multi-token path copies between host and device per layer, so it
  cannot be captured in CUDA graphs.
- Its Triton kernels are slow on RDNA3. At 380k tokens the first token took
  621 s, against 371 s with fp16.

So we wrote our own backend: same family of ideas, a few changes to the
format, and every kernel in HIP. Against TurboQuant on the same hardware it
comes out ahead on all three things we care about. It holds as many tokens or
more at each size: at about 200 bytes per slot the two hold 2.07M and 2.05M
tokens, and our 216-byte format holds 6% more than TurboQuant's 230-byte one.
It loses less: 2.5× less excess NLL at 380k at the same size, and GSM8K
stays at fp16 level (91.8-92.4 against 89.8). And it is faster: per layer at
380k, decode is 4.6× faster, MTP verification 11×, a prefill chunk takes
30% less time, and the first token of a 380k prompt arrives 2.1× sooner.

We have run it in production since October 2, 2026, and we would like to
propose it upstream. We would also like it to be more than an RDNA3 side
project: one compressed KV format for the whole AMD line, with a short
written contract that says what each architecture needs to implement. That
is the part where we most need your opinion, and AMD's help.

## Why it matters for AMD

The KV cache is usually what limits how many long requests a GPU can serve,
and on AMD it has been the hardest part to shrink: the options below 8 bits
were built for CUDA or fall back to Triton. A native compressed cache changes
that, and at any scale, because the saving is a ratio of bytes. In the same
memory it holds 4.7× more tokens than fp16 and 2.4× more than fp8 or int8,
whether that memory is a 24 GB 7900 XTX or a 192 GB MI300X. The cost is small:
no measurable change on GSM8K, and a next-token NLL increase of about 0.001
nats at 380k that stays flat as the context grows.

The smaller cache is also faster. At long context attention is limited by
memory bandwidth, so reading 4.7× fewer bytes is where most of the 4× decode
speedup comes from, as long as the kernels read the packed cache directly
instead of expanding it first. On our four 7900 XTX that turned a box that
held one long request into one that serves about four at 512k, with decode at
127 tok/s at that length.

With the kernels this tight, attention stops being the part of the step that
grows with the context. With fp16 at 380k, attention took over the decode
step and generation fell to 2.7 tok/s. With Octave KV, going from 128k to
512k (four times the context) only takes decode from 153 to 127 tok/s; most
of the step is the rest of the model again, the same weights and all-reduce
you pay at short context. Prefill shows the same thing: at 100k all the
backends we tried are within 8% of each other, because the GEMMs and the
all-reduce dominate. Long context stops being a special, expensive case and
becomes close to the normal one.

Getting this much out of the hardware makes AMD GPUs, consumer cards and
Instinct alike, more competitive for long-context serving. We think a native
compressed cache is one of the pieces that can make AMD a first choice for
long-context serving rather than an alternative: the capacity gain holds on
every card, and on the one we could measure, long context costs close to what
short context does. We would like every ROCm user to have it without writing
their own kernels, which is why we want the format to cover the whole line.
We have now measured speed on two architectures: RDNA3 and, since October 20,
MI300X, where Octave KV holds about twice the tokens of AITER's fp8 cache at
the same speed (see "MI300X" under Numbers).

## What it is

`ROCM_OCTAVE` is an attention backend for the full-attention layers. You turn
it on with the cache dtype, `--kv-cache-dtype octave_k3v3` (or
`octave_k3v4`, `octave_k3v3_compact`). The name comes from the 3-bit codes:
each one indexes an eight-level codebook.

Each (token, KV head) is stored as one packed slot. Before quantizing we flip
signs at random and apply a Walsh-Hadamard rotation, which makes the
coordinates close to Gaussian, so a fixed Lloyd-Max codebook for N(0, 1) fits
any model without calibration. The kernels apply the codebook with one
`v_perm_b32` per four codes. Each vector gets one scale (four on the blocked
K layout), chosen so that `x · x̂ = |x|²`. We started with a least-squares
scale and it was clearly worse: it shrinks every vector a little, the softmax
gets flatter, and NLL at 380k came out 2-3× higher.

The three formats differ in how they treat K. V is always rotated over the
whole head:

| Cache dtype | K | V | Bytes per slot (head 256) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | whole head rotated, 3-bit | 3-bit | 196 |
| `octave_k3v3` | 4 blocks of 64: RoPE block 4-bit, the rest 3-bit | 3-bit | 216 |
| `octave_k3v4` | as above | 4-bit | 248 |

For reference, `turboquant_3bit_nc` is 198 bytes, `turboquant_k3v4_nc` 230,
int8 per-token-head 520 and fp16 1024.

Decode, MTP verification and prefill all read the packed cache directly;
there is no dequantized copy of the prefix. MTP verification was the case we
cared most about: the query tokens of one request share every K/V read, and
the whole decode path is captured in CUDA graphs. The backend has its own
metadata builder, which computes the per-query maps on the device without
host syncs.

## Written for the GPU

Most of the speed does not come from the format, it comes from writing each
kernel for what an AMD GPU does well, instead of going through Triton. A few
examples from the RDNA3 kernels:

- The codebook costs nothing. Each code is an index into an eight-entry
  table, and one `v_perm_b32` turns four codes into four int8 values. Nothing
  is dequantized to fp16 in memory; the cache stays packed until it is in
  registers.
- The products run on the matrix units straight from those codebook values.
  In prefill, QK is an int8 WMMA with one scale per 64-dim block applied
  afterwards; in decode the values go into fp16 WMMA with a constant offset
  that is removed in the softmax. PV uses fp16 WMMA with the V scale folded
  into the probabilities. The portable tier does the same with
  `v_dot4_i32_iu8` (`v_dot4_i32_i8` on gfx9).
- In decode, the query tokens of one request (the 4 tokens of an MTP
  verification, for instance) share every K/V tile, so verifying 4 tokens
  costs almost the same as decoding 1. Pairs of lanes share matrix fragments
  through a DPP swap.
- In prefill, 8 loader waves unpack 16-token tiles into double-buffered LDS
  one tile ahead of 16 compute waves, and the compute waves synchronize on LDS
  only, so the loaders' global reads stay in flight. The GQA heads of one KV
  head share every tile.
- Nothing waits for the host: the metadata is computed on the device, and the
  whole decode path, MTP included, is captured in CUDA graphs.

This is also why the backend is per architecture. The same ideas map to MFMA
and wave64 on CDNA, but the kernel that gets the most out of a MI300 is not
the one that gets the most out of a 7900 XTX. On MI300X (gfx942), for
instance:
- QK runs on the int8 MFMA with the query split into two int8 halves.
- V is widened to fp16 with a single `v_perm` that turns each codebook byte
  into an exact fp16 denormal, which the MI300 MFMA keeps.
- The decode is compiled with its accumulators in VGPRs so it keeps two waves
  per SIMD.

## The reference and the tests

The PyTorch reference in `vllm/v1/attention/ops/rocm_octave.py` defines the
byte layout, and every kernel is tested against it. There is no Triton
fallback on purpose. If an architecture is missing a kernel the backend
refuses to start and says which one, instead of running slowly without
anyone noticing.

## Numbers

Everything below was measured on 4× RX 7900 XTX (gfx1100), Qwen3.8-27B GPTQ
W4A16, TP4, 8 GB of KV cache per GPU, `--max-num-seqs 6`,
`--max-num-batched-tokens 2048`, CUDA graphs on. Only the cache dtype changes
between rows.

### Capacity and quality

GSM8K uses `tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py` (chat, thinking off, 500
questions, temperature 0.6, no MTP so that TurboQuant is correct; the noise
is about ±1.2 points). NLL is the next-token NLL over a single 380k-token
document.

| KV cache | Bytes | KV tokens | GSM8K | NLL over fp16 at 380k |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fp16 | 1024 | 445,825 | 91.8 | — |
| `turboquant_k3v4_nc` | 230 | 1,790,625 | 89.8 | +0.00155 |
| `turboquant_3bit_nc` | 198 | 2,053,571 | — | +0.00368 |
| `octave_k3v4` | 248 | 1,678,832 | 91.4 | +0.00086 |
| `octave_k3v3` | 216 | 1,897,520 | 92.4 | +0.00125 |
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | 196 | 2,068,468 | 91.8 | +0.00150 |

GSM8K cannot tell Octave KV from fp16. The NLL is where the formats separate.
At the size of `turboquant_3bit_nc`, the compact format loses 2.5× less, about
what `turboquant_k3v4_nc` loses with 34 more bytes. The blocked formats also
stay flat as the context grows; TurboQuant's error grows with it.

### Speed

Per layer, one TP4 shard (6 query heads, 1 KV head) at 380k tokens of
context, with `benchmarks/attention_benchmarks`:

| | fp16 | `turboquant_k3v4_nc` | `octave_k3v3_compact` | `octave_k3v3` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| decode, 1 token | 2370 µs | 2565 µs | 563 µs | 614 µs |
| MTP verify, 4 tokens | 48.8 ms | 6.65 ms | 0.58 ms | 0.62 ms |
| prefill, 2048-token chunk | 125.6 ms | 86.6 ms | 60.8 ms | 63.9 ms |

End to end with `vllm bench serve` (cold prefix, different seed per length,
MTP on), time to first token:

| | fp16 | `turboquant_k3v4_nc` | `octave_k3v3_compact` | `octave_k3v3` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100k | 61.5 s | 59.9 s* | 57.2 s | 56.7 s |
| 380k | 371 s | 621 s | 297 s | 300 s |

\* The first TurboQuant request at 100k took 155 s, probably a Triton compile
for new shapes; we report the second one.

At 100k the prefill is dominated by the model's GEMMs and all-reduce, so the
attention backend matters less. At 380k decode with MTP runs at 152 tok/s
with `octave_k3v3_compact` against 2.7 tok/s with fp16.


### Sparse attention: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (update, Oct 7)

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (`qwen4_exp`) uses sparse attention (QSA) in its
full-attention layers: each token attends to the 2048 positions an indexer
picks. The PR now has a sparse decode that reads the packed cache through
those top-k indices, so Octave KV can be the main KV cache there too.

4x RX 7900 XTX, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next GPTQ W4A16 (asymmetric, g32), TP4, fp16,
`--max-num-batched-tokens 512`, no prefix caching. NLL from
`prompt_logprobs` over 12 documents of ~8k tokens, split at position 2048
(where top-k starts to drop tokens), and over 24 short documents. Nats over
fp16; mean NLL repeats to about ±0.003 nats between runs.

| KV cache | KV tokens | NLL pos >= 2048 | NLL pos < 2048 | NLL short |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fp16 | 47,409 | 1.0856 | 1.6707 | 1.1788 |
| `octave_k3v3` | 155,930 | +0.0395 | +0.0851 | +0.0708 |
| `octave_k3v3` + fp16 window | 155,930 | +0.0163 | noise | +0.0085 |

This model is much harder on a 3-bit cache than the 27B. The protocol is not
the same as the 380k NLL above, but the gap is clear. Looking at real Q/K, its
attention is far sharper: the spread between median and p99 logits is 6-9
nats, the last 64 tokens take 35-80% of the attention mass in most layers,
and the first 4 take 15-40% in a few. When a few tokens carry most of the
mass, their quantization error is not averaged out over many others. Both
halves contribute (quantizing only V costs more than quantizing only K), and
giving K 4 bits did not move the result.

The window keeps the first 4 and the last 64 tokens in fp16 as well, in small
tables keyed by cache slot (~18 MB per layer, no change in capacity), and an
exact kernel adds them to the sparse decode as one more split. It removes
most of the loss. It lives in the QSA path only for now; see step 4 of the
plan and question 4.

These numbers come from our fork: the fp16 port of QSA and two fixes to the
RDNA3 W4A16 MoE path for compressed-tensors checkpoints go in separate PRs.

### MI300X (update, Oct 20)

AMD lent us an MI300X, and the PR now has native gfx942 kernels: MFMA
prefill and an MFMA decode. Everything else is shared with RDNA3.

1× MI300X, Qwen3.8-27B W4A16 (compressed-tensors, int4, group 32; to reproduce, [`cyankiwi/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4`](https://huggingface.co/cyankiwi/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4) is a public checkpoint with the same scheme and architecture, so KV token counts will differ only slightly), TP1, fp16, MTP k=3,
`--max-model-len 131072`; only the cache dtype changes between rows.
- GSM8K: chat, thinking off, 200 questions.
- NIAH: 16 look-alike keys in one 126k document, asked at 32k, 64k and 126k
  (28 questions).
- Speed: `vllm bench serve` with random prompts.
- The fp8 row is AITER's flash attention, forced with
  `--attention-backend ROCM_AITER_FA`. Without it vLLM picks `ROCM_ATTN` even
  with `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`.

| KV cache | KV tokens | GSM8K | NIAH | decode at 126k | TPOT 1 user, 8k / 32k / 100k | 16 users, 8k |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `octave_k3v3` | 7,014,973 | 98.0 | 28/28 | 52 tok/s | 15 / 18 / 16 ms | 221 tok/s |
| `octave_k3v4` | 6,391,547 | 97.5 | 28/28 | 52 tok/s | 15 / 15 / 19 ms | 226 tok/s |
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | 7,446,005 | 97.0 | 28/28 | 50 tok/s | 16 / 18 / 16 ms | 211 tok/s |
| fp8, `ROCM_AITER_FA` | 3,597,048 | 97.0 | 28/28 | 50 tok/s | 15 / 17 / 16 ms | 235 tok/s |
| fp16, `ROCM_ATTN` | 1,952,899 | 97.0 | 28/28 | 6 tok/s | 22 / 45 / 108 ms | 120 tok/s |

NIAH in detail. The haystack is vLLM's own Python source, tokenized and cut
to 126k tokens. 16 keys are inserted every ~7.7k tokens, each a line such as
`# PROJECT KEY Aldebaran: WK3DEGZD`, with star names as look-alike labels
and random 8-character values. The same document is then cut at 32k, 64k
and 126k, which hold 4, 8 and 16 keys. For each key present the model is
asked, thinking off, to answer only that key's value; an answer counts if it
contains the exact value. Keys sit between 3% and 95% of the context. We
also check whether an answer returns another key's value: none did.

| KV cache | 32k (4 keys) | 64k (8 keys) | 126k (16 keys) | another key's value returned |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `octave_k3v3` | 4/4 | 8/8 | 16/16 | 0 |
| `octave_k3v4` | 4/4 | 8/8 | 16/16 | 0 |
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | 4/4 | 8/8 | 16/16 | 0 |
| fp8, `ROCM_AITER_FA` | 4/4 | 8/8 | 16/16 | 0 |
| fp16, `ROCM_ATTN` | 4/4 | 8/8 | 16/16 | 0 |

The task is easy for this model at 128k, so all rows saturate. It shows that
the 3-bit cache loses no retrieval up to the model's served window here,
not that it beats fp8. The harder test is the 800k curve in the RFC, where
the keys start to blur only past 640k, from the model and not from the cache.

`vllm bench serve` in detail. Random prompts (`--dataset-name random`),
512 output tokens with `--ignore-eos`, `--seed 0`, no prefix reuse. Runs:
- 6 prompts at 8k, 4 at 32k and 3 at 100k, one at a time;
- 64 prompts at 8k with 16 concurrent.

No request failed. Each cell is median TTFT / median TPOT / output tok/s.
Random tokens give MTP a low acceptance, so TPOT is higher than on real
text, the same for every row.

| KV cache | 8k, 1 user | 32k, 1 user | 100k, 1 user | 8k, 16 users |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `octave_k3v3` | 1.55 s / 15.3 ms / 51.3 | 5.99 s / 18.1 ms / 33.4 | 20.2 s / 15.6 ms / 17.9 | 3.34 s / 62.1 ms / 221 |
| `octave_k3v4` | 1.55 s / 15.4 ms / 52.4 | 6.06 s / 15.3 ms / 35.8 | 20.2 s / 19.2 ms / 17.1 | 3.95 s / 57.0 ms / 226 |
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | 1.57 s / 16.2 ms / 50.2 | 6.73 s / 17.6 ms / 32.4 | 20.1 s / 15.6 ms / 17.9 | 3.27 s / 57.2 ms / 211 |
| fp8, `ROCM_AITER_FA` | 1.57 s / 15.2 ms / 49.3 | 5.53 s / 17.1 ms / 34.1 | 18.6 s / 16.2 ms / 19.0 | 3.29 s / 49.9 ms / 235 |
| fp16, `ROCM_ATTN` | 1.64 s / 22.5 ms / 36.8 | 5.78 s / 44.6 ms / 16.9 | 23.1 s / 108.4 ms / 6.2 | 7.26 s / 112.4 ms / 120 |

Without MTP, to compare with UltraQuant, which needs bf16 here:

| KV cache | 8k, 1 user | 32k, 1 user | 100k, 1 user | 8k, 16 users |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `octave_k3v3` (fp16) | 1.57 s / 51.9 ms / 18.2 | 5.28 s / 52.2 ms / 16.0 | 19.1 s / 52.6 ms / 11.1 | 10.9 s / 82.0 ms / 157 |
| `ultraquant_4bit` (bf16) | 1.84 s / 58.5 ms / 16.1 | 6.24 s / 66.0 ms / 12.8 | 20.3 s / 87.5 ms / 7.9 | 14.0 s / 94.5 ms / 135 |

Without MTP the Octave TPOT is flat at ~52 ms from 8k to 100k: on gfx942 the
step is the W4A16 GEMMs, and attention adds almost nothing as the context
grows.

On one MI300X that is 53 concurrent requests of 128k with `octave_k3v3`,
against 27 with fp8 and 15 with fp16. For one request Octave KV runs at
AITER's speed, and per layer its decode is faster from 32k on (65 vs 103 µs
at 128k). AITER is still ahead with 16 users at 8k and in time to first token
at 100k (18.6 vs 20.2 s), which points at our prefill over a cached prefix.

We also ran UltraQuant (#57057) on the same setup, in bf16 as it requires.
On gfx942 its FlyDSL decode is not used (it is written for gfx950 and does
not cover 6 query heads per KV head), so it runs its Triton fallback:
- With MTP k=3 the output was not usable: GSM8K 1.0%, NIAH 0/28, answers
  repeating their first characters.
- Without MTP it is correct: 7,730,626 tokens, GSM8K 98.0, NIAH 28/28.
  `octave_k3v3` without MTP holds 9,437,184 tokens and decodes at 19.0 vs
  10.4 tok/s at 126k.

This says nothing about UltraQuant on gfx950, which is the hardware it was
written for.

### In production

We switched two boxes from int8 per-token-head to `octave_k3v3` (it is still
called `splitq_k3v3` in our fork). On the same image and flags, checked on a
local copy before switching:

| | int8 per-token-head | `octave_k3v3` |
|---|---|---|
| KV cache tokens | 961,194 | 2,142,148 |
| Decode step, 1 / 2 / 4 users, short context | 15.91 / 18.05 / 23.02 ms | 16.19 / 18.41 / 23.26 ms |
| MTP acceptance | 67.6-68.2% | 67.6-68.0% |

At short context we pay 1-2% per step, probably the fixed cost of the
rotations (we have not profiled it). What we gain is capacity, and speed at
long context. Both boxes now serve 512k-token contexts, with room for about
four such requests at once.

One thing that will surprise other users of hybrid models: vLLM sizes the
scheduler block so that one attention page matches one GDN state page. A
smaller KV slot makes the block longer, 1,584 tokens with int8 and 3,792 with
`octave_k3v3`. Flags that must be a multiple of the block, such as
`--prefix-cache-retention-interval`, have to follow it or the engine will not
start, and the prefix cache becomes coarser: the next turn of a conversation
can recompute up to one block.

### How far the context goes

We were curious whether the 3-bit cache would be what limits context, so we
raised `max_model_len` to 820k and built one document from vLLM's own source
code, with 16 look-alike keys ("CLAVE DEL PROYECTO <star>: <8 chars>") every
50k tokens. At each length we asked for every key present. The model was
trained to 262k and we did not scale RoPE:

| Context | Keys retrieved | Decode with MTP |
|---|---|---|
| 128k | 3/3 | 153 tok/s |
| 256k | 5/5 | 140 tok/s |
| 512k | 10/10 | 127 tok/s |
| 640k | 13/13 | 107 tok/s |
| 800k | 13/16 | 95 tok/s |

At 800k the model starts to answer three of the keys with the most recent
one. It confuses them, it does not produce garbage. This is one document and
an easy task, so we read it as an upper bound, but it suggests the format is
not the bottleneck: retrieval holds until the model itself starts to blur.

## A contract per architecture

Most of the backend is portable HIP that runs on wave32 and wave64 alike: the
cache store, the split-KV reduce, the rotation and a dot4 decode. What each
architecture has to add is one native prefill kernel and, if it wants to be
fast, a decode on its matrix instructions. Following the review on the PR,
Octave is built and selected only on the architectures it has been validated
on, gfx1100 and gfx942, and each new one is added once it passes the tests
and an end-to-end run. This is where things stand:

| Target | GPUs | Decode | Prefill |
|---|---|---|---|
| gfx1100 (RDNA3) | RX 7900 XTX/XT/GRE, PRO W7900/W7800 | WMMA | WMMA, in this PR |
| gfx942 (CDNA3) | MI300X/MI325X | MFMA | MFMA, in this PR |
| gfx1101-1103 (RDNA3) | RX 7800/7700/7600, PRO W7700/W7600 | — | same kernels as gfx1100, not yet validated |
| gfx1150/1151 (RDNA3.5) | Ryzen AI 300, Ryzen AI Max (Strix Halo) | portable | missing; same WMMA as RDNA3, so probably only wider guards |
| gfx1200/1201 (RDNA4) | RX 9070/9060, Radeon AI PRO R9700 | portable | missing; needs a port of the WMMA kernels to the gfx12 layout |
| gfx950 (CDNA4) | MI350X/MI355X | portable | missing; the gfx942 kernels plus the new FP8/FP4 MFMA |
| gfx90a (CDNA2) | MI210/MI250X | portable | missing; a new kernel on MFMA |

"Portable" means the shared HIP kernels would compile there, but the backend
is not built or selected on those targets until they are validated; the test
suite runs the portable decode next to the native one on gfx1100 and gfx942.

A new kernel can be HIP or FlyDSL. FlyDSL looks like a good fit for CDNA, and
it would add a runtime dependency, which is one of our open questions below.
Whatever the language, it keeps the signature of `octave_prefill`, passes
`tests/kernels/attention/test_rocm_octave.py` against the reference, and is
is added to the CMake guard, `_kernel_tier` and `supports_compute_capability`. For every new path we also break
the kernel on purpose once and check that the tests catch it.

The backend states what it does not support, and vLLM rejects it at startup:
head sizes other than 256 for now, sliding windows, ALiBi, sinks, soft-cap,
and bidirectional attention over image tokens. One limit depends on the
tensor-parallel size rather than on the model: the decode handles 1, 2, 4, 6
or 8 query heads per KV head on each GPU, so Qwen3.5-122B needs TP 4 or more.

This is what we would like to ask AMD for, if the direction makes sense to
you:

1. A review of the format and the contract, as a common basis for compressed
   KV caches on ROCm.
2. Help with gfx950 and the RDNA4 port. gfx942 is done, thanks to the MI300X
   AMD lent us. We are happy to review against the tests and to help with
   the format side.
3. Running `test_rocm_octave.py` on the AMD CI runners.
4. Access to a gfx1151 and a gfx1201 machine, which we cannot test today.

## Models

Today the kernels need head size 256 with 64 RoPE dims, which is the
Qwen3-Next / Qwen3.5 / 3.6 / 3.8 family, dense and MoE. We run Qwen3.8-27B,
and since October 7 also Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, whose sparse attention (QSA)
uses Octave KV as its main cache through a sparse decode (see "Sparse
attention" above). The 35B-A3B, 80B-A3B, 9B and 4B models of that family have
the same shape but we have not run them.

Most other models use head size 128. Those with partial RoPE (GLM-4.5/4.6,
MiniMax-M2) fit the blocked layout as it is, and those with full RoPE (Llama,
Qwen3, Mistral and others) can use the compact layout, which does not care
about RoPE. Templating the kernels on head size is our next step. We also
tried Gemma 4 26B-A4B; it does not start on gfx1100 even with Triton and fp16,
because of its 512-dim heads, so it would need its own kernels.

## Plan

1. This PR: the backend, the three formats, the shared kernels, and the
   decode and prefill for RDNA3 (gfx1100) and MI300X (gfx942), for head size
   256.
2. Head size 128, validated on models that fit our boxes
   (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, and GLM-4.5-Air if it fits).
3. The rest of the AMD line, following the contract, hopefully with AMD.
4. Keeping the first and the last tokens in fp16. On real Q/K/V of the 27B,
   keeping the first 16 and the last 256 cuts the attention error of the
   compact format from 14.6% to 5.9%. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next it is not
   optional: keeping the first 4 and the last 64 takes the NLL cost from
   +0.040 to +0.016 nats after position 2048, and from +0.071 to +0.009 on
   short documents (Oct 7, see "Sparse attention"). A first version lives in
   the QSA path of the PR. It is not specific to this backend, so we would
   still rather design the general mechanism with you than grow it inside
   one.

## Questions for you

1. Is a backend tied to one attention shape acceptable for a first PR (as the
   MLA backends are), with head size 128 as a follow-up?
2. Is "native kernels only, fail at startup otherwise" the right policy for a
   ROCm-only backend, or would you rather have a slow portable prefill?
3. Would a FlyDSL dependency be acceptable for the CDNA kernels, and how
   should it be declared?
4. Should the fp16 window from step 4 be a general KV-cache mechanism in
   vLLM?
5. On hybrid models, should flags tied to the block size (like the
   retention interval) be given in tokens and rounded by vLLM instead of
   being rejected?

## Related work

TurboQuant (#38479) gave us the starting point. We differ in the V quantizer
(Lloyd-Max instead of uniform min/max), the norm-preserving scale, the
RoPE-aware K blocks, and in reading the packed cache in every phase with
native kernels. The compact layout rotates the whole K head at 3 bits like
`turboquant_3bit_nc`, which makes the comparison direct; we have not isolated
which of the differences matters most.

Other related work: UltraQuant (#57057, FP4 with FlyDSL on gfx950, built on
TurboQuant), KVarN (#46613 / #46812, Triton, int4 K / int2 V), #43835 (HIP
int8/int4 per-token-head for CDNA), #40396 (a Triton decode for TurboQuant on
MI300X), #53231 (TurboQuant for Gemma 4 on ROCm) and #59132
(`ROCM_SEGMENTED_ATTN`, Triton attention for RDNA with fp16/bf16 KV, which
covers many of the shapes we reject).

We used AI assistance to write kernels, tests and this text: Claude, and
Qwen3.8-27B itself, served on these same boxes, so the model helped build the
cache it now runs on. Every number here was measured on the hardware
described, and I have reviewed the code and can answer for it.

cc @tjtanaa @dllehr-amd @hongxiayang @AndreasKaratzas @BowenBao @mgehre-amd
(ROCm) · @LucasWilkinson @MatthewBonanni (attention backends) · @sighingnow
(Qwen models, since these kernels target the Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 attention shape)

title: [Performance]: Avoid runtime routed_scaling_factor multiply between all-reduce and GEMM (MoE)
body: ### Proposal to improve performance On ROCm (confirmed on AMD Instinct MI350X / gfx950), for any MoE model that sets `apply_routed_scale_to_output=True`, `MoERunner.forward()` in `vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/runner/moe_runner.py` applies the model's `routed_scaling_factor` as a standalone elementwise multiply positioned directly between the routed-output all-reduce and the subsequent output-transform GEMM. Under `torch.compile`, this multiply compiles to its own kernel launch (`triton_poi_fused_mul_2` in the traces below), introducing a small but measurable stall on the critical path between a collective-communication op and a GEMM — exactly where launch/synchronization overhead is most expensive relative to useful work. This was identified during an MI350-vs-B200 comparative performance gap analysis: no equivalent stall was observed on B200 for the same workload, pointing at this as a ROCm/AITER-path-specific inefficiency rather than an architectural requirement of the model. ### Confirmed code path (traced end-to-end in `moe_runner.py`) In `MoERunner.forward()`, the following methods execute in this exact order: 1. `_maybe_reduce_routed_output_before_transform()` → calls `tensor_model_parallel_all_reduce(fused_output)` 2. `_maybe_reduce_shared_expert_output()` → separate reduce for the shared-expert path 3. `_maybe_apply_routed_scale_to_output()` → `fused_output *= self.routed_scaling_factor` (BF16/FP32 branch; the FP16 branch instead scales the shared-expert output inversely to avoid overflow) 4. `apply_routed_output_transform()` → the model's output-side projection (for NemotronH's latent-space MoE, this is `fc2_latent_proj`, a `ReplicatedLinear` projecting `moe_latent_size` back to `hidden_size`) 5. `_maybe_reduce_final_output()` Step 3 sits directly between step 1 (the all-reduce) and step 4 (the GEMM), matching the observed stall position exactly. ### Observed trace evidence Three kernels run back-to-back with no gap on the GPU stream: | Kernel | Duration | Role | |---|---:|---| | `aiter::cross_device_reduce_2stage` | 7.24us | AITER's custom two-stage cross-device all-reduce (not RCCL/NCCL — a peer-to-peer kernel using `RankSignals`/`Signal*`) | | `triton_poi_fused_mul_2` | 4.80us | The `routed_scaling_factor` multiply (Inductor-generated) | | `gemm_a16w16_kernel_BLOCK_SIZE_M_32...` |10.68us | The output-transform GEMM (`fc2_latent_proj`) | ### Report of performance regression _No response_ ### Misc discussion on performance This is a performance characteristic of the MoE runner's op ordering, not a crash — it reproduces on any model/config where `apply_routed_scale_to_output=True` and the fused output is BF16/FP32, run on ROCm with the AITER backend and `torch.compile` enabled. ### environment - Hardware: AMD Instinct MI350X (gfx950), 8x GPU node - ROCm: hip_runtime_version 70253211, roctracer 4.1 - Model: nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-BF16 (NemotronH architecture) - Parallelism: Tensor Parallel, ranks 0-2 captured (TP0/TP1/TP2), - AITER: enabled (confirmed via aiter-namespaced kernel names present in trace, e.g. aiter::cross_device_reduce_2stage) - torch.compile: active (NemotronHForCausalLM is decorated with @support_torch_compile; triton_poi_fused_mul_2 is an Inductor-generated kernel name, not hand-written Triton) ``` ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [ROCm][AMD] Qwen3.8-Flash-Next gfx950 / MI355X Performance Optimization
body:
### Proposal to improve performance

This issue is the gfx950 / MI355X performance optimization plan and tracker for `amd/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Quark-MXFP4` (`qwen4_exp`: GatedDeltaNet in 36 layers, QuerySparse Attention in 12, HyperConnection gated residual, MXFP4 MoE). The work below lands as PRs on main.

Related: #57149 (Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B on MI355X). 

CC:
@tjtanaa, @jhartika-amd, @maeehart, @nholmber, @damien-lejeune, @SamiAario-AMD

Tasks:

| Area | Uplift item | Expected uplift | Primary metric | Status | vLLM PR | Dependency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
