title: [Performance]: [MRV2][PP]: Post sampled-result receives closer to T+PP consumption
body: ## Proposal to improve performance ### TL;DR - In MRV2 pipeline parallelism, non-last ranks can post sampled-result receives several local feedback steps before consumption. A receiver-side NCCL kernel can remain active while independent model work runs. - Deferring PP4 receivers by three feedback steps improved output throughput by approximately 18% on a short-generation, prefill-heavy workload and by 4--6% on two decode-heavy workload classes, with all requests completing. - Moving a due delayed receive from before to after the current model execution produced another 4.8% gain on the prefill-heavy workload in a same-configuration comparison and nearly eliminated sampled-result receive/model overlap in the captured PP0 window. - The current best jointly tuned configuration combines delay 3, post-model launch, and a retuned PP partition. Relative to the earlier delay-3 configurations, it improves output throughput by approximately 5--11% across the three workload classes. Those numbers are combined tuning results, not isolated post-model effects. - Draft PR [#53948](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53948) currently contains the deferred-receive prototype only. The post-model ordering experiment is a separate follow-up prototype and is not yet in that PR. ### Summary Model Runner V2 pipeline parallelism returns sampled results from the last PP rank to every non-last rank. The CUDA implementation uses a sibling process group and side stream, as introduced by [#42187](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42187). However, a non-last rank posts its receive in local feedback step `T`, while the result is not consumed until `T + pp_size`. If the last rank has not produced the result yet, the receiver-side NCCL broadcast kernel can remain active across several intervening model executions. A side stream removes default-stream ordering, but does not isolate GPU execution and communication resources. The pending receive can therefore slow otherwise independent model work. If its CUDA event is still incomplete at `T + pp_size`, the main stream must also wait before applying the sampled result. This issue proposes an opt-in just-in-time receiver policy: - keep the last rank's source broadcast at its current point; - save receive metadata at feedback step `T`; - post non-last-rank receives closer to consumption; and - preserve the existing `T + pp_size` event wait as the correctness fallback. For `pp_size=4`, the first prototype uses delay 3: ```text Current: T post recv [possibly resident----------------------] consume at T+4 Deferred: T save receive metadata T+3 post recv [-------] consume at T+4 ``` A follow-up variant keeps delay 3 but posts the due receive *after* the current model execution instead of immediately before it: ```text T+3 before-model: post recv -> model work -> consume later T+3 post-model: model work -> post recv -> consume later ``` The follow-up does not add another scheduler-step delay. It changes only the ordering within the due local step, reducing the final interval in which the receiver kernel can overlap model work. Implementation status: - Draft PR [#53948](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53948) contains the opt-in receiver-delay implementation. - The post-model ordering variant is currently a separate experimental patch. Its results should not be interpreted as validation of the current PR head. ### Trace-guided mechanism The following reconstruction shows the two distinct costs. The long receive lifetimes are not equivalent to wire-transfer time or to one continuous hard wait: several pending receives can overlap model work, and only an event that is still incomplete at consumption causes the correctness wait. An older causal reconstruction also shows why CPU `execute_model` annotations must not be read as GPU execution boundaries. GPU work can lag host enqueue, while a receiver-side broadcast remains active. The red spans below are receiver-kernel lifetimes, not approximately 900 ms of payload transfer. ### Three mechanisms that should not be conflated 1. **Pending-receive interference.** A receiver collective is active while independent model work runs. Deferred or post-model posting targets this cost. 2. **Correctness wait.** At `T + pp_size`, the main stream must wait if the sampled result is still unavailable. Receiver deferral must preserve this wait and must not hide an increase in it. 3. **EngineCore queue depth.** MRV2 normally queues `pp_size + 1` batches to overlap host scheduling and worker execution. This extra queue entry does not change the sampled-result consume cadence of `pp_size` steps or shorten an already-posted receive. ### What the traces establish In two immediate-receive PP4 profiles, roughly one third of eligible sampled results were still incomplete when observed at their `T+4` consume point. The resulting hard waits were large enough to be visible as pipeline holes. This does **not** prove that PP3 compute alone was late. An incomplete event means that the complete source/collective/receiver path had not finished. Source production, stream backlog, transport progress, or receiver progress can all contribute. Deferral also changes the meaning of this metric. With delay 3, the receiver joins near local step `T+3`, and receiver launch is ordered after already enqueued local main-stream work. An incomplete event at `T+4` can therefore also mean that the receiver was posted too late in physical time to finish. Immediate- and delay-3 unready rates must not be compared as if both measured only source lateness. Nsight Systems establishes overlap and receiver-stage slowdown, but it does not identify the exact contested GPU resource. SM residency, warp scheduling, cache or memory traffic, and NCCL progress remain hypotheses until supported by lower-level counters. ### Result provenance The headline historical delay-3 and post-model experiments used a derived artifact based on vLLM revision [`ac7509e2`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/ac7509e2b1db). They establish the performance mechanism on that source line, but they are not performance measurements of the current PR head on current `main`. PR #53948 was separately tested on an official nightly based on revision [`46638857`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/46638857fdbb30e0c232c9e8f9cb1ff6d6f545c3). For the same short-generation, prefill-heavy workload class, delay 3 produced a 16.1% relative gain over immediate receive. Absolute throughput was lower than on the older source line before and after enabling delay 3, so current-main performance remains a separate issue from the deferred-receive mechanism. ### Immediate receive versus delay 3 The primary experiment used the public Kimi-K3 model in a multi-node PP4 configuration with Model Runner V2, asynchronous scheduling, CUDA graphs, Marlin MoE, FlashInfer autotuning, no expert parallelism, and no prefix cache. Each row compares otherwise equivalent runs for that workload class; scheduling limits were tuned by class. | Generic workload class | Delay-3 output-throughput change | Completion | |---|---:|---:| | Short generation, prefill-heavy | **approximately +18%** | All requests | | Long generation, decode-heavy | **approximately +4%** | All requests | | Very long generation, decode-heavy | **approximately +5%** | All requests | For the prefill-heavy workload, a matched Nsight capture showed: | Metric | Observed change with delay 3 | |---|---:| | Interior PP0 gaps at least 500 ms | **Eliminated in the capture** | | Largest interior PP0 gap | **Reduced by approximately 76%** | | PP0 median model time | **Reduced by approximately 21%** | | PP1 median model time | **Reduced by approximately 30%** | | PP2 median model time | **Reduced by approximately 22%** | | PP3 median model time | Approximately unchanged | The unchanged PP3 time is consistent with the mechanism: PP3 is the source, whereas PP0--PP2 are early receivers. All three non-last ranks participate; PP0 tends to expose the pause most clearly because it reaches the feedback dependency first, while PP1 and PP2 can hide part of the wait behind upstream activation dependencies. ### Before-model versus post-model launch Delay 3 still leaves approximately one local scheduler step in which the receive can overlap model execution. A follow-up prefill-heavy experiment moved the due receive from before to after current model execution. The following full-window runs used the same short-generation, prefill-heavy workload, image, PP partition, scheduling limits, receive delay, and concurrency. Both runs completed all requests. | Due receive placement | Output throughput | Total throughput | p50 latency | p99 latency | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Before model execution | Baseline | Baseline | Baseline | Baseline | | **After model execution** | **+4.8%** | **+4.8%** | **-5.9%** | **-5.5%** | These are same-configuration runs, not a serialized same-allocation A/B, so the result should be reproduced before treating 4.8% as a general gain. A separate pair of Nsight captures provides stronger mechanism evidence but is not a throughput A/B: both used delay 3 and the same PP partition, while the sequence-admission limit differed. | Receive placement | PP0 model time | PP1 | PP2 | PP3 | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Before model execution | Baseline | Baseline | Baseline | Baseline | | **After model execution** | **approximately -21%** | Approximately unchanged | Approximately unchanged | Approximately unchanged | In those captured windows: - PP0 sampled-result broadcast/model-compute overlap was nearly eliminated; - recurring large PP0 gaps became one residual large gap; and - that remaining gap was dominated by pipeline `SendRecv`, not the sampled-result broadcast. PP0 improved while PP1--PP3 remained nearly unchanged, which is consistent with removing the last due-receive overlap from PP0 model execution. The result also changes the stage balance: PP2 becomes the slowest stage, so a PP partition tuned around the interfered PP0 time may need retuning after this optimization. With the previously tuned PP partition, post-model placement improved the long-generation workload by 2.4%, below the approximately 3% single-run repeatability threshold, and regressed the very-long-generation workload by 1.5%. This shows that receive placement alone is not a universal win. Both workloads reached 100% KV usage and performed repeated preemptions, so stage balance, KV capacity, and recomputation also matter. Retuning the PP partition after removing PP0 receive interference produced the following best full-window results. The comparison baseline is the earlier delay-3 configuration for each workload. The current rows combine post-model placement with PP-stage retuning; the prefill-heavy row also changes the sequence-admission limit. | Generic workload class | Change versus earlier delay-3 configuration | |---|---:| | Short generation, prefill-heavy | **approximately +11%** | | Long generation, decode-heavy | **approximately +10%** | | Very long generation, decode-heavy | **approximately +5%** | The prefill-heavy configuration was repeated with receive-wait telemetry and reproduced within 0.1%. The two decode-heavy rows are single full-window results. Because the partition changed, this table must not be cited as an isolated post-model A/B. It shows that stage balancing should be repeated after receive interference is removed. This optimization should remain opt-in until it is reproduced across models, allocations, and PP sizes. ### Current source behavior At the source revision used to open this issue, [`d591d1d5`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/d591d1d511b5f2a70ae34adfd5adc5c1956ecae2): - [`PPHandler.receive()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/d591d1d511b5f2a70ae34adfd5adc5c1956ecae2/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pp_utils.py#L126-L168) immediately posts sampled-token and count broadcasts on `broadcast_stream`; - the non-last-rank FIFO is pre-seeded with `pp_size` entries; and - [`get_prev_sampled_outputs()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/d591d1d511b5f2a70ae34adfd5adc5c1956ecae2/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pp_utils.py#L93-L124) later consumes the slot and calls `main_stream.wait_event(slot.event)`. The delay is a local PP feedback-step cadence, not a wall-clock interval. Variable stage durations can therefore leave very different physical lead times between receive posting and consumption. ### Why a side stream is not sufficient PR #42187 correctly removes stream and communicator serialization from normal PP traffic. An unmatched receiver-side collective can nevertheless remain active while waiting for the last rank to publish its data. Closed PR [#47686](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47686) describes related early receiver-side LL-kernel spinning and proposes packing feedback fields into fewer collectives. Packing reduces the number of kernels; later receive placement reduces their lifetime. The ideas are complementary. ### Prototype implementation Draft PR [#53948](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53948) adds the receiver-delay setting: ```bash VLLM_PP_DEFER_SAMPLED_TOKEN_RECV= ``` The prototype has these properties: 1. Delay `0` retains the current immediate-receive path, including stream and allocation ordering. 2. A nonzero delay requires CUDA, Model Runner V2, asynchronous scheduling, and `1 <= delay < pp_size`; invalid settings fail during configuration. 3. PP3 still posts its source broadcast immediately. Non-last ranks preserve the tensors, request-slot mapping, liveness mask, and generation snapshot, then post receives in FIFO order at `T + delay`. 4. Sender and receivers use the same skip predicate for non-final chunked prefills and requests that finish after sampling, preserving collective order and symmetry. 5. Consumption remains at `T + pp_size`. An unexpectedly unposted receive is launched defensively, and the existing event wait preserves correctness. 6. Pending receives are posted at idle boundaries and before shutdown. 7. Normal performance runs avoid event-query synchronization. Optional diagnostics measure readiness and main-stream wait time at consumption. The source can be posted before its matching receive without changing collective order, provided every participating rank executes the same FIFO of matching broadcasts and shutdown drains that FIFO before communicator destruction. The separate post-model follow-up prototype adds: ```bash VLLM_PP_POST_MODEL_SAMPLED_TOKEN_RECV=1 ``` It currently requires a nonzero receive delay and was tested with delay 3. It adds one ordering rule: when a delayed receive becomes due, launch it after the current model execution but before a boundary at which its result may be consumed, flushed, or destroyed. This setting and its implementation are not yet part of PR #53948. ### Correctness invariants and risks The implementation must preserve: - identical collective order, shape, row count, and dtype on all ranks; - association between step-`T` feedback and its saved request-slot mapping; - generation and liveness checks across abort, preemption, and slot reuse; - the existing `T + pp_size` decode-eligibility cadence; - non-final chunked-prefill behavior; - no unnecessary receive for requests that finish after the first sample; - explicit drain before shutdown or communicator destruction; and - safe CUDA-graph warmup and capture boundaries. Receiver deferral can move contention to the source rank if the source is posted much earlier than its matching receivers. Evaluation must measure both source- and receiver-side residency. Other risks include collective-order mismatch on empty steps, insufficient lead time on slower topologies, abort cleanup, and backend-specific stream/event behavior. Two historical failure modes are especially important: - independently choosing delays by PP rank broke collective FIFO order; and - delaying the source together with the receivers deadlocked. The safe baseline is therefore one common receiver delay, an immediate source, and an explicit finite drain. ### Required telemetry Performance results are difficult to interpret without aggregate counters. The opt-in diagnostic mode should report: - deferred launches; - idle-boundary flushes; - defensive consume fallbacks; - receives unready at `T + pp_size`; - total and maximum main-stream wait time at consumption; and - receives still pending at shutdown. The counters should avoid per-step logging and should not add event-query overhead to normal performance runs. ### Suggested public reproducer Use a public PP-compatible model and fixed synthetic prompts. Compare otherwise identical workloads: 1. `max_tokens=1`: the request finishes after final-prefill sampling, so no sampled result is needed for another decode step; 2. `max_tokens=2`: the first sampled token must return before the next decode step. Controls: - Model Runner V2; - `pipeline_parallel_size > 1`; - asynchronous scheduling; - fixed input length and `--ignore-eos`; - prefix caching disabled; - identical concurrency and request count; and - enough requests to exclude startup and drain effects. Compare three receiver policies while holding all other settings fixed: 1. immediate receive; 2. delayed receive before current model execution; and 3. delayed receive after current model execution. Capture Nsight Systems on at least the first and last PP ranks. Record: - receive-post time on each non-last rank; - source-post time on the last rank; - readiness at the next step and at `T + pp_size`; - time blocked by `main_stream.wait_event()`; - lifetime of the selected NCCL broadcast kernel; - overlap between that kernel and model kernels; and - model-kernel duration with and without a pending receive. ### Acceptance criteria - Identical deterministic outputs to current `main`. - No deadlock or collective mismatch during startup, steady state, empty steps, abort, preemption, finite drain, or shutdown. - Lower receiver-side NCCL/model-work overlap without harmful source-side residency. - No increase in hard-wait frequency or time at `T + pp_size`. - No material regression at low concurrency or for one-output requests. - Reproduced throughput and latency results across multiple allocations. - Validation on at least PP2 and PP4 before considering a default. ### Related upstream work - [#42187](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42187), merged: introduced the current MRV2 feedback cadence and sibling stream/process group. - [#47686](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47686), closed: proposed packing feedback fields and documented early receiver-side LL-kernel spinning. - [#50853](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/50853), open RFC: broader MRV2 PP composition and deferred-result transport. - [#50410](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50410), open prototype: balances admission across PP batches; it changes work availability rather than receive placement. - [#51650](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51650), merged: overlaps sampled-token broadcast with compute on XPU. ## Report of performance regression This is not presented as a regression. PR #42187 is necessary and improves PP overlap. This proposal targets residual contention when asynchronous receives are posted substantially before source data exists. ## Misc discussion on performance The intended changes affect receiver timing only. The sampled-result dependency, collective order, consume cadence, and correctness wait remain unchanged. ## Current environment The results above used a multi-node NVIDIA GPU environment with PP4, Model Runner V2, asynchronous scheduling, and CUDA graphs. The result-provenance section names the public vLLM source revisions. A public reproducer should add sanitized `collect_env.py` output with exact CUDA, NCCL, PyTorch, and driver revisions. No private hostnames, absolute filesystem paths, scheduler identifiers, credentials, or model artifacts are included in this draft. ## Validation status - [x] Searched related public issues and PRs. - [x] Confirmed the referenced source behavior at a pinned public commit. - [x] Separated receive placement, correctness waits, and queue depth. - [x] Opened draft prototype [#53948](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53948). - [x] Added focused tests for delay `0`, PP2/PP4 cadence, empty-step flushing, skip symmetry, fallback, and finite/idempotent drain. - [x] Completed end-to-end delay-3 runs with no failed benchmark requests in the three reported workloads. - [x] Measured the post-model launch variant on all three reported workloads and profiled its prefill-heavy overlap. - [x] Reproduced the best prefill-heavy combined configuration within 0.1%. - [ ] Publish the separate post-model implementation in PR #53948 or a dedicated follow-up PR. - [ ] Add a public-model synthetic reproducer. - [ ] Add sanitized `collect_env.py` output and public trace attachments. - [ ] Repeat the same-allocation prefill-heavy post-model A/B. - [ ] Validate GPU execution on PP2 and on current `main` before proposing an upstream default.

title: [Performance]: DSA indexer is computed redundantly on every TP rank (NVIDIA / CUDA)
body:
### Proposal to improve performance

On DeepSeek-V4-Flash the DSA indexer is executed in full on **every tensor-parallel rank**, so with
TP=8 seven eighths of that work is duplicated. It is **15.9 % of prefill GPU time** at ISL 131072 on
8×H100. The redundancy is recoverable by sharding the **query-row** dimension — rows are independent,
so only the int32 top-k indices need merging (16 MB, not the `q × N` logits tensor).

I implemented this out-of-tree and measured **+7.1 % prefill at ISL 65536 and +13.8 % at 131072**
(concurrency 1, intervals disjoint). I then hit a **reproducible, silent correctness regression at
concurrency > 1** that I could not localise after nine falsified hypotheses, so I am filing this
analysis rather than a PR. This box covers the optimisation and how I built it; **the correctness
problem, the offline harness that reproduces cleanly, and the attached code are in the
"Misc discussion on performance" box below.**

#### The deployment these numbers come from

**Everything here is NVIDIA CUDA:** 8×H100 (SM90), vLLM commit `6f91edf96d3f3272945809c04702380053bff4de`
(`0.26.1rc1.dev77+g6f91edf96`), DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, TP=8, `pcp=1, dcp=1`, `compress_ratio=4`,
`index_topk=512`, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, `--block-size 256`, `--max-num-batched-tokens 8192`,
`--max-model-len 262144`, backend `DeepseekV4FlashMLAAttention` → `flash_mla_sparse_fwd`.
Full `collect_env.py` output is in the environment box at the end.

#### How this relates to #30055

**[#30055](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/30055) ("[RFC]: Sharded Context Parallelism for
Deepseek DSA")** is the nearest existing discussion and should be read alongside this. I am filing
separately rather than commenting there because the two are different cases and one of its premises
needs correcting:

| | #30055 | this issue |
|---|---|---|
| hardware | **Ascend 910C NPU**; implementation in `vllm-ascend` (PRs #4702 / #2931), no PR into vllm main | **NVIDIA H100 / CUDA**, no numbers of this kind in that thread |
| where the redundancy is | *between CP ranks* — "every CP rank must independently execute the full Indexer logic" | *between TP ranks inside a single CP rank* (`pcp = dcp = 1`, so by #30055's description this deployment should have none — yet the indexer is 15.9 % of prefill) |
| premise | "the Indexer module … **cannot be parallelized via TP**" | half right — see §1: not by head, but **yes by query row** |
| status | open since 2025-12-04, no maintainer response | — |

I checked `main` today: `sparse_attn_indexer.py` still has no `get_tensor_model_parallel_rank/world_size`,
no TP-aware query-row partitioning, and no cross-TP merge of top-k indices. The only collective there
is `get_dcp_group().all_gather()`, which is the orthogonal (context) axis. **The redundancy is
unaddressed upstream**, and #30055's proposal would not remove it for a `pcp = dcp = 1` deployment.

#### 1. The premise "the Indexer cannot be parallelized via TP" is half right

It is right about one axis and wrong about the other, and the distinction is what makes the redundancy
recoverable:

| axis | shardable? | why |
|---|---|---|
| **index heads** (64) | ❌ **the RFC is right** | logits are *reduced over* the head dimension, so sharding heads forces an all-reduce of the whole `q × N` logits tensor **before** top-k. At ISL 131072 that is ~4.3 GB per layer per chunk — not viable. This is also why no logits all-reduce exists anywhere on the current path. |
| **query rows** | ✅ **shardable, and exactly** | top-k is computed per row and rows are independent, so partitioning rows cannot change any row's mathematical result. Only the int32 top-k indices need merging — **16 MB**, not `q × N × 4`. |

So the accurate statement is **"it cannot be sharded by head; it can be sharded by query row."**

#### 2. This also happens with a single CP rank — the RFC's framing excludes that case

The RFC describes redundancy *between CP ranks*: "every CP rank must independently execute the full
Indexer logic on its local sequence." My deployment runs `pcp = 1, dcp = 1` — **one CP rank** — so by
that description it should have no redundancy. It measures the indexer at **15.9 % of prefill GPU
time** at ISL 131072.

The redundancy is among the **8 TP ranks inside** that single CP rank. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash
(vLLM `6f91edf96`, i.e. `0.26.1rc1.dev77+g6f91edf96`, TP=8, SM90):

* both indexer projections are `ReplicatedLinear` (that class body has no tp/shard logic at all)
* the layer takes `config.index_n_heads` with **no** `// tp_size`
* the profiled kernel's template reports `num_heads=64` — the full count, on every rank
* there is **no logits all-reduce** anywhere on the call path

Those four together admit only one reading: every TP rank computes the complete, identical indexer.
**7/8 of that work is duplicate.** I confirmed on `main` today that this is still the case — no
`get_tensor_model_parallel_*` and no cross-TP top-k merge in `sparse_attn_indexer.py`.

#### 3. Measured payoff on CUDA

🔴 **All speedup numbers below are at concurrency 1.** The correctness regression only appears at
concurrency > 1, so the configuration where I measured the patch fast is **not** the configuration
where it is broken. See the "Report of performance regression" box for that split, and the
"Misc discussion" box for the defect itself.

Isolated screen, one H100 — sharding the query dimension keeps **78.7–83.0 %** of the ideal 8×, i.e.
a realisable **13.3–13.4 % of prefill**. End to end, 8 × H100, TP=8, **concurrency 1**,
`--max-num-batched-tokens 8192`, `--block-size 256`, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`:

| ISL | prefill improvement | concurrency |
|---|---|---|
| 65 536 | **+7.1 %** | 1 |
| 131 072 | **+13.8 %** | 1 |

Both intervals were disjoint from baseline (min/max, not medians). Note also that retention falls with
context: an isolated screen measured 48.7 % at ISL 16384, so a short-prompt deployment sees far less
than 13.8 %.

Merge cost at the measured `index_topk = 512`: `7808 × 512 × 4 B` = **16.0 MB** per indexer layer per
chunk, 5.7 GB per ISL-131072 request, ≈ **19 ms** at 300 GB/s bus bandwidth against ≈ 5760 ms saved —
**0.3 %**.

#### 4. How it was implemented — what the patch actually changes

Posting this because the mechanism is short and the *placement* is the whole difficulty. Anyone
implementing it properly will hit the same three constraints.

**Everything the patch touches**, and what it does to each. Nothing is edited in place — it is
installed as a vLLM general plugin behind one env var, so the two arms differ by exactly one variable
and every measurement stays attributable:

| upstream symbol | file | what the patch does | why there |
|---|---|---|---|
| `split_indexer_prefill_chunks` | `v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py` | wraps it; narrows each returned `query_slice` to this rank's share via `shard_query_slice` | it already returns `(req_slice, query_slice)` pairs and already sub-chunks the query dim, so narrowing makes the *unmodified* 250-line indexer loop compute only this rank's rows |
| `build_prefill_chunk_metadata` | same file | wraps it; sets `skip_kv_gather = False` on the **returned object** for the specs seam 1 recorded | the callee re-derives that flag from the slice it was handed and ORs the caller's value away (see (b) below) |
| `SparseAttnIndexer.forward_cuda` | `model_executor/layers/sparse_attn_indexer.py` | wraps it; after the original returns, one `all_reduce(MAX)` over `topk_indices_buffer[:n]` merges the ranks' rows | a class attribute looked up at call time, so rebinding takes effect — unlike the module-level function |
| — | — | **not touched:** the top-k kernel, the fp8 logits GEMM, the consumer, the metadata kernel, any weight layout | the point is that row partitioning needs none of them changed |

Net: **~40 lines of sharding logic.** The patch file is 975 lines because the other ~935 are nine
probes and audits added while chasing the regression — a coverage audit that counts writers per row, a
cross-rank value probe, an injection probe, alignment instrumentation. None of that belongs in a real
implementation.

**Where the redundancy is NOT removed:** the two `ReplicatedLinear` projections still run in full on
every rank. Sharding rows cuts the logits GEMM and the top-k, which is where the 15.9 % lives; the
projections are small by comparison. A proper in-tree implementation could go further.

**The obvious seam does not work.** Monkey-patching the module-level `sparse_attn_indexer` function
has no effect: `direct_register_custom_op(...)` captures the function object into the torch op
registry, and `SparseAttnIndexer.forward_cuda` dispatches through
`torch.ops.vllm.sparse_attn_indexer`. Rebinding the module global leaves the registered impl
untouched. So an out-of-tree implementation has to work at two points that are far apart in the code.

**Seam 1 — narrow the query slice** (`split_indexer_prefill_chunks`, `v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py`).
It already returns `(req_slice, query_slice)` pairs and already sub-chunks the query dimension to
respect the logits budget, so narrowing each returned `query_slice` to this rank's share makes the
*unmodified* indexer loop compute only this rank's rows — no vendored copy of the 250-line body:

```python
def shard_query_slice(start, stop, rank, world):
    """This rank's contiguous share of [start, stop). Proportional bounds, so row counts
    differ by at most one and every row is owned by exactly one rank — the property the
    merge relies on. Contiguous rather than strided: under causal masking later rows score
    more keys, but a 7808-row chunk against a prefix of up to 131072 makes the within-chunk
    ramp ±6 %, not ±100 %, so contiguous costs ~3 points and reuses the existing slicing."""
    n = stop - start
    if n <= 0 or world <= 1:
        return start, stop
    return start + (n * rank) // world, start + (n * (rank + 1)) // world
```

**Seam 2 — merge after the indexer runs** (`SparseAttnIndexer.forward_cuda`, a class attribute looked
up at call time, so rebinding it does take effect). `topk_indices_buffer` is pre-filled with `-1` and
valid indices are `>= 0`, so one `all_reduce(MAX)` over the buffer is the union — a row this rank
computed holds real values here and `-1` elsewhere:

```python
out = _orig_forward(self, hidden_states, q_quant, k, weights)
view = self.topk_indices_buffer[:n, :self.topk_tokens]
torch.distributed.all_reduce(view, op=torch.distributed.ReduceOp.MAX,
                             group=get_tp_group().device_group)
```

🔴 **Two guards this needs, both found the hard way:**

*(a) The union must not run inside CUDA-graph capture.* This wrapper sits outside the
`@eager_break_during_capture` that shields `sparse_attn_indexer`, so during capture warmup the
`all_reduce` was issued *inside* the capture and invalidated it (`cudaErrorStreamCaptureInvalidated`).
That failed **silently** for three rounds, leaving a corrupted graph — wrong top-k, no crash — which
is why four rewrites of an unrelated predicate changed nothing:

```python
if torch.cuda.is_current_stream_capturing():
    return out          # sound HERE only because this patch shards PREFILL chunks only, and
                        # prefill chunks (7808 rows) far exceed max_cudagraph_capture_size (384),
                        # so prefill executes eagerly and never replays from a graph.
```

*(b) Seam 1b — the callee ORs the caller's `skip_kv_gather` back on.* At
`build_prefill_chunk_metadata` the flag is re-derived from the slice it was handed:

```python
skip_kv_gather = skip_kv_gather or qs_start > 0
```

Because seam 1 narrows `query_slice` to `(lo, hi)` with `lo > 0` on ranks 1..N-1, that `or` turns the
flag back to True no matter what the caller passed. **Four successive predicate rewrites in the caller
were all OR-ed away**, which is why `cp_gather_indexer_k_quant_cache` measured 1/8 of baseline and the
sharded arm answered out of the prompt's filler: ranks 1..N-1 scored against a KV workspace nobody
filled. The value was being recomputed *downstream* of the argument being patched. Fix on the
constructed object instead:

```python
md = _orig_build(*args, **kwargs)
if md is not None and gather_flags[i]:
    md.skip_kv_gather = False          # or dataclasses.replace(md, skip_kv_gather=False)
```

And the gather predicate itself must come from the **original** spec, not the narrowed one — the
gather is about the KV range, which every rank needs identically; sharding only changes which query
*rows* a rank scores. Two earlier versions derived it from the narrowed bound (circular: ranks 1..7
skipped every gather) and from "this rank's first slice per req_range" (at BS=1 all 26 specs share
`req_range (0,1)`, so 17 request-chunks collapsed into one gather per rank). The correct predicate is
the original spec's `query_range.start == 0`, and it is **rank-independent**.

#### 5. What I would suggest to whoever implements this properly

* **Shard by query row, not by head** (§1).
* **Do not merge with `all_reduce(MAX)` on index values.** It is only correct while exactly one rank
  has written each row — a property of the operating point, not a structural guarantee. vLLM already
  contains a better-founded pattern: `_merge_dcp_topk_global` ships `(score, global_id)` candidate
  pairs and selects with a stable top-k, which is *provably* equivalent to all-gathering the full
  logit matrix. Payload roughly doubles (score must travel), which on the numbers in §3 moves the
  merge cost from 0.3 % to ~0.7 % of the saving — negligible.
* **Do not gate quality on mean log-prob or perplexity.** It reported `|A−B| = 0.0000` on a run whose
  needle retrieval had collapsed to 4/16 (Misc box, §A). Gate on free-generation trajectories and a
  discrete retrieval check, and **measure the same-config floor first** — three of my instruments were
  defeated by a floor I had not measured (Misc box, §D).
* **Treat decode as a regression check, not a second win.** Decode takes `top_k_per_row_decode` with
  ~BS query rows per step, so sharding by row leaves each rank a handful of rows and kernel-launch
  overhead eats the gain. Expected ≈ 0.
* The `skip_kv_gather` interaction is a real trap: `build_prefill_chunk_metadata` re-derives
  `skip_kv_gather = skip_kv_gather or qs_start > 0` from the slice it is handed, so narrowing the
  query slice silently turns the flag back on for every rank but rank 0, and each rank then scores
  against a KV workspace nobody filled. Four successive fixes to the *caller* were all OR-ed away.

### Report of performance regression

**No performance regression in vLLM itself** — nothing here is a slowdown introduced by an upstream
change, and I am not asking for a revert. Three measurement caveats belong under this heading anyway,
because each one is a way the proposal above could disappoint someone who takes the headline number
at face value:

| # | caveat | detail |
|--:|---|---|
| 1 | **The speedup and the defect were measured at different concurrencies, and they do not overlap.** | +7.1 % / +13.8 % is at **concurrency 1**. The correctness regression (4/16 retrieval vs stock 16/16) needs **concurrency 4**; at concurrency 1 it does not reproduce — the sharded arm retrieved 6/6. So I have **no throughput number at concurrency 4**, and no defect at concurrency 1. Read +13.8 % as "fast in a regime where I could not detect the bug", not as "works, with a known bug". |
| 2 | **The win shrinks sharply with context length.** | Isolated screen retention: **48.7 % at ISL 16384** vs 78.7–83.0 % at 65536–131072. A short-prompt deployment sees far less than 13.8 %, and possibly nothing. |
| 3 | **Decode is expected to be ≈ 0 and could regress.** | `top_k_per_row_decode` sees ~BS query rows per step; sharding rows leaves each rank a handful and kernel-launch overhead eats the gain. Anyone implementing this must measure decode as a guard, not as upside. I did not observe a decode regression, but I also did not shard decode. |

Method note, since it affects how comparable these numbers are: improvements are reported as
**disjoint min/max intervals** over repeated runs, not as a difference of medians.

### Misc discussion on performance

This box is the part I would most like input on: **why the optimisation above is not a PR.** It also
carries the attached code.

#### A. The blocker — a reproducible, silent correctness regression at concurrency > 1

I implemented query-row sharding as an **out-of-tree runtime patch** (two monkey-patched seams, not a
change to vLLM), measured the speedup, and then hit a quality regression I was unable to localise. I
am reporting it because it is the single most useful thing I have for anyone else who tries this — the
optimisation looks simple and has a silent failure mode.

**The regression:** needle-in-a-haystack retrieval drops to **4/16** against stock's **16/16**, at ISL
65 536, concurrency 4, greedy decoding (`temperature=0, top_p=1, seed=0`). Stock retrieves 16/16 on
two independent runs with **zero flips**. It is stable and reproducible.

Exact prompt construction, since the haystack composition matters (a natural-prose haystack may
behave differently — I did not test one):

```python
WORDS = ("alpha bravo charlie delta echo foxtrot golf hotel india juliet kilo lima mike november "
         "oscar papa quebec romeo sierra tango uniform victor whiskey xray yankee zulu").split()

def build_prompt(seed, approx_tokens=65536):
    rng = random.Random(seed)                       # seeds 1000..1015 -> the 16 prompts
    body = " ".join(rng.choice(WORDS) for _ in range(int(approx_tokens / 1.25)))
    return (f"MEMO-{seed:04d}: the authorisation code is QX-{seed:04d}-ZK7. "
            f"Remember it.\n\n{body}\n\nQuestion: what is the authorisation code?\nAnswer:")

# 16 prompts, 4 in flight at once, max_tokens=48, temperature=0, top_p=1, seed=0.
# "Retrieved" == the literal string f"QX-{seed:04d}-ZK7" appears in the completion.
```

The needle is at the **very start** of a ~65k-token prompt, so retrieval requires the longest possible
lookback — that is deliberate, and it is why this catches something perplexity does not.

**It is silent under the usual gates.** Mean per-token log-prob of the generated continuation was
*identical* to stock (`|A−B| = 0.0000`). A perplexity- or mean-logprob-based quality gate reports
"equivalent" and you ship it. Only a discrete check — does the retrieved string appear — sees it.
The failure shape is specific:

```
stock: QX-1003-ZK7      shard: QX-1003-K7                     serial correct, one char dropped
stock: QX-1001-ZK7      shard: QX-OM-77                       serial replaced by haystack filler
stock: QX-1005-ZK7      shard: QX-RO-QU-AL-QU-AL-QU-AL-...    degenerate filler repetition
```

`RO`/`QU`/`AL` are filler tokens from the haystack.

#### B. The instrument that finally gave a clean answer

Six full-model A/B runs drowned in the noise floors in §D. The one that worked runs **offline with no
model**: one fixed logits tensor, stock = a single `top_k_per_row_prefill` call over all rows, shard =
one call per simulated rank over its row slice plus the MAX merge. Same input by construction, no
43-layer accumulation, no scheduler, no collective — so any difference is the sharding arithmetic and
nothing else. **One GPU, seconds per case.** This should be the first experiment anyone runs, not the
eighth:

```python
# stock: one call over all rows
out_stock = torch.full((rows, topk), -1, dtype=torch.int32, device=dev)
ops.top_k_per_row_prefill(logits, ks, ke, out_stock, rows,
                          logits.stride(0), logits.stride(1), topk)

# sharded: one call per rank over its slice, into a -1-filled buffer, then MAX
per_rank = []
for r in range(world):
    lo, hi = shard_query_slice(0, rows, r, world)
    buf = torch.full((rows, topk), -1, dtype=torch.int32, device=dev)
    sub = logits[lo:hi]
    ops.top_k_per_row_prefill(sub, ks[lo:hi], ke[lo:hi], buf[lo:hi], hi - lo,
                              sub.stride(0), sub.stride(1), topk)
    per_rank.append(buf)
out_shard = per_rank[0]
for buf in per_rank[1:]:
    out_shard = torch.maximum(out_shard, buf)

# compare as SETS per row, bounded by what the consumer actually reads:
#   topk_len = min((pos + 1) // compress_ratio, topk)
# Rows with topk_len == 0 are chunk heads carrying no selection and MUST be excluded —
# including them manufactured a false candidate (see §C item 4).
```

🔴 **This harness is inherently single-request**, so by construction it cannot reproduce the
concurrency-4 defect. That is not a flaw — it is what makes it useful: it answers "is row sharding
arithmetically exact for one chunk of rows?" without any of the noise that made the full-model
comparisons unreadable. A clean result here narrows the search to things that only exist under
concurrency (batch composition, chunk grouping across requests, the metadata built for several specs
at once), which is exactly where I ran out of instruments.

Results on this harness, DeepSeek-V4-Flash shapes (`kv=4096`, `topk=512`, `compress_ratio=4`).
Exact reproduction parameters: `logits = torch.randn(rows, 4096, generator=Generator().manual_seed(1003))`,
`ks = 0`, `ke[p] = min((p+1)//4, 4096)`, `topk = 512`; the tie cases apply
`logits = (logits * 8).round() / 8` before anything else. `rows_with_selection` is the count of rows
where `min((pos+1)//4, 512) > 0`, i.e. excluding chunk heads.

| case | rows | world | ties | rows_with_selection | **SET differs** | order-only differs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8192 | 4 | no | 8189 | **0** | 6141 |
| 2 | 8192 | 4 | **yes** | 8189 | **4498** | 1643 |
| 3 | 8192 | 8 | no | 8189 | **0** | 6141 |
| 4 | 12287 | 4 | no | 12284 | **0** | 10235 |
| 4 | 12288 | 4 | no | 12285 | **0** | 10237 |
| 4 | 12289 | 4 | no | 12286 | **0** | 10237 |
| 4 | 16384 | 4 | no | 16381 | **0** | 14333 |
| 5 | 8192 | 8 | yes | 8189 | 4531 | 1610 |
| 5 | 12287 | 8 | yes | 12284 | 8177 | 2058 |
| 5 | 12288 | 8 | yes | 12285 | 8214 | 2022 |
| 5 | 12289 | 8 | yes | 12286 | 8190 | 2048 |
| 5 | 16384 | 8 | yes | 16381 | 12132 | 2201 |

**SET differs** counts rows where the two paths selected a different *set* of key indices — a real
divergence, because membership is what the attention consumer gathers. **order-only differs** counts
rows where both paths selected the same set but wrote it in a different order.

🔴 **Do not be alarmed by the `order-only` column.** Thousands of rows return the same *set* in a
different *order*, in every case including the clean ones. That is expected and harmless here: the
consumer (`_compute_global_topk_indices_and_lens_kernel`) maps each slot independently through
`block_table` and writes it back to the same offset, so membership is what the model sees and order is
not. If you compare these buffers with `==` instead of as sets you will see a huge false signal.

Rows 12289 and 16384 straddle `kSortingAlgorithmThreshold = 12288`, so they exercise the
insertion-path/radix-path split within one call — the `algo` column in the harness output confirms
which path each case took. They are clean without ties, which is what rules the algorithm switch out.

Every divergent row in the tie cases differs by **exactly one index** (symmetric difference 2), and
the first sits just past a rank boundary (row 2086 for `world=4`, whose rank0/rank1 boundary is 2048).
So the discriminating variable is exact ties — which is what sent me to measure tie density on the
live path (§C item 9), where it turned out to be zero.

#### C. Nine candidate mechanisms, each falsified with evidence

1. `all_reduce(MAX)` on the index buffer overwrites a correct value — impossible: an observed
   post-union value (264) was *smaller* than the pre-union value on the same row (1450), and MAX over
   a set containing 1450 cannot return 264.
2. Top-k lost on later forwards — this was my leading candidate for days and turned out to be an
   artifact of my own probe's re-arm guard.
3. Multi-writer rows breaking the union's one-writer premise — the writer-count audit's failures are
   all the benign replicated-decode case (`max_writers == world` on decode rows, which are not
   sharded).
4. Rows lost at a request boundary — recomputing all four ranks' absolute coverage gives
   **8192/8192 rows, zero gap**; the apparently-lost rows are a request's *chunk head*, where
   `compress_ratio=4` yields `cu_seqlen_ke = 0` and top-k legitimately selects nothing.
5. The sparse-MLA consumer being order-sensitive — `_compute_global_topk_indices_and_lens_kernel` is
   element-wise and position-preserving, so membership matters and order does not.
6. The top-k kernel's two-algorithm dispatch (`kSortingAlgorithmThreshold = 12288` in
   `csrc/libtorch_stable/sampler.cu`: insertion below, radix above) — sharding changes `num_rows` per
   rank and can move a row between algorithms, but the offline test in §B was clean across the
   boundary.
7. Sharding perturbing prefill more than ordinary nondeterminism — **stock-vs-stock** step-0 mean
   `|Δlogprob|` is **0.1360**, *larger* than shard-vs-stock's 0.0893, while stock still retrieves
   16/16 twice. Magnitude has no discriminating power here.
8. cuBLAS split-k / NCCL reduction order / TF32 — pinned all three by hand
   (`CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:16:8`, `NCCL_ALGO=allreduce:tree`, single channel and thread,
   `NVIDIA_TF32_OVERRIDE=0`); the regression persisted.
9. Tie-breaking order differing between sharded and unsharded kernel launches — **the best
   candidate.** Offline, with fixed input, quantising the logits to create exact ties yields 4498
   rows whose selected *set* differs (each by exactly one index); without ties it is 0. But measuring
   the **real** logits on the live path found **0 boundary ties across 1140 rows** with a median
   margin of 1e-3, three orders above fp8 resolution. Real mechanism, unreachable in production.

#### D. Why I could not localise it — the noise floors

Every numerical comparison is defeated by the same property: **this model does not reproduce itself,
and the noise grows with depth.** Same-config (stock vs stock) floors:

| instrument | concurrency | floor |
|---|---|---|
| decode step-0 mean \|Δlogprob\| | 4 | **0.1360** (the signal was 0.0893) |
| per-position top-1 token identity | 4 | **24.5 %** of positions flip |
| per-layer hidden-state fingerprint | 4 | L=0 **0**, L=1 6.8e-08, L=5 **1.8e-01**, L=33 **5.2e-01** (≈ ×100 per layer) |
| needle retrieval (discrete) | 4 | **16/16 twice, zero flips** — the only stable instrument, and it says *whether*, never *where* |

All four floors are at concurrency 4, i.e. measured in the regime where the defect exists — which is
the only regime where a floor is relevant, and also the regime where the floor is worst.

L=0 being bit-identical across arms confirms the inputs matched; the noise is accumulated.

There is also a structural dead end in cross-arm comparison: at **concurrency 1** the two arms can be
aligned exactly but **the regression does not reproduce**; at **concurrency 4** it reproduces but the
arms see different batch compositions, so no per-row comparison is valid.

#### E. Two routes to determinism, both dead

* `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` — **the server does not start**:
  `NotImplementedError: No MXFP4 MoE backend supports the deployment configuration`
  (`fused_moe/oracle/mxfp4.py`), all TP ranks. `enable_batch_invariant_mode()` replaces `torch.bmm`
  and sets `VLLM_USE_AOT_COMPILE=0`, after which no MXFP4 MoE backend's `is_supported_config` passes.
  **This looks like a genuine incompatibility worth its own issue** — batch-invariant mode appears
  unusable on any MXFP4-MoE model on SM90, independent of anything I am doing. Happy to file it
  separately if that is useful.
* Pinning only the environment half of that switch (no operator swaps) — the server starts, but stock
  still reproduced its own output on only 2 of 4 prompts. The residual nondeterminism is therefore
  outside cuBLAS split-k / NCCL order / TF32, i.e. in the fp8 logits GEMM (`torch.ops.vllm.*`),
  `top_k_per_row_prefill` (`torch.ops._C.*`), or the vendored `flash_mla_sparse_fwd` binary — none of
  which read those environment variables or dispatch through `aten::`.

**What would actually help:** a supported way to make this model bit-reproducible under concurrency,
or a pointer to an instrument that localises a prefill-side selection defect without depending on
numerical comparison across a 43-layer stack. Those are the two things I ran out of.

title: [Performance]: Avoid scanning the full KV block table
body:
## Summary

In the V1 scheduler path, `FullAttentionManager.get_num_common_prefix_blocks()` scans the allocated KV blocks to determine the common prefix.

With only a single allocated request, this scan can traverse the request's block table even though the resulting common-prefix information cannot enable cascade attention for the single-request case.

This was found during a **WOB** source audit. WOB is an experimental, novel way of improving source code for data processing. WOB is based on the idea that not all computation has equal marginal value. If a cheap mechanism can identify cases where additional work is unlikely to improve the result enough to justify its cost, that work can be selectively avoided.
 
WOB is mostly automated, directed by a human.

For long-context decode, the scan is repeated and its CPU cost grows linearly with the number of allocated KV blocks.

## Affected code

**File:**

```text
vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py
```

**Section:**

```text
class FullAttentionManager
```

**Method:**

```text
get_num_common_prefix_blocks()
```

Current implementation:

```python
def get_num_common_prefix_blocks(self, running_request_id: str) -> int:
    blocks = self.req_to_blocks[running_request_id]
    num_common_blocks = 0
    for block in blocks:
        if block.ref_cnt == len(self.req_to_blocks):
            num_common_blocks += 1
        else:
            break
    return num_common_blocks
```

## Current behaviour

For a single allocated request:

```python
len(self.req_to_blocks) == 1
```

and its allocated blocks normally have:

```python
block.ref_cnt == 1
```

The loop can therefore continue through the request's entire common-prefix block range.

The resulting `num_common_prefix_blocks` is propagated downstream for cascade-attention handling, but the FlashAttention cascade heuristic rejects cascade attention for batches with fewer than eight requests.

Consequently, in the single-request case the scheduler can pay the full block-table traversal cost for information that cannot enable cascade attention.

## Measured cost

I benchmarked the exact `FullAttentionManager.get_num_common_prefix_blocks()` method body extracted from the current source using AST, rather than a manually rewritten approximation.

Block size: 16 tokens.

| Context | Blocks scanned | Current implementation | Early return |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1,024 tokens | 64 | 3.61 µs | 0.105 µs |
| 4,096 tokens | 256 | 14.95 µs | 0.201 µs |
| 16,384 tokens | 1,024 | 60.65 µs | 0.105 µs |
| 65,536 tokens | 4,096 | 245.46 µs | 0.105 µs |

This is not an end-to-end vLLM latency benchmark, but it confirms linear CPU cost in the actual audited implementation.

During decode the calculation may occur repeatedly, so long-context single-request workloads can accumulate this scheduler-side work across generation steps.

## Proposed minimal modification

**File:**

```text
vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py
```

**Section:**

```text
FullAttentionManager.get_num_common_prefix_blocks()
```

Proposed implementation:

```python
def get_num_common_prefix_blocks(self, running_request_id: str) -> int:
    # A single allocated request cannot have a prefix shared with another
    # request, so avoid scanning its entire block table.
    if len(self.req_to_blocks) <= 1:
        return 0

    blocks = self.req_to_blocks[running_request_id]
    num_common_blocks = 0
    num_reqs = len(self.req_to_blocks)

    for block in blocks:
        if block.ref_cnt == num_reqs:
            num_common_blocks += 1
        else:
            break

    return num_common_blocks
```

Equivalent diff:

```diff
 def get_num_common_prefix_blocks(self, running_request_id: str) -> int:
+    # A single allocated request cannot have a prefix shared with another
+    # request, so avoid scanning its entire block table.
+    if len(self.req_to_blocks) <= 1:
+        return 0
+
     blocks = self.req_to_blocks[running_request_id]
     num_common_blocks = 0
+    num_reqs = len(self.req_to_blocks)
+
     for block in blocks:
-        if block.ref_cnt == len(self.req_to_blocks):
+        if block.ref_cnt == num_reqs:
             num_common_blocks += 1
         else:
             break
+
     return num_common_blocks
```

## Why this should be safe

This change does not alter:

- KV-cache allocation
- KV ownership
- block reference counts
- prefix-cache lookup at request ingress
- model execution
- token outputs

It only suppresses calculation of shared-prefix metadata when there is only one allocated request.

The intended invariant is:

```text
one allocated request
=> no cross-request common prefix is required
=> num_common_prefix_blocks = 0
```

## Suggested verification

A focused regression test could:

1. Create a `FullAttentionManager` with one allocated request.
2. Give that request a large block table.
3. Call `get_num_common_prefix_blocks()`.
4. Verify that it returns `0` without traversing the blocks.
5. Verify unchanged model and scheduler behaviour for single-request decode.

It would also be useful to benchmark scheduler CPU time for single-request decode at increasing context lengths.

A broader follow-up could investigate whether the common-prefix calculation can also be skipped for other small batches when the selected attention backend cannot use cascade attention, but that is separate from this minimal single-request optimisation.

## Environment / revision

**Repository:**

```text
vLLM upstream
```

**Branch:**

```text
main
```

**Revision:**

```text
4f3e255dca347c8611e8d6586f2e22a4c7ddd168
```

The source-extracted benchmark was run in an existing Conda environment with:

```text
Python 3.11.15
PyTorch 2.7.1+cu126
GTX 1080
CUDA available: yes
```

The available local hardware/environment cannot run the current vLLM checkout faithfully end to end, so the measurements above are source-extracted CPU measurements rather than an end-to-end serving benchmark.

title: [Performance]: higher Mooncake Store tail latency with all-HCA registration on 4-TP / 4-RNIC hosts
body:
### Proposal to improve performance

Could vLLM provide a supported way to preserve worker-level NIC affinity while still allowing multi-rail registration?

For a 4-TP / 4-RNIC host, the desired mapping is:

```text
TP0 -> mlx5_20
TP1 -> mlx5_21
TP2 -> mlx5_28
TP3 -> mlx5_29
```

For an 8-RNIC / 4-TP host, the same policy could allow two GPU-affine RNICs per worker:

```text
TP0 -> RNIC0,RNIC1
TP1 -> RNIC2,RNIC3
TP2 -> RNIC4,RNIC5
TP3 -> RNIC6,RNIC7
```

This retains multi-rail bandwidth without allowing every local TP worker to contend for every RNIC.

The motivation of #43799 is clear: hosts with more HCAs than GPUs should not leave available HCAs idle. However, in our 4-TP / 4-RNIC deployment, passing the same complete HCA list to every worker appears to remove worker-level rail isolation and increases tail latency.

We would appreciate guidance on:

1. Is per-worker HCA grouping an expected or supported deployment model?
2. Should this grouping be configured in vLLM before initializing `MooncakeDistributedStore`, or should it be handled by Mooncake Transfer Engine affinity policy?
3. Is there an existing recommended configuration for multi-NIC TP deployments that preserves GPU/NUMA affinity while avoiding cross-worker RNIC contention?

### Report of performance regression

## Report of performance regression

We observed higher Mooncake Store transfer tail latency after adopting the all-HCA worker registration introduced by [#43799](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43799).

Our deployment uses 4 TP workers and 4 RDMA NICs per host. The NIC order is GPU/NUMA-affine:

```text
mlx5_20,mlx5_21,mlx5_28,mlx5_29
```

Before #43799, each Mooncake Store worker selected the RNIC associated with its local physical GPU:

```text
TP0 -> mlx5_20
TP1 -> mlx5_21
TP2 -> mlx5_28
TP3 -> mlx5_29
```

After #43799, every TP worker passes the complete `device_name` CSV to `MooncakeDistributedStore` and registers all four RNICs.

## Configuration

The standalone `mooncake_client` is started with all four RNICs:

```bash
mooncake_client \
  --master_server_address=redis://<METADATA_HOST>:<PORT> \
  --host=<LOCAL_HOST_IP> \
  --device_names=mlx5_20,mlx5_21,mlx5_28,mlx5_29 \
  --port=<CLIENT_PORT> \
  --protocol=rdma \
  --metadata_server=redis://<METADATA_HOST>:<PORT> \
  --global_segment_size=256GB \
  --enable_offload=false \
  --enable_http_server=true \
  --http_port=<METRICS_PORT> \
  --graceful_unmount_seconds=10 \
  --threads=16
```

The Mooncake Store configuration used by each vLLM TP worker is:

```json
{
  "mode": "standalone-store",
  "metadata_server": "redis://<METADATA_HOST>:<PORT>",
  "master_server_address": "redis://<METADATA_HOST>:<PORT>",
  "global_segment_size": "0",
  "local_buffer_size": "8GB",
  "protocol": "rdma",
  "device_name": "mlx5_20,mlx5_21,mlx5_28,mlx5_29",
  "enable_offload": false
}
```

Therefore, with #43799, all four TP workers independently initialize a Transfer Engine with the same four-NIC `device_name` list.

## Observed behavior

With all-HCA registration, we observed intermittent transfer latency spikes. Under higher concurrent load, some Store reads exceeded the 10 s read lease and failed with `LEASE_EXPIRED`.

Examples from the all-HCA configuration:

| Metric | Observed range across hosts |
| --- | ---: |
| Typical transfer p50 | 16–20 ms |
| p90 | 49–119 ms |
| p99 | 153–859 ms |
| Maximum transfer time | 3–4 s in one run; up to 14.7 s in an earlier high-load run |
| Failure mode | `Slice timeout detected`, followed by `LEASE_EXPIRED` when total read time exceeded the 10 s lease |

We restored the previous per-worker GPU-affine RNIC selection locally. Each worker again registered only its own RNIC. This is an operational comparison rather than a fully controlled benchmark, but the tail latency became substantially more stable:

| Configuration | p50 | p90 | p99 | Maximum |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| All-HCA registration | 16–20 ms | 49–119 ms | 153–859 ms | 3–4 s, occasionally higher under load |
| Per-worker GPU-affine RNIC | 14–17 ms | 49–70 ms | 89–146 ms | 149–332 ms |

After restoring per-worker RNIC selection, we did not observe `LEASE_EXPIRED` during the sampled window.

### Misc discussion on performance

_No response_

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

```text
vLLM: main-derived build including #43799
Mooncake Store mode: standalone-store
Protocol: RDMA
Topology: 4 TP workers / 4 RDMA NICs per host
Configured local buffer: 8GB
Read lease TTL: 10 seconds
```

## Configuration

title: [Performance]: Best practices for preventing GPU OOM in production
body:
### Proposal to improve performance


We are using vLLM to serve large language models in a production environment.

Our primary requirement is **production stability and avoiding GPU OOM**, rather than maximizing GPU utilization or throughput.

We would like to ask the vLLM community and maintainers:

**What are the recommended best practices for configuring vLLM to minimize or prevent GPU OOM in production?**

In particular, we would appreciate guidance on:

* How to choose a safe `--gpu-memory-utilization`
* How to balance `--max-model-len`, `--max-num-seqs`, and `--max-num-batched-tokens`
* How much GPU memory safety margin should typically be reserved
* Whether `--kv-cache-memory-bytes` is recommended for production deployments
* How to account for GPU memory used by CUDA Graphs, activations, NCCL, workspaces, and other runtime components
* How to perform stress testing to validate that a configuration is safe before deploying it to production

We understand that there may be no configuration that can mathematically guarantee zero OOM under completely unbounded workloads.

Our goal is to establish a **systematic and reproducible production-sizing methodology** so that, given a fixed model, GPU configuration, `max-model-len`, and expected workload, we can determine a sufficiently safe vLLM configuration.

Any recommended production deployment guidelines, sizing formulas, profiling tools, or real-world best practices would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you!

title: [Performance]: MTP acceptance metrics fluctuate within a benchmark run for GLM-5.2-FP8 on 8×H200 with vLLM v0.24.0
body:
### Proposal to improve performance

At this stage, we are seeking clarification about the semantics and
expected variability of the MTP metrics reported by the vLLM server.
We do not yet have a proposed implementation change.

### Report of performance regression

We have not confirmed a regression between vLLM versions.

All results below were collected with vLLM v0.24.0+cu129. The aggregate
results of repeated benchmark runs are relatively stable, but the
10-second server-side MTP metrics fluctuate significantly within each run.

Therefore, this report is currently a performance question rather than a
confirmed version-to-version regression.

### Misc discussion on performance

## Description

When serving a local GLM-5.2-FP8 checkpoint with MTP speculative decoding
on 8× NVIDIA H200 GPUs, the server-side `SpecDecoding metrics` reported
every 10 seconds fluctuate significantly within a single benchmark run.

For example, with `num_speculative_tokens=2`, the reported mean acceptance
length changes approximately between 1.0 and 1.7. The per-position
acceptance rates also change significantly between reporting intervals.

We would like to understand whether this is expected because these metrics
are calculated over short reporting windows with changing request/batch
composition, or whether it indicates an issue with MTP, FP8 model
quantization, FP8 KV cache, or scheduling.

## Environment and configuration

- vLLM: `0.24.0+cu129`
- Container: `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.24.0-cu129-ubuntu2404`
- GPUs: `8× NVIDIA H200`, 143771 MiB each

- Model quantization: `fp8`

- Tensor parallel size: `8`

- Prefix caching: enabled

The server also reports the following warning for FP8 KV cache:

title: [Performance]: Improve Pixtral vision attention scaling for batched images
body:
### Proposal to improve performance

Pixtral concatenates the patch sequences for all images in an encoder batch, while attention remains semantically independent per image. On the default installation, where xFormers is unavailable, the model constructs a dense block-diagonal mask and applies SDPA to the combined sequence. The resulting attention work and mask storage scale poorly as more images are batched.

This issue proposes routing both Pixtral vision implementations through vLLM's `MMEncoderAttention`, using cumulative sequence lengths to preserve per-image boundaries. This would:

- use vLLM's existing multimodal attention backend selection, including FlashAttention, FlashInfer, Torch SDPA, Triton attention, and ROCm AITER;
- avoid materializing the dense combined-sequence mask;
- remove Pixtral's model-specific optional xFormers path; and
- preserve checkpoint compatibility, preprocessing, output ordering, and token counts.

Backend-specific packed metadata still needs to be respected. In particular, FlashInfer uses padded sequence-length metadata and transformed cumulative offsets, so the implementation delegates metadata construction to `MMEncoderAttention` rather than assuming the FlashAttention layout.


### Report of performance regression

Controlled local benchmark on an NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10), using BF16, the 24-layer Pixtral HF vision encoder, 840 x 840 images, three warmup iterations, and ten measured iterations. Both variants used the same branch parent, container, model configuration, and identically seeded random weights.

| Encoder batch | Unpatched base | Packed FlashAttention | Speedup |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 119.4 ms / 8.37 images/s | 95.9 ms / 10.43 images/s | 1.25x |
| 2 | 371.1 ms / 5.39 images/s | 213.4 ms / 9.37 images/s | 1.74x |
| 4 | 1187.4 ms / 3.37 images/s | 430.9 ms / 9.28 images/s | 2.76x |

Numerical validation against Torch SDPA used the same 24-layer, identically initialized encoder on mixed-size images:

| Backend | Max absolute difference | Cosine similarity |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| FlashAttention | 0.00220 | 0.999985 |
| FlashInfer | 0.00195 | 0.999980 |

A two-layer pretrained-weight check produced identical features when the same image was encoded alone or alongside a differently sized image. A full Mistral3 vLLM smoke test also loaded a real checkpoint, selected the requested FlashAttention vision backend, processed two differently sized images, and generated successfully.


### Misc discussion on performance

## Related work and design implications

- #40703 migrates Pixtral's current xFormers imports to `mslk` while intentionally preserving the existing attention design. This proposal is materially different and would supersede the need for that model-specific path if accepted.
- #38175 tracks full ViT CUDA graph support, and Pixtral/Mistral3 work has recently been claimed there. This proposal does not add encoder CUDA graph support, but metadata preparation may eventually move outside `forward` as part of that work.
- #43052 addresses a separate Pixtral/Mistral3 graph-mode failure.

Would maintainers prefer Pixtral to adopt the standard `MMEncoderAttention` path, or retain a model-specific `mslk` path? If `MMEncoderAttention` is preferred, should graph-friendly metadata preparation be included here or remain scoped to the CUDA graph work in #38175?

title: [Performance][MooncakeStoreConnector] Overlapping async cold-prefix loads cause duplicate Gets into distinct GPU blocks
body:
### Proposal to improve performance # [Performance][MooncakeStoreConnector] Overlapping async cold-prefix loads cause duplicate Gets into distinct GPU blocks > **Scope:** This report concerns duplicated work counts on the vLLM control path: external lookups, load metadata, GPU block allocations, receive-queue entries, and external Get submissions. It does not report latency, TTFT, completed network transfers, or measured NIC bytes. ## Summary When several requests on the same worker and tensor-parallel rank share a cold prefix, a request arriving while an earlier asynchronous load is still in flight cannot observe or join that load. Instead, each overlapping request: 1. performs its own external lookup; 2. allocates its own destination GPU block; 3. constructs its own `LoadSpec`; 4. enters the receive queue independently; and 5. submits its own external Get. For `N` overlapping requests sharing one block hash, the current path can therefore produce: ```text N lookups N LoadSpecs N receive-queue entries N external Get submissions N distinct destination GPU blocks ``` for one logically unique KV-cache block. ## Reproduction I used eight concurrent requests with: * the same worker; * the same TP rank; * the same cold prefix; and * the same block hash. The first Get was held behind a deterministic barrier. While it was blocked, the other seven requests completed lookup, destination-block allocation, `LoadSpec` construction, and receive-queue enqueue. The barrier was then released. The result on current upstream `main` was: | Observed operation | Count | | ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------: | | Requests | 8 | | Unique block hashes | **1** | | External lookups | 8 | | `LoadSpec`s | 8 | | Receive-queue entries | 8 | | `batch_get_into_multi_buffers` Get occurrences | 8 | | Distinct CUDA destination addresses | 8 | | Completed requests | 8, exactly once each | The barrier did not time out, and every request completed exactly once. This is duplicated work rather than a livelock, dropped completion, or memory leak. The probe used an intentionally small 256-byte logical block. Its raw output reports: ```text unique_logical_bytes = 256 requested_remote_bytes = 2048 actual_completed_remote_bytes = null ``` The `2048`-byte figure is not a production bandwidth measurement. It only reflects the submitted buffer sizes in this deterministic test: ```text requested Get bytes = overlapping request count × configured KV block bytes ``` The meaningful result is the duplication count, not the absolute byte value. ### Raw summary ```json { "requests": 8, "scope": "same worker / same rank", "unique_block_hashes": 1, "lookup_operations": { "cfc3ba9bee31343e6778d774e1c6b9e51c929668e69020f0770fde4326e21694": 8 }, "load_specs": { "cfc3ba9bee31343e6778d774e1c6b9e51c929668e69020f0770fde4326e21694": 8 }, "recv_queue_entries": { "cfc3ba9bee31343e6778d774e1c6b9e51c929668e69020f0770fde4326e21694": 8 }, "get_occurrences": { "cfc3ba9bee31343e6778d774e1c6b9e51c929668e69020f0770fde4326e21694": 8 }, "distinct_destination_addresses": 8, "request_completion_counts": { "id-1": 1, "id-2": 1, "id-3": 1, "id-4": 1, "id-5": 1, "id-6": 1, "id-7": 1, "id-8": 1 }, "barrier_timed_out": false, "unique_logical_bytes": 256, "requested_remote_bytes": 2048, "actual_completed_remote_bytes": null } ``` ## Method The probe preserves the existing receive path: ```text Scheduler → MooncakeStoreConnector → MooncakeStoreWorker → batch_get_into_multi_buffers ``` At the `batch_get_into_multi_buffers` boundary, it substitutes a deterministic, dictionary-backed Store stand-in. The duplicated lookups, block allocations, `LoadSpec`s, queue entries, and Get submissions all occur before or at that boundary. Replacing the backend removes transport timing variability while preserving: * the real scheduler-side connector path; * the real worker-side receive path; * the real receive queue; * the real load metadata construction; and * real CUDA KV-cache destination buffers. The probe therefore demonstrates duplicate Get submissions into distinct CUDA destinations, but it does not claim that all submitted Gets become distinct completed NIC transfers. ### Code-level observations consistent with the result * lookup state and futures are associated with request IDs; * `LoadSpec` state is maintained per request; * receive work is submitted per request; * there is no block-hash-indexed registry for an already-running load; * asynchronously loaded blocks are not available for ordinary local prefix matching until the load completes. As a result, requests entering the allocation path before the first load commits can independently allocate blocks and submit Gets for the same content hash. ## Environment Reproduced on current upstream `main` at: ```text 38a267cdd5b30841bb2e2913d67ba18544098c3a ``` The test passed with: ```text 1 passed, 17 warnings in 5.72s ``` The only test source added was: ```text tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_duplicate_load_probe.py ``` No production Python source files were modified. To run the current upstream Python source without rebuilding the complete local development environment, I reused ABI-compatible native-extension binaries from an existing vLLM build through local symbolic links. These extensions were needed to satisfy import-time dependencies; the probe does not exercise FlashAttention or other model execution kernels. ### Connector configuration ```json { "kv_connector": "MooncakeStoreConnector", "kv_role": "kv_consumer", "kv_connector_extra_config": { "load_async": true, "lookup_async": false } } ``` | Setting | Value | | ------------------------ | ---------: | | Tensor parallel size | 1 | | Worker TP rank | 0 | | Mooncake receive threads | 1 | | Concurrent requests | 8 | | Mooncake mode | `embedded` | | Configured transport | `tcp` | | Offload enabled | `false` | This reproduction uses `lookup_async: false`. I have not measured how enabling asynchronous lookup changes the frequency of the overlap in a production workload. ### Probe and raw log * Probe:[test_mooncake_store_duplicate_load_probe.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30546974/test_mooncake_store_duplicate_load_probe.py) * Raw log: [mooncake_dup_load_probe_upstream_main.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30546986/mooncake_dup_load_probe_upstream_main.log)

## Relation to duplicate local blocks in v1 vLLM v1 intentionally tolerates some duplicate local blocks because block tables are append-only. Once separate requests have allocated blocks for the same hash, those blocks are not retroactively merged, and the duplicates remain until their requests release them. This report does not claim that this local duplication is a correctness bug. The issue here is that, during a Mooncake asynchronous cold load, the duplication crosses the external-cache boundary. In addition to consuming duplicate GPU cache capacity, overlapping requests also perform duplicate: * external lookups; * load metadata construction; * receive-queue work; and * external Get submissions. Preventing the duplication before separate block allocations occur would avoid both the accepted local duplication and the additional connector work. ## Possible first fix: wait behind an in-flight owner A possible Mooncake-local first step would be a block-hash-indexed in-flight load registry in `MooncakeStoreScheduler`, conceptually: ```text block hash already has an in-flight load ↓ do not report an external miss do not allocate another destination block ↓ defer the later request ↓ owner load completes and its block becomes locally visible ↓ waiter retries normal prefix matching ``` For example: ```python inflight_loads: dict[BlockHash, OwnerState] ``` Important semantics would include: * **Do not report a miss.** Treating the block as unavailable would send the request through local prefill and recompute the prefix. * **Index ownership by block hash.** Requests may overlap on only part of a prefix. * **Use a bounded waiter deadline.** If the owner stalls, a waiter should eventually fall back to the current lookup/allocation/Get behavior. * **Release waiters on owner failure or cancellation.** * **Do not expose pending contents as usable.** A pending-block representation would need an explicit readiness state before the block could satisfy normal prefix matching. If completion is currently available only at request granularity, an initial implementation could still index ownership by block hash while waking waiters when the owner request's load finishes. ### Alternatives Another representation would be to register the destination block in the prefix cache as pending and make later requests wait for its readiness. That expresses the same ownership at block granularity rather than through scheduler-side request deferral. Coalescing only inside the Get layer and copying or fanning out to multiple destinations could reduce duplicate remote reads, but it would retain duplicate lookups, load metadata, queue entries, and GPU block allocations. ## Questions 1. Is this duplicated connector work known and intentionally accepted for the asynchronous Mooncake load path? 2. Would you prefer ownership and waiting to be implemented in `MooncakeStoreScheduler`, as a pending local-cache block state, or nearer the Get layer? 3. Would the deterministic probe be useful as a regression test once the intended semantics are agreed? The probe is self-contained and does not modify production code. I would be happy to upstream it as a regression test and implement the preferred ownership/fallback semantics. ### Report of performance regression _No response_ ### Misc discussion on performance _No response_ ### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary) ```text The output of `python collect_env.py` ``` ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Performance][ROCm]: Fused bf16→fp32 router GEMM falls back to a standalone copy kernel on ROCm
body:
### Proposal to improve performance

## Summary

The MoE router gate `GateLinear` is constructed with `out_dtype=torch.float32` (`grouped_topk` requires fp32 logits). The fused fp32-output GEMM tiers in `gate_linear.py` that fold the fp32 cast into the GEMM's BLAS epilogue are all gated on `current_platform.is_cuda()`. On ROCm the gate therefore falls through to the final tier — `F.linear` in bf16 followed by a separate `output.to(fp32)` — which emits a standalone bf16→fp32 elementwise copy kernel on every MoE layer, every step.

## Details

The relevant tier does `torch.mm(x, w.T, out_dtype=fp32)`, folding the fp32 cast into the GEMM epilogue. Its eligibility (`allow_cublas_router_gemm`) requires `allow_specialized_router_gemm`, which is CUDA + SM90/SM100 only. hipBLASLt supports the same `out_dtype` epilogue, so the CUDA-only gate is unnecessarily strict.

In a kernel trace this shows up as a standalone

```
at::native::vectorized_elementwise_kernel<..., bfloat16tofloat32_copy_kernel ...>
```

running between the router GEMM and `grouped_topk`, once per MoE layer per step.

## Proposed change

Add ROCm (bias-free, bf16 weight, fp32 out) as an alternative enabling condition for `allow_cublas_router_gemm`, in both `__init__` and `set_out_dtype` (out_dtype can be set late, so both sites must agree). CUDA behavior is unchanged — the added disjunct is `current_platform.is_rocm() and ...`, which is `False` on CUDA. The fused tier then fires on ROCm and the fp32 logits come straight out of the GEMM.

## Numerical accuracy

Verified on gfx942: `torch.mm(bf16, bf16.T, out_dtype=fp32)` matches an fp32 reference to ~6e-5.

## Scope

Router gate only. It does not touch the expert GEMMs or any other bf16→fp32 intermediate in the graph (genuine fp32 intermediates in the attention-residual path are left alone).

## Environment

- Platform: ROCm / hipBLASLt (validated on gfx942)
- File: `vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/router/gate_linear.py`
